paragraphs: This paper shows how an oscillating cortical model can function as an associative memory. Its architecture contains excitatory neurons with local inhibitory feedback, creating nonlinear oscillators. Long-range connections between these oscillators are exclusively excitatory. The authors motivate this minimal coupling arrangement using known anatomy.

A local Hebb-like rule adjusts primary and higher-order synapses at the ends of the long-range connections. Through this learning rule, the network stores patterns of oscillation amplitudes of the kinds observed in olfactory and visual cortex. Memory is therefore expressed through structured rhythmic activity, rather than requiring every stored pattern to be a fixed, unchanging state.

The rule comes from a more general projection algorithm for recurrent analog networks. That algorithm analytically guarantees content-addressable storage of continuous periodic sequences without spurious attractors. The stated capacity is N/2 Fourier components for N nodes, counting components of periodic signals rather than simply counting memories. The result connects an anatomically motivated oscillator network with a mathematical account of reliable storage.
summary.tldr: An anatomically motivated oscillator network stores rhythmic activity patterns using a local learning rule derived from a guaranteed periodic-memory construction.

title: Associative Memory in a Simple Model of Oscillating Cortex

The theory of 'P.cS-completeness gives strong evidence that such a separation is unlikely for nonpla(cid:173) nar Hopfield networks, and it is demonstrated that this is also the case for several restricted classes of nonplanar Hopfield networks, including those who interconnection graphs are the class of bipar(cid:173) tite graphs, graphs of degree 3, the dual of the knight's graph, the 8-neighbor mesh, the hypercube , the butterfly, the cube-connected cycles, and the shuffle-exchange graph.

paragraphs: The paper examines whether letting a Hopfield network settle into a stable state is faster than computing a stable state on a conventional computer. These are different procedures for reaching the same kind of result. A network follows its own dynamics, whereas a computer can use an algorithm that need not reproduce that trajectory.

For planar Hopfield networks, the authors establish a substantial separation. Some such networks require exponential time to converge, yet a conventional computer can find a stable state of any planar Hopfield network in polynomial time. Thus, the time taken by the physical or simulated settling process need not reflect the computational difficulty of finding a stable configuration.

The situation changes for nonplanar networks. Complexity-theoretic evidence suggests that an analogous separation is unlikely, including for several restricted connection patterns such as bipartite graphs, degree-three graphs, hypercubes, and meshes. The findings therefore make connectivity central to the comparison: the strong advantage proved for conventional computation applies to planar networks, while broader architectures encounter a different complexity barrier.
summary.tldr: Conventional computers can find stable states exponentially faster than some planar Hopfield networks converge, with no comparable separation expected for nonplanar networks.

title: Are Hopfield Networks Faster than Conventional Computers?

abstract: In many applications, such as credit default prediction and medical im(cid:173) age recognition, test inputs are available in addition to the labeled train(cid:173) ing examples. We propose a method to incorporate the test inputs into learning. Our method results in solutions having smaller test errors than that of simple training solution, especially for noisy problems or small training sets.
originalAbstract: In many applications, such as credit default prediction and medical im(cid:173) age recognition, test inputs are available in addition to the labeled train(cid:173) ing examples. We propose a method to incorporate the test inputs into learning. Our method results in solutions having smaller test errors than that of simple training solution, especially for noisy problems or small training sets.

paragraphs: This paper considers a learning setting in which the inputs requiring predictions are already available alongside labeled training examples. Credit default prediction and medical image recognition are given as motivating applications. The central question is whether those test inputs can help shape the learned solution before their outcomes are known.

The authors propose a method that incorporates test inputs into learning. These inputs supply information about the cases on which the model will be evaluated, while the labeled examples provide the known input-output relationships. The approach therefore uses the available prediction cases as part of the learning problem, making their input information relevant to the fitted solution.

The paper reports smaller test errors than a simple solution based on training alone, with particularly strong benefits for noisy problems or small training sets. Those findings identify situations where the additional input information is especially useful. The contribution is the use of an available source of information—the test cases themselves—to improve predictions when labeled training evidence is limited or noisy.
summary.tldr: Incorporating available test inputs into learning reduces test error, especially with noisy data or small labeled training sets.

title: Incorporating Test Inputs into Learning

abstract: We present a novel generic approach to the problem of Event Related Potential identification and classification, based on a competitive N eu(cid:173) ral Net architecture. The network weights converge to the embedded signal patterns, resulting in the formation of a matched filter bank. The network performance is analyzed via a simulation study, exploring identification robustness under low SNR conditions and compared to the expected performance from an information theoretic perspective. The classifier is applied to real event-related potential data recorded during a classic odd-ball type paradigm; for the first time, within(cid:173) session variable signal patterns are automatically identified, dismiss(cid:173) ing the strong and limiting requirement of a-priori stimulus-related selective grouping of the recorded data. 902 D. H. Lange, H. T. Siegelmann, H. Pratt and G. F. Inbar

paragraphs: The paper tackles the problem of identifying event-related brain responses when recordings contain noise and the response patterns can change during a session. Its approach uses a competitive neural network to discover patterns within the recordings, rather than requiring the data to be divided into stimulus-related groups beforehand.

As learning proceeds, the network weights converge toward the signal patterns embedded in the data. Those learned weights form a bank of matched filters: each filter is suited to detecting a particular pattern. This connects learning and identification directly, because the patterns the network discovers become the templates it uses to recognize responses.

The authors investigate robustness at low signal-to-noise ratios through simulations and compare performance with information-theoretic expectations. They also apply the classifier to recordings from an odd-ball experiment. The reported result is automatic identification of patterns that vary within a session, removing the stated requirement for advance stimulus-based grouping and allowing the recorded signals themselves to determine the categories.
summary.tldr: A competitive neural network learns brain-response templates and identifies changing patterns without advance stimulus-based grouping.

title: A Generic Approach for Identification of Event Related Brain Potentials via a Competitive Neural Network Structure

abstract: We provide an abstract characterization of boosting algorithms as gradient decsent on cost-functionals in an inner-product function space. We prove convergence of these functional-gradient-descent algorithms under quite weak conditions. Following previous theo(cid:173) retical results bounding the generalization performance of convex combinations of classifiers in terms of general cost functions of the margin, we present a new algorithm (DOOM II) for performing a gradient descent optimization of such cost functions. Experiments on several data sets from the UC Irvine repository demonstrate that DOOM II generally outperforms AdaBoost, especially in high noise situations, and that the overfitting behaviour of AdaBoost is predicted by our cost functions.

We prove convergence of these functional-gradient-descent algorithms under quite weak conditions. Following previous theo(cid:173) retical results bounding the generalization performance of convex combinations of classifiers in terms of general cost functions of the margin, we present a new algorithm (DOOM II) for performing a gradient descent optimization of such cost functions. Experiments on several data sets from the UC Irvine repository demonstrate that DOOM II generally outperforms AdaBoost, especially in high noise situations, and that the overfitting behaviour of AdaBoost is predicted by our cost functions.

paragraphs: This paper interprets boosting algorithms as gradient descent over functions. Instead of viewing boosting only as a sequence of classifier-building steps, it describes those steps as attempts to reduce a cost assigned to the combined prediction function. The mathematical setting is a function space equipped with an inner product.

The authors prove convergence of these functional gradient methods under conditions they characterize as quite weak. They then introduce DOOM II, which performs gradient descent on costs defined through classification margins. Its motivation draws on earlier theoretical bounds relating the generalization performance of convex classifier combinations to such margin-based costs.

Experiments on several UC Irvine datasets show that DOOM II generally outperforms AdaBoost, with a particular advantage in high-noise situations. The proposed cost functions also predict AdaBoost's overfitting behavior in the reported study. These findings connect the theoretical interpretation to algorithm design: choosing and optimizing a margin-based cost can change empirical behavior, although the reported comparison does not establish superiority on every dataset.
summary.tldr: Viewing boosting as functional gradient descent yields convergence results and DOOM II, which generally beats AdaBoost in the reported experiments.

title: Boosting Algorithms as Gradient Descent

abstract: Nested sampling is a new Monte Carlo method by Skilling [1] intended for general Bayesian computation. Nested sampling provides a robust alternative to annealing-based methods for computing normalizing constants. It can also generate estimates of other quantities such as posterior expectations. The key technical requirement is an ability to draw samples uniformly from the prior sub ject to a constraint on the likelihood. We provide a demonstration with the Potts model, an undirected graphical model.
originalAbstract: Nested sampling is a new Monte Carlo method by Skilling [1] intended for general Bayesian computation. We provide a demonstration with the Potts model, an undirected graphical model.

paragraphs: The paper demonstrates nested sampling on the Potts model, an undirected graphical model. Nested sampling is a Monte Carlo approach intended for general Bayesian computation. Its main role here is computing normalizing constants, the quantities needed to turn relative probabilistic weights into a normalized distribution.

The authors present the method as a robust alternative to approaches based on annealing. Its scope also includes estimating posterior expectations, so the same computational approach can address both normalization and averages under a posterior distribution. The Potts-model example serves as a concrete demonstration of these Bayesian computation ideas in a graphical-model setting.

The crucial technical requirement is the ability to sample uniformly from the prior while enforcing a constraint on the likelihood. That requirement specifies the sampling operation an implementation must be able to carry out. The contribution connects a general computational method to the Potts model and highlights the operation on which it depends. The stated robustness is a motivation for using nested sampling, while the concrete result supplied here is its demonstration in that model.
summary.tldr: The paper demonstrates nested sampling for Potts models, emphasizing likelihood-constrained prior sampling as its key computational requirement.

title: Nested sampling for Potts models

abstract: We introduce a new algorithm for off-policy temporal-difference learning with function approximation that has lower variance and requires less knowledge of the behavior policy than prior methods. We develop the notion of a recognizer, a filter on actions that distorts the behavior policy to produce a related target policy with low-variance importance-sampling corrections. We also consider target policies that are deviations from the state distribution of the behavior policy, such as potential temporally abstract options, which further reduces variance. This paper introduces recognizers and their potential advantages, then develops a full algorithm for linear function approximation and proves that its updates are in the same direction as on-policy TD updates, which implies asymptotic convergence. Even though our algorithm is based on importance sampling, we prove that it requires absolutely no knowledge of the behavior policy for the case of state-aggregation function approximators.

We develop the notion of a recognizer, a filter on actions that distorts the behavior policy to produce a related target policy with low-variance importance-sampling corrections. We also consider target policies that are deviations from the state distribution of the behavior policy, such as potential temporally abstract options, which further reduces variance. This paper introduces recognizers and their potential advantages, then develops a full algorithm for linear function approximation and proves that its updates are in the same direction as on-policy TD updates, which implies asymptotic convergence. Even though our algorithm is based on importance sampling, we prove that it requires absolutely no knowledge of the behavior policy for the case of state-aggregation function approximators.

paragraphs: This paper develops temporal-difference learning for a target policy using behavior generated by another policy. Its algorithm uses function approximation while reducing variance and requiring less information about the behavior policy than earlier methods. The central device is a recognizer, which filters actions to produce a related target policy.

Because the target is constructed through this filtering relationship, importance-sampling corrections can have low variance. The paper also considers targets that depart from the behavior policy's state distribution, including potential temporally extended options, to reduce variance further. The target's relationship to the observed behavior is therefore an active part of the algorithm's design.

For linear function approximation, the authors develop a complete algorithm and prove that its updates have the same direction as on-policy TD updates, implying asymptotic convergence. A stronger information requirement result holds for state aggregation: despite using importance sampling, the algorithm needs no knowledge of the behavior policy in that case. These guarantees connect the proposed variance reduction mechanism to a concrete learning procedure.
summary.tldr: Action recognizers enable lower-variance off-policy TD learning, with convergence results and no behavior-policy knowledge required for state aggregation.

title: Off-policy Learning with Options and Recognizers

abstract: We are at the beginning of the multicore era. Computers will have increasingly many cores (processors), but there is still no good programming framework for these architectures, and thus no simple and unified way for machine learning to take advantage of the potential speed up. In this paper, we develop a broadly applicable parallel programming method, one that is easily applied to many different learning algorithms. Our work is in distinct contrast to the tradition in machine learning of designing (often ingenious) ways to speed up a single algorithm at a time. Specifically, we show that algorithms that fit the Statistical Query model [15] can be written in a certain "summation form," which allows them to be easily parallelized on multicore computers. We adapt Google's map-reduce [7] paradigm to demonstrate this parallel speed up technique on a variety of learning algorithms including locally weighted linear regression (LWLR), k-means, logistic regression (LR), naive Bayes (NB), SVM, ICA, PCA, gaussian discriminant analysis (GDA), EM, and backpropagation (NN). Our experimental results show basically linear speedup with an increasing number of processors.

We adapt Google's map-reduce [7] paradigm to demonstrate this parallel speed up technique on a variety of learning algorithms including locally weighted linear regression (LWLR), k-means, logistic regression (LR), naive Bayes (NB), SVM, ICA, PCA, gaussian discriminant analysis (GDA), EM, and backpropagation (NN). Our experimental results show basically linear speedup with an increasing number of processors.

paragraphs: Many learning algorithms could benefit from multiple processors, but implementing a separate parallelization strategy for each algorithm creates repeated work. This paper develops a common programming method for multicore machines. Its central contribution is identifying a computational structure shared by a broad class of learning algorithms.

The authors show that algorithms fitting the Statistical Query model can be expressed in a particular summation form. That structure allows work to be divided across processors and the resulting contributions to be combined. They adapt the map-reduce paradigm to turn this observation into a reusable approach to parallel machine learning.

Demonstrations cover algorithms including logistic regression, k-means, naive Bayes, SVMs, PCA, EM, and neural-network backpropagation. Across their experiments, the authors report approximately linear speedup as processor counts increase. This supports the practical value of the shared formulation for the tested settings. The theoretical applicability rests on the Statistical Query connection, while the reported scaling provides empirical evidence that one framework can accelerate several different learning procedures.
summary.tldr: A shared summation form enables map-reduce parallelization of many learning algorithms, with approximately linear speedups in experiments.

title: Map-Reduce for Machine Learning on Multicore

abstract: A central question in game theory and artificial intelligence is how a rational agent should behave in a complex environment, given that it cannot perform unbounded computations. We study strategic aspects of this question by formulating a simple model of a game with additional costs (computational or otherwise) for each strategy. First we connect this to zero-sum games, proving a counter-intuitive generalization of the classic min-max theorem to zero-sum games with the addition of strategy costs. We then show that potential games with strategy costs remain potential games. Both zero-sum and potential games with strategy costs maintain a very appealing property: simple learning dynamics converge to equilibrium.
originalAbstract: A central question in game theory and artificial intelligence is how a rational agent should behave in a complex environment, given that it cannot perform unbounded computations. We study strategic aspects of this question by formulating a simple model of a game with additional costs (computational or otherwise) for each strategy. First we connect this to zero-sum games, proving a counter-intuitive generalization of the classic min-max theorem to zero-sum games with the addition of strategy costs. We then show that potential games with strategy costs remain potential games. Both zero-sum and potential games with strategy costs maintain a very appealing property: simple learning dynamics converge to equilibrium.

paragraphs: An agent facing a complex environment cannot perform unlimited computation before choosing how to act. This paper studies that constraint through games in which each strategy carries an additional cost. The cost may represent computation or another expense associated with the strategy. This makes the burden of choosing and using a strategy part of the strategic problem itself.

The authors first investigate games that are zero-sum before these strategy costs are added. They prove a generalization of the classical min-max theorem for this setting, describing the result as counterintuitive. They also examine potential games and establish that adding strategy costs preserves their status as potential games.

A shared consequence is that simple learning dynamics converge to equilibrium in both of the studied settings with strategy costs. This matters because bounded rationality raises questions about both desirable decisions and how agents can reach stable behavior. The model provides a way to incorporate resource costs while retaining convergence properties for these particular game families.
summary.tldr: Adding strategy costs models bounded rationality while preserving equilibrium convergence in the studied game families.

title: An Approach to Bounded Rationality

abstract: We give a new class of outer bounds on the marginal polytope, and propose a cutting-plane algorithm for efficiently optimizing over these constraints. When combined with a concave upper bound on the entropy, this gives a new variational inference algorithm for probabilistic inference in discrete Markov Random Fields (MRFs). Valid constraints on the marginal polytope are derived through a series of projections onto the cut polytope. As a result, we obtain tighter upper bounds on the log-partition function. We also show empirically that the approximations of the marginals are significantly more accurate when using the tighter outer bounds. Finally, we demonstrate the advantage of the new constraints for finding the MAP assignment in protein structure prediction.
originalAbstract: We give a new class of outer bounds on the marginal polytope, and propose a cutting-plane algorithm for efficiently optimizing over these constraints. When combined with a concave upper bound on the entropy, this gives a new variational inference algorithm for probabilistic inference in discrete Markov Random Fields (MRFs). Valid constraints on the marginal polytope are derived through a series of projections onto the cut polytope. As a result, we obtain tighter upper bounds on the log-partition function. We also show empirically that the approximations of the marginals are significantly more accurate when using the tighter outer bounds. Finally, we demonstrate the advantage of the new constraints for finding the MAP assignment in protein structure prediction.

paragraphs: Inference in a discrete Markov random field involves finding probabilities consistent with a joint model. The marginal polytope describes the allowable marginal probabilities, but working with it motivates tractable outer approximations. This paper introduces additional constraints that make those approximations tighter, reducing the set of candidate marginals admitted by the relaxation.

The constraints are derived through projections onto the cut polytope. A cutting-plane algorithm supports efficient optimization over them. Combined with a concave upper bound on entropy, this produces a variational inference algorithm. Tightening the feasible approximation yields tighter upper bounds on the log-partition function, a quantity involved in normalizing the model’s probabilities.

The authors also report that marginal estimates become significantly more accurate experimentally when the tighter bounds are used. They demonstrate benefits for finding the most probable joint assignment, known as MAP inference, in protein structure prediction. The paper therefore connects stronger constraints to both a mathematical improvement in upper bounds and observed improvements in inference quality.
summary.tldr: Tighter outer bounds on valid marginals improve variational bounds and empirically strengthen marginal and MAP inference.

title: New Outer Bounds on the Marginal Polytope

abstract: We prove strong noise-tolerance properties of a potential-based boosting algorithm, similar to MadaBoost (Domingo and Watanabe, 2000) and SmoothBoost (Servedio, 2003). Our analysis is in the agnostic framework of Kearns, Schapire and Sellie (1994), giving polynomial-time guarantees in presence of arbitrary noise. A remarkable feature of our algorithm is that it can be implemented without reweighting examples, by randomly relabeling them instead. Our boosting theorem gives, as easy corollaries, alternative derivations of two recent non-trivial results in computational learning theory: agnostically learning decision trees (Gopalan et al, 2008) and agnostically learning halfspaces (Kalai et al, 2005). Experiments suggest that the algorithm performs similarly to Madaboost.
originalAbstract: We prove strong noise-tolerance properties of a potential-based boosting algorithm, similar to MadaBoost (Domingo and Watanabe, 2000) and SmoothBoost (Servedio, 2003). Our analysis is in the agnostic framework of Kearns, Schapire and Sellie (1994), giving polynomial-time guarantees in presence of arbitrary noise. A remarkable feature of our algorithm is that it can be implemented without reweighting examples, by randomly relabeling them instead. Our boosting theorem gives, as easy corollaries, alternative derivations of two recent non-trivial results in computational learning theory: agnostically learning decision trees (Gopalan et al, 2008) and agnostically learning halfspaces (Kalai et al, 2005). paragraphs: Boosting combines weaker learning procedures into a stronger learner. This paper analyzes a potential-based boosting algorithm in the agnostic setting, where the analysis allows arbitrary noise. The central theoretical contribution is a set of strong noise-tolerance properties with polynomial-time guarantees within that framework.

A distinctive implementation feature is that the algorithm can randomly relabel examples instead of changing their weights. This provides another way to alter the learning problem presented during boosting. The paper relates the algorithm to MadaBoost and SmoothBoost, while establishing its own guarantees through the potential-based analysis.

The boosting theorem also yields alternative derivations of existing nontrivial results for agnostically learning decision trees and halfspaces. Those consequences show that the theorem has applications beyond analysis of the boosting procedure itself. Experiments suggest performance similar to MadaBoost. The theoretical and experimental claims play different roles: the analysis establishes noise-tolerance guarantees in its formal setting, while the experiments indicate comparable practical behavior to a related method rather than an empirical improvement over it.
summary.tldr: A potential-based boosting algorithm has agnostic noise-tolerance guarantees and can operate by randomly relabeling examples.

title: Potential-Based Agnostic Boosting

abstract: In order to learn effective control policies for dynamical systems, policy search methods must be able to discover successful executions of the desired task. While random exploration can work well in simple domains, complex and high-dimensional tasks present a serious challenge, particularly when combined with high-dimensional policies that make parameter-space exploration infeasible. We present a method that uses trajectory optimization as a powerful exploration strategy that guides the policy search. A variational decomposition of a maximum likelihood policy objective allows us to use standard trajectory optimization algorithms such as differential dynamic programming, interleaved with standard supervised learning for the policy itself. We demonstrate that the resulting algorithm can outperform prior methods on two challenging locomotion tasks.

While random exploration can work well in simple domains, complex and high-dimensional tasks present a serious challenge, particularly when combined with high-dimensional policies that make parameter-space exploration infeasible. We present a method that uses trajectory optimization as a powerful exploration strategy that guides the policy search. A variational decomposition of a maximum likelihood policy objective allows us to use standard trajectory optimization algorithms such as differential dynamic programming, interleaved with standard supervised learning for the policy itself. We demonstrate that the resulting algorithm can outperform prior methods on two challenging locomotion tasks.

paragraphs: Policy search needs to discover successful task executions before it can learn effective control behavior. Random exploration can do this in simple settings, but complex tasks and high-dimensional policies make searching through policy parameters difficult. This paper uses trajectory optimization to guide exploration toward useful executions of the task.

The method starts from a variational decomposition of a maximum-likelihood policy objective. That decomposition allows standard trajectory optimization methods, including differential dynamic programming, to alternate with supervised learning of the policy. The trajectory step searches for successful behavior, and the supervised step uses that guidance to train the policy itself.

This arrangement connects optimization of task executions with optimization of the controller that should produce them. It gives policy learning a structured source of exploration in settings where random parameter search is challenging. The authors demonstrate that the resulting algorithm can outperform prior methods on two demanding locomotion tasks, providing empirical support for this combination in the evaluated control problems.
summary.tldr: Alternating trajectory optimization with supervised policy learning guides exploration and can outperform prior methods on two challenging locomotion tasks.

title: Variational Policy Search via Trajectory Optimization

abstract: We introduce RNADE, a new model for joint density estimation of real-valued vectors. Our model calculates the density of a datapoint as the product of one-dimensional conditionals modeled using mixture density networks with shared parameters. RNADE learns a distributed representation of the data, while having a tractable expression for the calculation of densities. A tractable likelihood allows direct comparison with other methods and training by standard gradient-based optimizers. We compare the performance of RNADE on several datasets of heterogeneous and perceptual data, finding it outperforms mixture models in all but one case.
originalAbstract: We introduce RNADE, a new model for joint density estimation of real-valued vectors. Our model calculates the density of a datapoint as the product of one-dimensional conditionals modeled using mixture density networks with shared parameters. RNADE learns a distributed representation of the data, while having a tractable expression for the calculation of densities. A tractable likelihood allows direct comparison with other methods and training by standard gradient-based optimizers. We compare the performance of RNADE on several datasets of heterogeneous and perceptual data, finding it outperforms mixture models in all but one case.

paragraphs: RNADE estimates a joint probability density for vectors of real-valued observations. It constructs that density as a product of one-dimensional conditional densities. This breaks a multidimensional estimation problem into linked predictions for individual coordinates while preserving an explicit expression for the density of a complete observation.

Each conditional is modeled with a mixture density network, and the networks share parameters. The model also learns a distributed representation of the data. The central combination is a learned neural representation together with density calculations that remain tractable.

A tractable likelihood permits training with standard gradient-based optimizers and direct likelihood comparisons with other density estimators. The paper evaluates RNADE on several datasets covering heterogeneous and perceptual data. It outperforms mixture models in all but one of the evaluated cases. That exception preserves the empirical scope of the finding: RNADE performs better across most of these comparisons, without establishing a universal advantage. The work shows how neural conditional models can be assembled into a practical joint density estimator.
summary.tldr: RNADE combines shared neural conditional density models into a tractable joint density estimator that beats mixture models on most tested datasets.

title: RNADE: The real-valued neural autoregressive density-estimator

abstract: The sparse additive model for text modeling involves the sum-of-exp computing, with consuming costs for large scales. Moreover, the assumption of equal background across all classes/topics may be too strong. This paper extends to propose sparse additive model with low rank background (SAM-LRB), and simple yet efficient estimation. Particularly, by employing a double majorization bound, we approximate the log-likelihood into a quadratic lower-bound with the sum-of-exp terms absent. The constraints of low rank and sparsity are then simply embodied by nuclear norm and $\ell_1$-norm regularizers. Interestingly, we find that the optimization task in this manner can be transformed into the same form as that in Robust PCA. Consequently, parameters of supervised SAM-LRB can be efficiently learned using an existing algorithm for Robust PCA based on accelerated proximal gradient. Besides the supervised case, we extend SAM-LRB to also favor unsupervised and multifaceted scenarios. Experiments on real world data demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of SAM-LRB, showing state-of-the-art performances.

paragraphs: Sparse additive text models face expensive sums of exponentials, and assuming an identical background across all classes or topics can be restrictive. This paper introduces SAM-LRB, which replaces that shared-background assumption with a low-rank background. It pairs the more flexible model with an estimation procedure designed to reduce computational cost.

A double majorization bound turns the log-likelihood into a quadratic lower-bound approximation without the costly sum-of-exponentials terms. Nuclear-norm and l1-norm regularizers impose low-rank and sparse structure. The resulting optimization takes the same form as a Robust PCA problem, allowing supervised SAM-LRB parameters to be learned using an existing accelerated proximal-gradient algorithm.

The authors also extend the model to unsupervised and multifaceted settings. Experiments on real-world data report effective and efficient learning, with state-of-the-art performance. The approach matters because it addresses model flexibility and optimization together: it relaxes a strong background assumption while converting the fitting problem into a form supported by an established optimization method.
summary.tldr: SAM-LRB adds a low-rank background to sparse text models and enables efficient fitting through a Robust PCA optimization form.

title: Sparse Additive Text Models with Low Rank Background

abstract: Let $f: \{-1,1\}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a polynomial with at most $s$ non-zero real coefficients. We give an algorithm for exactly reconstructing $f$ given random examples from the uniform distribution on $\{-1,1\}^n$ that runs in time polynomial in $n$ and $2^{s}$ and succeeds if the function satisfies the \textit{unique sign property}: there is one output value which corresponds to a unique set of values of the participating parities. This sufficient condition is satisfied when every coefficient of $f$ is perturbed by a small random noise, or satisfied with high probability when $s$ parity functions are chosen randomly or when all the coefficients are positive. Learning sparse polynomials over the Boolean domain in time polynomial in $n$ and $2^{s}$ is considered notoriously hard in the worst-case. Our result shows that the problem is tractable for almost all sparse polynomials. Then, we show an application of this result to hypergraph sketching which is the problem of learning a sparse (both in the number of hyperedges and the size of the hyperedges) hypergraph from uniformly drawn random cuts. We also provide experimental results on a real world dataset.

The proposed algorithm runs in time polynomial in n and 2^s, where n is the input dimension, and succeeds under a sufficient condition called the unique sign property.

They also report experiments on a real-world dataset, connecting the conditional polynomial-learning result to recovering sparse graph-like structure from random observations.
summary.tldr: A sufficient uniqueness condition enables exact sparse-polynomial recovery from random examples, with an application to hypergraph sketching.

title: Sparse Polynomial Learning and Graph Sketching

abstract: In this work we aim at extending theoretical foundations of lifelong learning. Previous work analyzing this scenario is based on the assumption that the tasks are sampled i.i.d. from a task environment or limited to strongly constrained data distributions. Instead we study two scenarios when lifelong learning is possible, even though the observed tasks do not form an i.i.d. sample: first, when they are sampled from the same environment, but possibly with dependencies, and second, when the task environment is allowed to change over time. In the first case we prove a PAC-Bayesian theorem, which can be seen as a direct generalization of the analogous previous result for the i.i.d. case. For the second scenario we propose to learn an inductive bias in form of a transfer procedure. We present a generalization bound and show on a toy example how it can be used to identify a beneficial transfer algorithm.

paragraphs: Lifelong learning studies how experience across tasks can help with learning additional tasks. Earlier theoretical analyses often assumed tasks were sampled independently from a fixed environment, or imposed strong restrictions on data distributions. This paper extends the foundations to two settings where the observed tasks are not an independent, identically distributed sample.

In the first setting, tasks still come from the same environment but may depend on one another. The authors prove a PAC-Bayesian theorem that directly generalizes an earlier result for independent tasks. This separates the assumption of a common task environment from the stronger requirement that every sampled task be independent of the others.

In the second setting, the task environment itself can change over time. The authors propose learning an inductive bias represented as a transfer procedure, provide a generalization bound, and use a toy example to show how the bound can identify a beneficial transfer algorithm. The contribution supplies theoretical routes for learning across dependent tasks and changing environments within the analyzed scenarios.
summary.tldr: The paper extends lifelong-learning theory to dependent tasks and changing task environments through generalization bounds and learned transfer procedures.

title: Lifelong Learning with Non-i.i.d. Tasks

abstract: This paper develops a general approach, rooted in statistical learning theory, to learning an approximately revenue-maximizing auction from data. We introduce t-level auctions to interpolate between simple auctions, such as welfare maximization with reserve prices, and optimal auctions, thereby balancing the competing demands of expressivity and simplicity. We prove that such auctions have small representation error, in the sense that for every product distribution F over bidders’ valuations, there exists a t-level auction with small t and expected revenue close to optimal. We show that the set of t-level auctions has modest pseudo-dimension (for polynomial t) and therefore leads to small learning error. One consequence of our results is that, in arbitrary single-parameter settings, one can learn a mechanism with expected revenue arbitrarily close to optimal from a polynomial number of samples.

paragraphs: Learning a revenue-maximizing auction from data requires balancing flexibility with learnability. A simple auction family may miss profitable mechanisms, while a more expressive family can be harder to learn reliably. This paper introduces t-level auctions to provide a controlled range between simple auction formats and optimal auctions.

The analysis separates two sources of error. Representation error measures how much revenue is lost by restricting attention to the chosen auction family. For every product distribution over bidders' valuations, the authors show that an auction with small t can obtain expected revenue close to optimal. The contribution explains why a carefully chosen intermediate auction family can be expressive enough to approximate optimal revenue while remaining statistically learnable.
summary.tldr: T-level auctions balance expressivity and statistical complexity, enabling near-optimal expected revenue learning with polynomially many samples in the studied settings.

title: On the Pseudo-Dimension of Nearly Optimal Auctions

abstract: Abstract Subjective expected utility theory assumes that decision-makers possess unlimited computational resources to reason about their choices; however, virtually all decisions in everyday life are made under resource constraints---i.e. decision-makers are bounded in their rationality. Here we experimentally tested the predictions made by a formalization of bounded rationality based on ideas from statistical mechanics and information-theory. We systematically tested human subjects in their ability to solve combinatorial puzzles under different time limitations. We found that our bounded-rational model accounts well for the data. The decomposition of the fitted model parameter into the subjects' expected utility function and resource parameter provide interesting insight into the subjects' information capacity limits. Our results confirm that humans gradually fall back on their learned prior choice patterns when confronted with increasing resource limitations.

The decomposition of the fitted model parameter into the subjects' expected utility function and resource parameter provide interesting insight into the subjects' information capacity limits. paragraphs: People usually make decisions with limited time and computational resources. This paper studies that constraint through a formal model of bounded rationality, drawing on statistical mechanics and information theory. Its aim is to explain choices when a decision-maker cannot devote unlimited effort to evaluating every possibility.

The researchers tested people solving combinatorial puzzles under different time limits. This let them examine how behavior changed as the available decision-making resources became more restricted. They fitted the bounded-rationality model to the observations and separated its fitted parameter into an expected-utility component and a resource component, offering insight into participants' information-capacity limits.

The model accounted well for the experimental data. As time constraints became more severe, participants increasingly returned to choice patterns they had previously learned. This finding connects limited deliberation with greater reliance on prior behavior. Within the studied puzzle tasks, the results support a quantitative account of how preferences and available resources jointly shape decisions, and explain why tightening time limits changes the pattern of choices people make.
summary.tldr: Puzzle experiments support a bounded-rationality model in which tighter time limits lead people to rely more on learned choice patterns.

title: Human Decision-Making under Limited Time

abstract: Spectral decomposition of the Koopman operator is attracting attention as a tool for the analysis of nonlinear dynamical systems. Dynamic mode decomposition is a popular numerical algorithm for Koopman spectral analysis; however, we often need to prepare nonlinear observables manually according to the underlying dynamics, which is not always possible since we may not have any a priori knowledge about them. In this paper, we propose a fully data-driven method for Koopman spectral analysis based on the principle of learning Koopman invariant subspaces from observed data. To this end, we propose minimization of the residual sum of squares of linear least-squares regression to estimate a set of functions that transforms data into a form in which the linear regression fits well. We introduce an implementation with neural networks and evaluate performance empirically using nonlinear dynamical systems and applications.

paragraphs: Koopman spectral analysis offers a way to study nonlinear dynamical systems through functions of their states. Dynamic mode decomposition is a numerical tool for this analysis, but it often requires manually chosen nonlinear observables. Choosing those functions can be difficult when the underlying dynamics are not known in advance.

The paper proposes learning the observables directly from data, guided by the idea of a Koopman invariant subspace. It seeks functions that transform observations into a representation where linear regression fits the dynamics well. The optimization criterion is the residual sum of squares from linear least-squares regression, so the quality of the linear fit directly guides representation learning.

The authors implement this approach with neural networks and evaluate it empirically on nonlinear dynamical systems and applications. Its central contribution is a data-driven alternative to manually preparing observables. The reported evaluation examines the learned representation in use; the abstract does not claim that the optimization always discovers an exactly invariant subspace for arbitrary dynamics.
summary.tldr: The method learns nonlinear observables from data by seeking a representation whose dynamics admit a good linear least-squares fit.

title: Learning Koopman Invariant Subspaces for Dynamic Mode Decomposition

abstract: There is significant recent interest to parallelize deep learning algorithms in order to handle the enormous growth in data and model sizes. While most advances focus on model parallelization and engaging multiple computing agents via using a central parameter server, aspect of data parallelization along with decentralized computation has not been explored sufficiently. In this context, this paper presents a new consensus-based distributed SGD (CDSGD) (and its momentum variant, CDMSGD) algorithm for collaborative deep learning over fixed topology networks that enables data parallelization as well as decentralized computation. Such a framework can be extremely useful for learning agents with access to only local/private data in a communication constrained environment. We analyze the convergence properties of the proposed algorithm with strongly convex and nonconvex objective functions with fixed and diminishing step sizes using concepts of Lyapunov function construction. We demonstrate the efficacy of our algorithms in comparison with the baseline centralized SGD and the recently proposed federated averaging algorithm (that also enables data parallelism) based on benchmark datasets such as MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.

paragraphs: The paper studies how multiple computing agents can train a deep model together while each has access to local data. Its focus is decentralized computation over a fixed communication network. This setting is relevant when communication is constrained and agents cannot rely on a central parameter server to coordinate every update.

The authors introduce consensus-based distributed stochastic gradient descent, called CDSGD, and a momentum version, CDMSGD. Consensus supplies the mechanism for coordinating agents, while distributed training allows them to work with different portions of the data. The proposed framework combines these two elements so collaboration can follow the available network connections.

The analysis covers strongly convex and nonconvex objectives, with both fixed and diminishing step sizes. It uses Lyapunov functions to study convergence. Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 demonstrate the algorithms' effectiveness in comparisons with centralized SGD and federated averaging. Together, the theoretical analysis and experiments support decentralized training as a useful approach for agents operating within a fixed network.
summary.tldr: Consensus-based SGD lets agents train collaboratively over a fixed network using local data, with convergence analysis and benchmark evaluation.

title: Collaborative Deep Learning in Fixed Topology Networks

abstract: Many real world tasks such as reasoning and physical interaction require identification and manipulation of conceptual entities. A first step towards solving these tasks is the automated discovery of distributed symbol-like representations. In this paper, we explicitly formalize this problem as inference in a spatial mixture model where each component is parametrized by a neural network. Based on the Expectation Maximization framework we then derive a differentiable clustering method that simultaneously learns how to group and represent individual entities. We evaluate our method on the (sequential) perceptual grouping task and find that it is able to accurately recover the constituent objects. We demonstrate that the learned representations are useful for next-step prediction.

paragraphs: Reasoning about a scene or interacting with it requires identifying entities that can be considered individually. This paper studies an early step toward that ability: discovering distributed representations that behave like symbols for distinct entities. The challenge is to learn both which observations belong together and how each resulting group should be represented.

The authors formulate this as inference in a spatial mixture model, with a neural network parameterizing each component. From the expectation maximization framework, they derive a differentiable clustering method that jointly learns grouping and representation. This ties the formation of individual entities to the process of learning useful descriptions of them.

Evaluations on perceptual grouping, including sequential grouping, show that the method can accurately recover the constituent objects in the tested inputs. The learned representations also prove useful for predicting the next step. These findings support object discovery as a practical representation-learning objective: the resulting groups capture entities in the input and provide information useful beyond the grouping task itself.
summary.tldr: Neural Expectation Maximization jointly learns to group observations into entities and represent them for tasks such as next-step prediction.

title: Neural Expectation Maximization

abstract: The study of cross-domain mapping without supervision has recently attracted much attention. Much of the recent progress was enabled by the use of adversarial training as well as cycle constraints. The practical difficulty of adversarial training motivates research into non-adversarial methods. In a recent paper, it was shown that cross-domain mapping is possible without the use of cycles or GANs. Although promising, this approach suffers from several drawbacks including costly inference and an optimization variable for every training example preventing the method from using large training sets. We present an alternative approach which is able to achieve non-adversarial mapping using a novel form of Variational Auto-Encoder. Our method is much faster at inference time, is able to leverage large datasets and has a simple interpretation.

paragraphs: Unsupervised cross-domain mapping seeks a mapping between domains without supervision. Much of the progress discussed in this paper relies on adversarial training and cycle constraints. Because adversarial training can be difficult in practice, the authors investigate a different route based on a new form of variational autoencoder.

Their starting point is earlier evidence that mapping across domains can work without cycles or generative adversarial networks. That earlier approach has practical costs: inference is expensive, and it assigns a separate optimization variable to every training example. The latter requirement prevents it from making use of large training sets, creating a scaling problem in addition to the cost of applying the trained method.

The proposed variational-autoencoder approach achieves non-adversarial mapping while addressing those stated drawbacks. The authors report much faster inference, the ability to use large datasets, and a simple interpretation. These claims make the contribution primarily about the practicality of non-adversarial mapping: a promising alternative becomes easier to apply and better able to benefit from more training data.
summary.tldr: A new variational-autoencoder approach enables non-adversarial cross-domain mapping with faster inference and support for large datasets.

title: Non-Adversarial Mapping with VAEs

abstract: Feature hashing, also known as {\em the hashing trick}, introduced by Weinberger et al. (2009), is one of the key techniques used in scaling-up machine learning algorithms. Loosely speaking, feature hashing uses a random sparse projection matrix $A : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ (where $m \ll n$) in order to reduce the dimension of the data from $n$ to $m$ while approximately preserving the Euclidean norm. Every column of $A$ contains exactly one non-zero entry, equals to either $-1$ or $1$. Weinberger et al. showed tail bounds on $\|Ax\|_2^2$. Specifically they showed that for every $\varepsilon, \delta$, if $\|x\|_{\infty} / \|x\|_2$ is sufficiently small, and $m$ is sufficiently large, then \begin{equation*}\Pr[ \; | \;\|Ax\|_2^2 - \|x\|_2^2\; | < \varepsilon \|x\|_2^2 \;] \ge 1 - \delta \;.\end{equation*} These bounds were later extended by Dasgupta et al. (2010) and most recently refined by Dahlgaard et al. (2017), however, the true nature of the performance of this key technique, and specifically the correct tradeoff between the pivotal parameters $\|x\|_{\infty} / \|x\|_2, m, \varepsilon, \delta$ remained an open question. We settle this question by giving tight asymptotic bounds on the exact tradeoff between the central parameters, thus providing a complete understanding of the performance of feature hashing. We complement the asymptotic bound with empirical data, which shows that the constants "hiding" in the asymptotic notation are, in fact, very close to $1$, thus further illustrating the tightness of the presented bounds in practice.

Each original coordinate contributes to one output coordinate with a random positive or negative sign. The central question is how much this inexpensive transformation changes the vector’s squared Euclidean length, and how reliably that change can be controlled.

The answer depends on four quantities: the largest coordinate relative to the vector’s length, the compressed dimension, the tolerated relative error, and the allowed failure probability. Earlier results gave sufficient conditions connecting these quantities, but left their precise tradeoff unresolved. This paper supplies tight asymptotic bounds describing that tradeoff.

The result clarifies the performance of feature hashing by connecting properties of the input vector to the compression size needed for a desired accuracy and reliability. The authors also compare the theory with empirical data. Those observations indicate that the constants hidden in the asymptotic bounds are close to one, supporting the practical tightness of the analysis in the examined settings.
summary.tldr: Tight asymptotic bounds characterize how feature hashing trades compressed dimension and input concentration against norm-preservation accuracy and failure probability.

title: Fully Understanding The Hashing Trick

abstract: In this paper, we show that SVRG and SARAH can be modified to be fundamentally faster than all of the other standard algorithms that minimize the sum of $n$ smooth functions, such as SAGA, SAG, SDCA, and SDCA without duality. Most finite sum algorithms follow what we call the ``span assumption'': Their updates are in the span of a sequence of component gradients chosen in a random IID fashion. In the big data regime, where the condition number $\kappa=O(n)$, the span assumption prevents algorithms from converging to an approximate solution of accuracy $\epsilon$ in less than $n\ln(1/\epsilon)$ iterations. SVRG and SARAH do not follow the span assumption since they are updated with a hybrid of full-gradient and component-gradient information. We show that because of this, they can be up to $\Omega(1+(\ln(n/\kappa))_+)$ times faster. In particular, to obtain an accuracy $\epsilon = 1/n^\alpha$ for $\kappa=n^\beta$ and $\alpha,\beta\in(0,1)$, modified SVRG requires $O(n)$ iterations, whereas algorithms that follow the span assumption require $O(n\ln(n))$ iterations. Moreover, we present lower bound results that show this speedup is optimal, and provide analysis to help explain why this speedup exists. With the understanding that the span assumption is a point of weakness of finite sum algorithms, future work may purposefully exploit this to yield faster algorithms in the big data regime.

title: Breaking the Span Assumption Yields Fast Finite-Sum Minimization

abstract: A key task in Bayesian machine learning is sampling from distributions that are only specified up to a partition function (i.e., constant of proportionality). One prevalent example of this is sampling posteriors in parametric distributions, such as latent-variable generative models. However sampling (even very approximately) can be #P-hard. Classical results (going back to Bakry and Emery) on sampling focus on log-concave distributions, and show a natural Markov chain called Langevin diffusion mix in polynomial time. However, all log-concave distributions are uni-modal, while in practice it is very common for the distribution of interest to have multiple modes. In this case, Langevin diffusion suffers from torpid mixing. We address this problem by combining Langevin diffusion with simulated tempering. The result is a Markov chain that mixes more rapidly by transitioning between different temperatures of the distribution. We analyze this Markov chain for a mixture of (strongly) log-concave distributions of the same shape. In particular, our technique applies to the canonical multi-modal distribution: a mixture of gaussians (of equal variance). Our algorithm efficiently samples from these distributions given only access to the gradient of the log-pdf. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first result that proves fast mixing for multimodal distributions.

Established sampling guarantees cover log-concave distributions, which have a single mode. Distributions with several modes create a different challenge: Langevin diffusion can move too slowly between their separate high-probability regions.

Changing temperature helps the process move between regions that are difficult to traverse at a fixed temperature, addressing the slow mixing that motivates the work.

The authors prove efficient sampling for mixtures of strongly log-concave distributions with the same shape, including Gaussian mixtures with equal variance. Their algorithm requires access only to the gradient of the log probability density. The contribution is a fast-mixing guarantee for this specified multimodal family, extending the theoretical reach of Langevin-based sampling beyond the single-mode setting. The shared-shape assumption is part of the scope of the analysis.
summary.tldr: Combining Langevin diffusion with simulated tempering enables provably efficient sampling for a specified family of multimodal distributions.

title: Beyond Log-concavity: Provable Guarantees for Sampling Multi-modal Distributions using Simulated Tempering Langevin Monte Carlo

abstract: We introduce a new neural network-based continual learning algorithm, dubbed as Uncertainty-regularized Continual Learning (UCL), which builds on traditional Bayesian online learning framework with variational inference. We focus on two significant drawbacks of the recently proposed regularization-based methods: a) considerable additional memory cost for determining the per-weight regularization strengths and b) the absence of gracefully forgetting scheme, which can prevent performance degradation in learning new tasks. In this paper, we show UCL can solve these two problems by introducing a fresh interpretation on the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence term of the variational lower bound for Gaussian mean-field approximation. Based on the interpretation, we propose the notion of node-wise uncertainty, which drastically reduces the number of additional parameters for implementing per-weight regularization. Moreover, we devise two additional regularization terms that enforce \emph{stability} by freezing important parameters for past tasks and allow \emph{plasticity} by controlling the actively learning parameters for a new task. Through extensive experiments, we show UCL convincingly outperforms most of recent state-of-the-art baselines not only on popular supervised learning benchmarks, but also on challenging lifelong reinforcement learning tasks. The source code of our algorithm is available at https://github.com/csm9493/UCL.

summary.tldr: UCL uses node-wise uncertainty and adaptive regularization to reduce memory overhead while balancing retention and adaptation across sequential tasks.

title: Uncertainty-based Continual Learning with Adaptive Regularization

abstract: A key challenge in crowdsourcing is inferring the ground truth from noisy and unreliable data. To do so, existing approaches rely on collecting redundant information from the crowd, and aggregating it with some probabilistic method. However, oftentimes such methods are computationally inefficient, are restricted to some specific settings, or lack theoretical guarantees. In this paper, we revisit the problem of binary classification from crowdsourced data. Specifically we propose Streaming Bayesian Inference for Crowdsourcing (SBIC), a new algorithm that does not suffer from any of these limitations. First, SBIC has low complexity and can be used in a real-time online setting. Second, SBIC has the same accuracy as the best state-of-the-art algorithms in all settings. Third, SBIC has provable asymptotic guarantees both in the online and offline settings.

Existing approaches can make this aggregation computationally expensive, restrict the settings they handle, or provide insufficient theoretical assurance. This paper focuses on the case where each item has one of two possible classes.

The proposed algorithm, Streaming Bayesian Inference for Crowdsourcing, is designed to process this evidence with low computational complexity. Its streaming formulation allows use in a real-time online setting, making it suitable for updating classification inferences as crowd information arrives. Computational efficiency is therefore part of the algorithm's central contribution alongside its inference quality.

The authors report accuracy matching the best state-of-the-art algorithms across the settings considered. They also establish asymptotic guarantees for both online and offline use. These results connect efficient ongoing aggregation with theoretical support and competitive accuracy, addressing several weaknesses of earlier approaches within the paper's binary crowdsourced-classification problem.
summary.tldr: SBIC efficiently aggregates noisy binary crowd labels online while matching leading accuracy and providing asymptotic guarantees.

title: Streaming Bayesian Inference for Crowdsourced Classification

abstract: Many real-world data represent sequences of interdependent events unfolding over time. They can be modeled naturally as realizations of a point process. Despite many potential applications, existing point process models are limited in their ability to capture complex patterns of interaction. Hawkes processes admit many efficient inference algorithms, but are limited to mutually excitatory effects. Non- linear Hawkes processes allow for more complex influence patterns, but for their estimation it is typically necessary to resort to discrete-time approximations that may yield poor generative models. In this paper, we introduce the first general class of Bayesian point process models extended with a nonlinear component that allows both excitatory and inhibitory relationships in continuous time. We derive a fully Bayesian inference algorithm for these processes using Polya-Gamma augmentation and Poisson thinning. We evaluate the proposed model on single and multi-neuronal spike train recordings. Results demonstrate that the proposed model, unlike existing point process models, can generate biologically-plausible spike trains, while still achieving competitive predictive likelihoods.

paragraphs: Event sequences often contain interactions: one event can make another more or less likely. The authors introduce a Bayesian point-process family with a nonlinear component that captures both excitation and inhibition in continuous time. They derive a fully Bayesian inference algorithm using Polya-Gamma augmentation and Poisson thinning. These mathematical tools support inference for the proposed model while preserving its continuous-time treatment of event occurrence.

Evaluation uses recordings of neuronal spikes from both single neurons and multiple neurons. The model generates biologically plausible spike trains while maintaining competitive predictive likelihoods, a combination the authors contrast with existing point-process models. This distinction matters because assigning good probabilities to observed data and generating realistic new sequences are different aspects of model quality. The reported results support the proposed approach on both fronts.
summary.tldr: A nonlinear Bayesian point-process model captures excitation and inhibition in continuous time and generates plausible neuronal spike trains with competitive predictive likelihoods.

title: Mutually Regressive Point Processes

abstract: We study deep neural networks with polynomial activations, particularly their expressive power. For a fixed architecture and activation degree, a polynomial neural network defines an algebraic map from weights to polynomials. The image of this map is the functional space associated to the network, and it is an irreducible algebraic variety upon taking closure. This paper proposes the dimension of this variety as a precise measure of the expressive power of polynomial neural networks. We obtain several theoretical results regarding this dimension as a function of architecture, including an exact formula for high activation degrees, as well as upper and lower bounds on layer widths in order for deep polynomials networks to fill the ambient functional space. We also present computational evidence that it is profitable in terms of expressiveness for layer widths to increase monotonically and then decrease monotonically. Finally, we link our study to favorable optimization properties when training weights, and we draw intriguing connections with tensor and polynomial decompositions.

paragraphs: This paper asks how architecture determines the range of functions a neural network can express when its activations are polynomials. With architecture and activation degree fixed, changing the weights produces different polynomial functions. The authors study the geometry of that collection as a precise way to characterize expressive power.

The map from weights to output polynomials is algebraic, and the closure of its image forms an irreducible algebraic variety. The paper proposes the dimension of this variety as its expressivity measure. It derives architecture-dependent results, including an exact dimension formula for high activation degrees and upper and lower width bounds for filling the ambient functional space.

This architectural observation is presented as evidence, alongside the theoretical results about dimension. The paper also connects the analysis with favorable training optimization properties and with tensor and polynomial decompositions, linking network design to mathematical descriptions of which functions its parameters can represent.
summary.tldr: The paper measures polynomial-network expressivity through algebraic dimension and derives how architecture and activation degree shape that dimension.

title: On the Expressive Power of Deep Polynomial Neural Networks

abstract: Monte-Carlo planning, as exemplified by Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), has demonstrated remarkable performance in applications with finite spaces. In this paper, we consider Monte-Carlo planning in an environment with continuous state-action spaces, a much less understood problem with important applications in control and robotics. We introduce POLY-HOOT, an algorithm that augments MCTS with a continuous armed bandit strategy named Hierarchical Optimistic Optimization (HOO) (Bubeck et al., 2011). Specifically, we enhance HOO by using an appropriate polynomial, rather than logarithmic, bonus term in the upper confidence bounds. Such a polynomial bonus is motivated by its empirical successes in AlphaGo Zero (Silver et al., 2017b), as well as its significant role in achieving theoretical guarantees of finite space MCTS (Shah et al., 2019). We investigate, for the first time, the regret of the enhanced HOO algorithm in non-stationary bandit problems. Using this result as a building block, we establish non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for POLY-HOOT: the value estimate converges to an arbitrarily small neighborhood of the optimal value function at a polynomial rate. We further provide experimental results that corroborate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo tree search has worked well in finite spaces, but planning with continuous states and actions is less understood. POLY-HOOT addresses this setting by combining tree search with Hierarchical Optimistic Optimization, a bandit strategy that handles a continuous range of choices. The aim is both an algorithm and a finite-computation account of its behavior.

The method modifies the bandit strategy's upper confidence bounds by using a polynomial exploration bonus in place of a logarithmic one. The authors analyze the enhanced strategy in non-stationary bandit problems, where the quantities being learned can change. That regret analysis supplies a building block for understanding the complete planner.

The resulting non-asymptotic guarantee shows that POLY-HOOT's value estimate approaches an arbitrarily small neighborhood of the optimal value function at a polynomial rate. This states how convergence progresses, rather than only describing behavior in an unlimited-computation limit. Experiments corroborate the theoretical findings, supporting the combination of continuous-action bandit search and the modified exploration bonus.
summary.tldr: POLY-HOOT combines Monte Carlo tree search with a modified continuous bandit strategy and establishes polynomial-rate value convergence guarantees.

title: POLY-HOOT: Monte-Carlo Planning in Continuous Space MDPs with Non-Asymptotic Analysis

abstract: QMIX is a popular $Q$-learning algorithm for cooperative MARL in the centralised training and decentralised execution paradigm. In order to enable easy decentralisation, QMIX restricts the joint action $Q$-values it can represent to be a monotonic mixing of each agent's utilities. However, this restriction prevents it from representing value functions in which an agent's ordering over its actions can depend on other agents' actions. To analyse this representational limitation, we first formalise the objective QMIX optimises, which allows us to view QMIX as an operator that first computes the $Q$-learning targets and then projects them into the space representable by QMIX. This projection returns a representable $Q$-value that minimises the unweighted squared error across all joint actions. We show in particular that this projection can fail to recover the optimal policy even with access to $Q^*$, which primarily stems from the equal weighting placed on each joint action. We rectify this by introducing a weighting into the projection, in order to place more importance on the better joint actions. We propose two weighting schemes and prove that they recover the correct maximal action for any joint action $Q$-values, and therefore for $Q^*$ as well. Based on our analysis and results in the tabular setting we introduce two scalable versions of our algorithm, Centrally-Weighted (CW) QMIX and Optimistically-Weighted (OW) QMIX and demonstrate improved performance on both predator-prey and challenging multi-agent StarCraft benchmark tasks (Samvelyan et al., 2019).

paragraphs: QMIX supports centralized training and decentralized decisions by combining individual agents’ utilities monotonically. This makes decentralization convenient but limits the joint values it can represent. In particular, it cannot capture every situation where one agent’s preference among actions changes depending on what other agents do.

The paper analyzes QMIX as a projection of learning targets into its representable value functions. Its ordinary squared-error projection weights every joint action equally and can miss the optimal policy even when given the true optimal values. Weighted QMIX instead emphasizes better joint actions. The authors propose two weighting schemes and prove that their projections recover the correct maximizing action for any joint action values.

Both show improved performance on predator-prey and challenging multi-agent StarCraft tasks. The distinction between results matters: correct action recovery is proved for the analyzed weighting schemes, while the scalable algorithms are supported by experiments. The approach targets which decisions survive approximation, rather than requiring exact representation of every joint value.
summary.tldr: Weighted QMIX emphasizes better joint actions during value approximation, with action-recovery guarantees in its analysis and improved benchmark performance.

title: Weighted QMIX: Expanding Monotonic Value Function Factorisation for Deep Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: This article develops a Bayesian optimization (BO) method which acts directly over raw strings, proposing the first uses of string kernels and genetic algorithms within BO loops. Recent applications of BO over strings have been hindered by the need to map inputs into a smooth and unconstrained latent space. Learning this projection is computationally and data-intensive. Our approach instead builds a powerful Gaussian process surrogate model based on string kernels, naturally supporting variable length inputs, and performs efficient acquisition function maximization for spaces with syntactic constraints. Experiments demonstrate considerably improved optimization over existing approaches across a broad range of constraints, including the popular setting where syntax is governed by a context-free grammar.

paragraphs: BOSS tackles Bayesian optimization when candidate inputs are strings, potentially with different lengths and strict syntax. Existing approaches discussed in the paper first learn a mapping from strings into a smooth, unconstrained latent space. Building that mapping can require substantial data and computation, creating an additional burden before optimization can proceed effectively.

The proposed method works directly with raw strings. It constructs a Gaussian process surrogate using string kernels and uses genetic algorithms within the Bayesian optimization loop. The kernel-based surrogate naturally accommodates variable-length inputs, while the acquisition optimization procedure searches spaces subject to syntactic restrictions.

Experiments show considerably better optimization than existing approaches across a broad range of constraints, including syntax specified by a context-free grammar. The result supports direct string modeling as a useful alternative to learning a latent projection. Its significance is the combination of a string-aware predictive model and an efficient search procedure that can respect the structure of valid candidates.
summary.tldr: BOSS combines string kernels and genetic search to optimize raw, variable-length strings under syntactic constraints.

title: BOSS: Bayesian Optimization over String Spaces

abstract: We introduce a method called TracIn that computes the influence of a training example on a prediction made by the model. The idea is to trace how the loss on the test point changes during the training process whenever the training example of interest was utilized. We provide a scalable implementation of TracIn via: (a) a first-order gradient approximation to the exact computation, (b) saved checkpoints of standard training procedures, and (c) cherry-picking layers of a deep neural network. In contrast with previously proposed methods, TracIn is simple to implement; all it needs is the ability to work with gradients, checkpoints, and loss functions. The method is general. It applies to any machine learning model trained using stochastic gradient descent or a variant of it, agnostic of architecture, domain and task. We expect the method to be widely useful within processes that study and improve training data.
