paragraphs: A model's prediction reflects its training data, but identifying which examples contributed to that prediction is a separate problem. This paper introduces TracIn, a method for estimating the influence of a particular training example. Its starting point is to track changes in the loss on a test point whenever that training example is used during learning.

Computing that training-history contribution directly can be costly. TracIn makes the calculation scalable through a first-order gradient approximation, saved checkpoints from standard training, and selection of particular neural-network layers. These choices turn the basic idea of tracing loss changes into an implementation built around gradients, checkpoints, and loss functions.

The method applies to models trained by stochastic gradient descent or its variants, without tying the formulation to a particular architecture, application domain, or task. Its significance is a practical route from an individual prediction back to the training examples that influenced it. The authors anticipate usefulness for studying and improving training data; the abstract presents that broader impact as an expectation.
summary.tldr: TracIn estimates training-example influence by approximating changes in a test point's loss along gradient-based training using saved checkpoints.

title: Estimating Training Data Influence by Tracing Gradient Descent

abstract: Self-attention architectures, which are rapidly pushing the frontier in natural language processing, demonstrate a surprising depth-inefficient behavior: previous works indicate that increasing the internal representation (network width) is just as useful as increasing the number of self-attention layers (network depth). We theoretically predict a width-dependent transition between depth-efficiency and depth-inefficiency in self-attention. We conduct systematic empirical ablations on networks of depths 6 to 48 that clearly reveal the theoretically predicted behaviors, and provide explicit quantitative suggestions regarding the optimal depth-to-width allocation for a given self-attention network size. The race towards beyond 1-Trillion parameter language models renders informed guidelines for increasing self-attention depth and width in tandem an essential ingredient. Our guidelines elucidate the depth-to-width trade-off in self-attention networks of sizes up to the scale of GPT3 (which is too deep for its size), and beyond, marking an unprecedented width of 30K as optimal for a 1-Trillion parameter self-attention network.

paragraphs: Making a self-attention network larger leaves a design choice: add more layers or widen the representations inside them. Earlier findings suggested that width could be as useful as depth, challenging the expectation that additional layers always provide a particularly efficient use of capacity. This paper studies how that tradeoff changes with network width.

The theoretical analysis predicts a width-dependent transition between regimes where depth is efficient and where it is inefficient. Systematic experiments varying networks from 6 to 48 layers reveal the predicted behaviors. The authors use these results to provide quantitative guidance for allocating depth and width at a given overall network size.

The guidance extends to very large self-attention models. Under the paper's analysis, GPT3 is too deep for its size, and a width of 30,000 is identified as optimal for a one-trillion-parameter self-attention network. These are conclusions of the proposed allocation guidelines. The broader implication is that depth and width should be increased together according to their interaction, rather than treating more layers as an independently reliable route to efficient scaling.
summary.tldr: Theory and experiments identify a width-dependent limit to the benefits of depth in self-attention and guide depth-to-width allocation.

title: Limits to Depth Efficiencies of Self-Attention

abstract: This paper proposes a method to visualize the discrimination power of intermediate-layer visual patterns encoded by a DNN. Specifically, we visualize (1) how the DNN gradually learns regional visual patterns in each intermediate layer during the training process, and (2) the effects of the DNN using non-discriminative patterns in low layers to construct disciminative patterns in middle/high layers through the forward propagation. Based on our visualization method, we can quantify knowledge points (i.e. the number of discriminative visual patterns) learned by the DNN to evaluate the representation capacity of the DNN. Furthermore, this method also provides new insights into signal-processing behaviors of existing deep-learning techniques, such as adversarial attacks and knowledge distillation.

paragraphs: A neural network’s intermediate layers encode visual patterns, but their usefulness for distinguishing inputs can be difficult to inspect. This paper proposes a visualization method centered on that discriminative power. It examines the network from two complementary perspectives: how patterns emerge over training and how patterns are combined as information moves through the layers.

The first perspective tracks regional visual patterns learned within each intermediate layer during training. The second shows how patterns in lower layers that are not themselves discriminative can contribute to discriminative patterns in middle or higher layers. This helps explain how the usefulness of a representation can depend on what later computation builds from it.

The method also counts discriminative visual patterns as knowledge points, providing a way to assess representation capacity. The authors use the visualizations to gain insights into signal-processing behavior associated with adversarial attacks and knowledge distillation. The contribution connects visual inspection with a quantitative description of learned patterns and their role in the network’s processing.
summary.tldr: A visualization method tracks how discriminative visual patterns emerge during training and are constructed across network layers.

title: Visualizing the Emergence of Intermediate Visual Patterns in DNNs

abstract: We consider the problem of online learning in the presence of distribution shifts that occur at an unknown rate and of unknown intensity. We derive a new Bayesian online inference approach to simultaneously infer these distribution shifts and adapt the model to the detected changes by integrating ideas from change point detection, switching dynamical systems, and Bayesian online learning. Using a binary ‘change variable,’ we construct an informative prior such that--if a change is detected--the model partially erases the information of past model updates by tempering to facilitate adaptation to the new data distribution. Furthermore, the approach uses beam search to track multiple change-point hypotheses and selects the most probable one in hindsight. Our proposed method is model-agnostic, applicable in both supervised and unsupervised learning settings, suitable for an environment of concept drifts or covariate drifts, and yields improvements over state-of-the-art Bayesian online learning approaches.

paragraphs: An online learner continually updates its model as data arrives, but earlier observations may become less relevant when the data distribution changes. This paper addresses shifts whose frequency and strength are unknown. It develops a Bayesian approach that jointly infers whether a change has occurred and adapts the model to the new conditions.

A binary change variable controls an informative prior. When the method detects a change, tempering partially removes the influence of previous model updates, making room for new evidence. Beam search maintains several possible histories of change points, and the method selects the most probable history in hindsight. This allows uncertainty about when changes happened to remain part of inference.

The approach combines ideas from change-point detection, switching dynamical systems, and Bayesian online learning. It is model-agnostic and applies to supervised or unsupervised learning, including concept drift and covariate drift. The reported improvements over existing Bayesian online approaches support the value of connecting change detection directly to selective forgetting and subsequent adaptation.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian online learner detects irregular distribution shifts and selectively weakens past information to adapt.

title: Detecting and Adapting to Irregular Distribution Shifts in Bayesian Online Learning

abstract: Real-world data universally confronts a severe class-imbalance problem and exhibits a long-tailed distribution, i.e., most labels are associated with limited instances. The naïve models supervised by such datasets would prefer dominant labels, encounter a serious generalization challenge and become poorly calibrated. We propose two novel methods from the prior perspective to alleviate this dilemma. First, we deduce a balance-oriented data augmentation named Uniform Mixup (UniMix) to promote mixup in long-tailed scenarios, which adopts advanced mixing factor and sampler in favor of the minority. Second, motivated by the Bayesian theory, we figure out the Bayes Bias (Bayias), an inherent bias caused by the inconsistency of prior, and compensate it as a modification on standard cross-entropy loss. We further prove that both the proposed methods ensure the classification calibration theoretically and empirically. Extensive experiments verify that our strategies contribute to a better-calibrated model, and their combination achieves state-of-the-art performance on CIFAR-LT, ImageNet-LT, and iNaturalist 2018.
originalAbstract: Real-world data universally confronts a severe class-imbalance problem and exhibits a long-tailed distribution, i.e., most labels are associated with limited instances. The naïve models supervised by such datasets would prefer dominant labels, encounter a serious generalization challenge and become poorly calibrated. We propose two novel methods from the prior perspective to alleviate this dilemma. First, we deduce a balance-oriented data augmentation named Uniform Mixup (UniMix) to promote mixup in long-tailed scenarios, which adopts advanced mixing factor and sampler in favor of the minority. Second, motivated by the Bayesian theory, we figure out the Bayes Bias (Bayias), an inherent bias caused by the inconsistency of prior, and compensate it as a modification on standard cross-entropy loss. We further prove that both the proposed methods ensure the classification calibration theoretically and empirically. Extensive experiments verify that our strategies contribute to a better-calibrated model, and their combination achieves state-of-the-art performance on CIFAR-LT, ImageNet-LT, and iNaturalist 2018.

paragraphs: Long-tailed recognition involves many classes with few examples and a smaller number of dominant classes. Training directly on that imbalance can favor common labels, weaken generalization, and produce poor calibration. This paper approaches the problem through class priors, connecting the frequency of labels to both data augmentation and the training loss.

The first method, Uniform Mixup or UniMix, adjusts how examples are selected and mixed to favor minority classes. The second, Bayias, addresses a bias attributed to inconsistent priors. Motivated by Bayesian reasoning, it compensates for that bias by modifying standard cross-entropy loss. The methods therefore intervene at different points: construction of training examples and evaluation of prediction errors.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical support for classification calibration with both methods. Experiments find better-calibrated models, and combining the techniques achieves state-of-the-art performance on CIFAR-LT, ImageNet-LT, and iNaturalist 2018. The results support addressing class imbalance through complementary changes to sampling, mixing, and loss design, rather than relying on ordinary training to overcome dominant-class preferences on its own.
summary.tldr: Minority-oriented mixup and a prior-bias correction improve calibration and recognition performance on the reported long-tailed benchmarks.

title: Towards Calibrated Model for Long-Tailed Visual Recognition from Prior Perspective

abstract: Though data augmentation has rapidly emerged as a key tool for optimization in modern machine learning, a clear picture of how augmentation schedules affect optimization and interact with optimization hyperparameters such as learning rate is nascent. In the spirit of classical convex optimization and recent work on implicit bias, the present work analyzes the effect of augmentation on optimization in the simple convex setting of linear regression with MSE loss.We find joint schedules for learning rate and data augmentation scheme under which augmented gradient descent provably converges and characterize the resulting minimum. Our results apply to arbitrary augmentation schemes, revealing complex interactions between learning rates and augmentations even in the convex setting. Our approach interprets augmented (S)GD as a stochastic optimization method for a time-varying sequence of proxy losses. This gives a unified way to analyze learning rate, batch size, and augmentations ranging from additive noise to random projections. From this perspective, our results, which also give rates of convergence, can be viewed as Monro-Robbins type conditions for augmented (S)GD.

paragraphs: Data augmentation changes the examples used during training, but its optimization effects depend on how those changes interact with the learning rate. This paper studies that interaction in linear regression with mean squared error. The convex setting allows a precise analysis while still revealing complicated behavior when augmentation and optimization schedules evolve together.

The authors interpret augmented gradient methods as stochastic optimization over a changing sequence of proxy losses. This creates a common framework for examining learning rate, batch size, and different augmentation mechanisms. The analysis covers arbitrary augmentation schemes, with additive noise and random projections illustrating the range of transformations considered.

The paper identifies joint learning-rate and augmentation schedules that guarantee convergence, characterizes the resulting minimum, and provides convergence rates. These are conditional guarantees about compatible schedules, rather than a claim that every augmentation schedule converges. Viewed through the proxy-loss framework, the results provide stochastic-approximation-style conditions for augmented gradient descent. Their significance is that augmentation affects the optimization process itself, including where it converges, even in this simple convex learning problem.
summary.tldr: A proxy-loss analysis explains how augmentation and learning-rate schedules jointly determine convergence in linear regression.

title: How Data Augmentation affects Optimization for Linear Regression

abstract: The audio-visual video parsing task aims to temporally parse a video into audio or visual event categories. However, it is labor intensive to temporally annotate audio and visual events and thus hampers the learning of a parsing model. To this end, we propose to explore additional cross-video and cross-modality supervisory signals to facilitate weakly-supervised audio-visual video parsing. The proposed method exploits both the common and diverse event semantics across videos to identify audio or visual events. In addition, our method explores event co-occurrence across audio, visual, and audio-visual streams. We leverage the explored cross-modality co-occurrence to localize segments of target events while excluding irrelevant ones. The discovered supervisory signals across different videos and modalities can greatly facilitate the training with only video-level annotations. Quantitative and qualitative results demonstrate that the proposed method performs favorably against existing methods on weakly-supervised audio-visual video parsing.

paragraphs: Audio-visual video parsing identifies when different audible or visible events occur within a video. Providing detailed temporal labels for both sound and imagery is labor-intensive. This paper instead learns with annotations attached to whole videos, seeking additional supervisory information in relationships between videos and between their audio and visual streams.

Across videos, the method uses both shared event meanings and differences in event content to help identify what is audible or visible. Across modalities, it examines event co-occurrence in audio, visual, and combined audio-visual streams. These co-occurrence signals help locate segments containing a target event while excluding segments that are irrelevant. Both kinds of relationships provide guidance beyond the coarse video-level labels.

Quantitative and qualitative evaluations show favorable performance relative to existing weakly supervised parsing methods. The result supports using structure already present across the training videos and modalities to improve temporal localization. Its practical significance lies in extracting more useful supervision from video-level annotations when detailed event-by-event timing labels are costly to obtain.
summary.tldr: Relationships across videos and audio-visual streams provide extra supervision for locating events using only video-level labels.

title: Exploring Cross-Video and Cross-Modality Signals for Weakly-Supervised Audio-Visual Video Parsing

abstract: Since Nesterov's seminal 1983 work, many accelerated first-order optimization methods have been proposed, but their analyses lacks a common unifying structure. In this work, we identify a geometric structure satisfied by a wide range of first-order accelerated methods. Using this geometric insight, we present several novel generalizations of accelerated methods. Most interesting among them is a method that reduces the squared gradient norm with $\mathcal{O}(1/K^4)$ rate in the prox-grad setup, faster than the $\mathcal{O}(1/K^3)$ rates of Nesterov's FGM or Kim and Fessler's FPGM-m.

This paper identifies a geometric structure shared by a wide range of accelerated methods. The contribution is a common way to understand how these methods work, alongside a basis for constructing additional algorithms.

The authors use that geometric insight to derive several generalizations of accelerated methods. Their highlighted result concerns making the squared gradient norm small in a proximal-gradient setting. This focuses on reducing the strength of the remaining local optimization signal, giving a specific measure by which the new method can be compared with existing accelerated approaches.

The proposed method achieves an O(1/K⁴) rate for that quantity, compared with O(1/K³) for Nesterov’s FGM and Kim and Fessler’s FPGM-m. The faster decay is the stated mathematical advantage in the specified setting. More broadly, the work shows how a shared geometric account can produce concrete algorithmic improvements, rather than serving only as a retrospective explanation of existing methods.
summary.tldr: A shared geometric structure of accelerated optimization yields a method with faster squared-gradient-norm decay in the proximal-gradient setting.

title: A Geometric Structure of Acceleration and Its Role in Making Gradients Small Fast

abstract: Vision transformer networks have shown superiority in many computer vision tasks. In this paper, we take a step further by proposing a novel generative vision transformer with latent variables following an informative energy-based prior for salient object detection. Both the vision transformer network and the energy-based prior model are jointly trained via Markov chain Monte Carlo-based maximum likelihood estimation, in which the sampling from the intractable posterior and prior distributions of the latent variables are performed by Langevin dynamics. Further, with the generative vision transformer, we can easily obtain a pixel-wise uncertainty map from an image, which indicates the model confidence in predicting saliency from the image. Different from the existing generative models which define the prior distribution of the latent variables as a simple isotropic Gaussian distribution, our model uses an energy-based informative prior which can be more expressive to capture the latent space of the data. We apply the proposed framework to both RGB and RGB-D salient object detection tasks. Extensive experimental results show that our framework can achieve not only accurate saliency predictions but also meaningful uncertainty maps that are consistent with the human perception.

The purpose of this prior is to describe the latent space more expressively than the simple isotropic Gaussian distributions used by the generative approaches discussed in the abstract.

The Transformer and prior are trained jointly through maximum likelihood estimation using Markov chain Monte Carlo. Because the latent prior and posterior are intractable, the method uses Langevin dynamics to perform the required sampling. The latent-variable formulation also allows the system to produce a confidence-related uncertainty value for each image pixel.

The authors apply the framework to both ordinary color images and images accompanied by depth information. Their experiments report accurate saliency predictions and meaningful uncertainty maps consistent with human perception. The contribution therefore combines object saliency estimation with an indication of where the model is less certain, supported by a more expressive learned distribution over its latent variables.
summary.tldr: A generative vision Transformer with a learned energy-based prior produces accurate saliency predictions and meaningful pixel-level uncertainty maps.

title: Learning Generative Vision Transformer with Energy-Based Latent Space for Saliency Prediction

abstract: Delusive attacks aim to substantially deteriorate the test accuracy of the learning model by slightly perturbing the features of correctly labeled training examples. By formalizing this malicious attack as finding the worst-case training data within a specific $\infty$-Wasserstein ball, we show that minimizing adversarial risk on the perturbed data is equivalent to optimizing an upper bound of natural risk on the original data. This implies that adversarial training can serve as a principled defense against delusive attacks. Thus, the test accuracy decreased by delusive attacks can be largely recovered by adversarial training. To further understand the internal mechanism of the defense, we disclose that adversarial training can resist the delusive perturbations by preventing the learner from overly relying on non-robust features in a natural setting. Finally, we complement our theoretical findings with a set of experiments on popular benchmark datasets, which show that the defense withstands six different practical attacks. Both theoretical and empirical results vote for adversarial training when confronted with delusive adversaries.

paragraphs: A delusive attack changes the features of training examples slightly while leaving their labels correct. Its goal is to make a learner perform poorly on ordinary test data. Because the labels remain intact, the damage comes from what the altered examples encourage the model to learn.

The paper formalizes the attacker as choosing worst-case training data within a particular infinity-Wasserstein ball, which constrains the permitted changes. Within this formulation, minimizing adversarial risk on the corrupted data is equivalent to optimizing an upper bound on ordinary risk for the original data. This relationship supplies a theoretical reason to use adversarial training as a defense.

The authors also examine how the defense works. In a natural setting, adversarial training can prevent excessive dependence on non-robust features that delusive perturbations exploit. Experiments on benchmark datasets show the defense withstanding six practical attacks and largely recovering the test accuracy lost to corruption. These findings support adversarial training for the studied threat, with the theoretical justification tied to the specified attack formulation.
summary.tldr: Adversarial training offers a theoretically motivated defense against small training-data perturbations designed to damage ordinary test accuracy.

title: Better Safe Than Sorry: Preventing Delusive Adversaries with Adversarial Training

abstract: The partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) provides a general framework for modeling an agent's decision process with state uncertainty, and online planning plays a pivotal role in solving it. A belief is a distribution of states representing state uncertainty. Methods for large-scale POMDP problems rely on the same idea of sampling both states and observations. That is, instead of exact belief updating, a collection of sampled states is used to approximate the belief; instead of considering all possible observations, only a set of sampled observations are considered. Inspired by this, we take one step further and propose an online planning algorithm, Adaptive Online Packing-guided Search (AdaOPS), to better approximate beliefs with adaptive particle filter technique and balance estimation bias and variance by fusing similar observation branches. Theoretically, our algorithm is guaranteed to find an $\epsilon$-optimal policy with a high probability given enough planning time under some mild assumptions. We evaluate our algorithm on several tricky POMDP domains, and it outperforms the state-of-the-art in all of them.

Inspired by this, we take one step further and propose an online planning algorithm, Adaptive Online Packing-guided Search (AdaOPS), to better approximate beliefs with adaptive particle filter technique and balance estimation bias and variance by fusing similar observation branches. paragraphs: Planning under partial observability means choosing actions without knowing the exact state of the world. A POMDP represents this uncertainty through a belief: a probability distribution over possible states. Large problems make exact belief updates and consideration of every possible observation difficult, so planning methods approximate both using samples.

AdaOPS improves this sampling-based approach in two connected ways. It uses an adaptive particle filter to improve the sampled representation of a belief. It also combines branches of the planning search associated with similar observations. Combining branches balances estimation bias and variance, addressing how the planner uses its limited samples as well as how it represents uncertainty.

The theoretical result is conditional: under assumptions described as mild, sufficient planning time gives a high probability of finding a policy within a specified tolerance of optimality. Experiments on several challenging POMDP domains report better performance than the state of the art in every tested domain. Together, these findings support adaptive belief approximation and observation grouping as useful components of online planning.
summary.tldr: AdaOPS improves planning under state uncertainty through adaptive belief sampling and merging similar observation branches.

title: Adaptive Online Packing-guided Search for POMDPs

abstract: Learning in the brain is poorly understood and learning rules that respect biological constraints, yet yield deep hierarchical representations, are still unknown. Here, we propose a learning rule that takes inspiration from neuroscience and recent advances in self-supervised deep learning. Learning minimizes a simple layer-specific loss function and does not need to back-propagate error signals within or between layers. Instead, weight updates follow a local, Hebbian, learning rule that only depends on pre- and post-synaptic neuronal activity, predictive dendritic input and widely broadcasted modulation factors which are identical for large groups of neurons. The learning rule applies contrastive predictive learning to a causal, biological setting using saccades (i.e. rapid shifts in gaze direction). We find that networks trained with this self-supervised and local rule build deep hierarchical representations of images, speech and video.

paragraphs: How the brain could learn deep, hierarchical representations remains poorly understood. This paper proposes a learning rule inspired by neuroscience and self-supervised learning. Each layer minimizes its own loss, without requiring error signals to be backpropagated either within that layer or between different layers.

Weight updates follow a local Hebbian rule. They depend on activity before and after a synaptic connection, predictive input to dendrites, and modulation factors broadcast identically to large groups of neurons. This specifies the information the proposed updates use, connecting the learning mechanism to biological constraints rather than requiring conventional error propagation through the network.

The method adapts contrastive predictive learning to a causal biological setting involving saccades, the rapid movements that shift gaze. Networks trained with the resulting local, self-supervised rule develop deep hierarchical representations of images, speech, and video. The findings demonstrate that this proposed learning mechanism can build such representations across the tested data types, contributing a candidate approach to biologically inspired deep learning.
summary.tldr: A biologically inspired local learning rule builds deep image, speech, and video representations without backpropagating errors within or between layers.

title: Local plasticity rules can learn deep representations using self-supervised contrastive predictions

abstract: With the development of machine learning techniques, the attention of research has been moved from single-modal learning to multi-modal learning, as real-world data exist in the form of different modalities. However, multi-modal models often carry more information than single-modal models and they are usually applied in sensitive scenarios, such as medical report generation or disease identification. Compared with the existing membership inference against machine learning classifiers, we focus on the problem that the input and output of the multi-modal models are in different modalities, such as image captioning. This work studies the privacy leakage of multi-modal models through the lens of membership inference attack, a process of determining whether a data record involves in the model training process or not. To achieve this, we propose Multi-modal Models Membership Inference (M$^4$I) with two attack methods to infer the membership status, named metric-based (MB) M$^4$I and feature-based (FB) M$^4$I, respectively. More specifically, MB M$^4$I adopts similarity metrics while attacking to infer target data membership. FB M$^4$I uses a pre-trained shadow multi-modal feature extractor to achieve the purpose of data inference attack by comparing the similarities from extracted input and output features. Extensive experimental results show that both attack methods can achieve strong performances. Respectively, 72.5% and 94.83% of attack success rates on average can be obtained under unrestricted scenarios. Moreover, we evaluate multiple defense mechanisms against our attacks. The source code of M$^4$I attacks is publicly available at https://github.com/MultimodalMI/Multimodal-membership-inference.git.

This paper studies that privacy question for multimodal systems whose inputs and outputs have different forms, such as image-captioning models. That setting differs from attacks on classifiers because the attacker must relate information across modalities rather than examine a conventional class prediction.

The proposed M4I framework contains two attacks. The metric-based version uses similarity measures to infer whether a target example belonged to the training data. The feature-based version uses a pretrained shadow multimodal feature extractor, comparing similarities between extracted input and output features. Both approaches use cross-modal relationships as evidence of membership.

The experiments report average attack success rates of 72.5% for the metric-based method and 94.83% for the feature-based method under unrestricted scenarios. Those conditions are part of the reported result, so the figures should be interpreted within that setting. The authors also evaluate multiple defenses. The work demonstrates a privacy risk associated with training-data membership in models that connect different types of information.
summary.tldr: Two M4I attacks use cross-modal similarities to infer training-data membership, achieving strong reported success under unrestricted scenarios.

title: M$^4$I: Multi-modal Models Membership Inference

abstract: This paper shows that masked generative adversarial network (MaskedGAN) is robust image generation learners with limited training data. The idea of MaskedGAN is simple: it randomly masks out certain image information for effective GAN training with limited data. We develop two masking strategies that work along orthogonal dimensions of training images, including a shifted spatial masking that masks the images in spatial dimensions with random shifts, and a balanced spectral masking that masks certain image spectral bands with self-adaptive probabilities. The two masking strategies complement each other which together encourage more challenging holistic learning from limited training data, ultimately suppressing trivial solutions and failures in GAN training. Albeit simple, extensive experiments show that MaskedGAN achieves superior performance consistently across different network architectures (e.g., CNNs including BigGAN and StyleGAN-v2 and Transformers including TransGAN and GANformer) and datasets (e.g., CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, 100-shot, AFHQ, FFHQ and Cityscapes).

paragraphs: Training an image-generating adversarial network with limited data can lead to trivial solutions and training failures. MaskedGAN addresses this by randomly hiding some image information during training. The purpose is to make learning from the available images more demanding and encourage attention to the image as a whole.

The method combines two complementary masking strategies. Shifted spatial masking removes information across spatial dimensions with random shifts. Balanced spectral masking removes selected spectral bands using probabilities that adapt during training. Because the strategies act on different dimensions of image information, their combination provides a broader learning challenge than either type of masking alone.

The experiments report consistently superior performance across the tested architectures and datasets. These include convolutional models such as BigGAN and StyleGAN-v2, transformer models such as TransGAN and GANformer, and datasets ranging from CIFAR and ImageNet to faces and street scenes. The results support masking as a broadly applicable training intervention for the limited-data generation settings examined.
summary.tldr: MaskedGAN improves image generation with limited data by combining spatial and spectral masking during adversarial training.

title: Masked Generative Adversarial Networks are Data-Efficient Generation Learners

abstract: In many contexts, simpler models are preferable to more complex models and the control of this model complexity is the goal for many methods in machine learning such as regularization, hyperparameter tuning and architecture design. In deep learning, it has been difficult to understand the underlying mechanisms of complexity control, since many traditional measures are not naturally suitable for deep neural networks. Here we develop the notion of geometric complexity, which is a measure of the variability of the model function, computed using a discrete Dirichlet energy. Using a combination of theoretical arguments and empirical results, we show that many common training heuristics such as parameter norm regularization, spectral norm regularization, flatness regularization, implicit gradient regularization, noise regularization and the choice of parameter initialization all act to control geometric complexity, providing a unifying framework in which to characterize the behavior of deep learning models.

paragraphs: Many machine learning techniques aim to keep models simple, but traditional measures of complexity do not fit deep neural networks naturally. This paper develops geometric complexity as a way to describe variability in the function a network represents. It measures complexity using a discrete Dirichlet energy, placing attention on the model's functional behavior.

The authors combine theoretical arguments with empirical results to examine how common training choices affect this measure. They consider parameter-norm and spectral-norm regularization, flatness regularization, implicit gradient regularization, noise regularization, and parameter initialization. Their analysis shows that these different mechanisms all act to control geometric complexity.

The significance is a shared framework for interpreting methods that otherwise appear to constrain different aspects of learning. Weight restrictions, noise, initialization, and properties of the optimization process can all be examined through their influence on function variability. This provides a way to characterize complexity control in deep learning and connect familiar training heuristics to a common notion of simplicity.
summary.tldr: Geometric complexity provides a common measure through which several regularization methods and training choices control neural-network function variability.

title: Why neural networks find simple solutions: The many regularizers of geometric complexity

abstract: As modern machine learning models continue to advance the computational frontier, it has become increasingly important to develop precise estimates for expected performance improvements under different model and data scaling regimes. Currently, theoretical understanding of the learning curves that characterize how the prediction error depends on the number of samples is restricted to either large-sample asymptotics ($m\to\infty$) or, for certain simple data distributions, to the high-dimensional asymptotics in which the number of samples scales linearly with the dimension ($m\propto d$). There is a wide gulf between these two regimes, including all higher-order scaling relations $m\propto d^r$, which are the subject of the present paper. We focus on the problem of kernel ridge regression for dot-product kernels and present precise formulas for the mean of the test error, bias, and variance, for data drawn uniformly from the sphere with isotropic random labels in the $r$th-order asymptotic scaling regime $m\to\infty$ with $m/d^r$ held constant. We observe a peak in the learning curve whenever $m \approx d^r/r!$ for any integer $r$, leading to multiple sample-wise descent and nontrivial behavior at multiple scales. We include a colab notebook that reproduces the essential results of the paper.
originalAbstract: As modern machine learning models continue to advance the computational frontier, it has become increasingly important to develop precise estimates for expected performance improvements under different model and data scaling regimes. Currently, theoretical understanding of the learning curves that characterize how the prediction error depends on the number of samples is restricted to either large-sample asymptotics ($m\to\infty$) or, for certain simple data distributions, to the high-dimensional asymptotics in which the number of samples scales linearly with the dimension ($m\propto d$). There is a wide gulf between these two regimes, including all higher-order scaling relations $m\propto d^r$, which are the subject of the present paper. We focus on the problem of kernel ridge regression for dot-product kernels and present precise formulas for the mean of the test error, bias, and variance, for data drawn uniformly from the sphere with isotropic random labels in the $r$th-order asymptotic scaling regime $m\to\infty$ with $m/d^r$ held constant. We observe a peak in the learning curve whenever $m \approx d^r/r!$ for any integer $r$, leading to multiple sample-wise descent and nontrivial behavior at multiple scales. We include a colab notebook that reproduces the essential results of the paper.

paragraphs: Learning curves describe how prediction error changes as more training examples become available. This paper investigates kernel ridge regression in scaling regimes between familiar large-sample analyses and high-dimensional analyses where sample count grows linearly with dimension. It considers higher-order relationships in which the sample count grows like an integer power of dimension.

For dot-product kernels, the authors derive precise formulas for average test error, bias, and variance. Their setting assumes inputs drawn uniformly from a sphere and isotropic random labels. The asymptotic analysis lets the sample count grow while holding its ratio to the rth power of dimension constant, making each order of scaling a distinct regime to study.

The resulting learning curves have a peak near a sample count of d^r / r! for each integer order r. This produces multiple episodes of descent as the number of samples increases, with nontrivial behavior at several scales. Within the stated distributional and scaling assumptions, the formulas give a more detailed account of performance changes than a single linear relationship between sample count and dimension can provide.
summary.tldr: Precise kernel regression formulas reveal repeated learning-curve peaks when sample counts scale as successive powers of input dimension.

title: Precise Learning Curves and Higher-Order Scalings for Dot-product Kernel Regression

abstract: Curriculum Reinforcement Learning (CRL) aims to create a sequence of tasks, starting from easy ones and gradually learning towards difficult tasks. In this work, we focus on the idea of framing CRL as interpolations between a source (auxiliary) and a target task distribution. Although existing studies have shown the great potential of this idea, it remains unclear how to formally quantify and generate the movement between task distributions. Inspired by the insights from gradual domain adaptation in semi-supervised learning, we create a natural curriculum by breaking down the potentially large task distributional shift in CRL into smaller shifts. We propose GRADIENT which formulates CRL as an optimal transport problem with a tailored distance metric between tasks. Specifically, we generate a sequence of task distributions as a geodesic interpolation between the source and target distributions, which are actually the Wasserstein barycenter. Different from many existing methods, our algorithm considers a task-dependent contextual distance metric and is capable of handling nonparametric distributions in both continuous and discrete context settings. In addition, we theoretically show that GRADIENT enables smooth transfer between subsequent stages in the curriculum under certain conditions. We conduct extensive experiments in locomotion and manipulation tasks and show that our proposed GRADIENT achieves higher performance than baselines in terms of learning efficiency and asymptotic performance.

paragraphs: Curriculum reinforcement learning trains an agent through a sequence of tasks that moves toward a difficult target. This paper asks how to define that progression when the starting and target tasks are distributions rather than single tasks. Its guiding idea is to divide a potentially large distribution shift into smaller, more manageable stages.

The proposed method, GRADIENT, formulates curriculum construction as an optimal transport problem. It uses a contextual distance that depends on the tasks and builds intermediate distributions through geodesic interpolation, expressed using Wasserstein barycenters. This gives the progression a mathematical structure: each stage occupies an intermediate position between the source and target under the chosen task distance.

The authors prove smooth transfer between successive stages under specified conditions, so that guarantee is conditional rather than automatic for every curriculum. In locomotion and manipulation experiments, the method improves both learning efficiency and eventual performance relative to the evaluated baselines. The contribution connects a principled way of measuring task movement with a practical procedure for generating training stages.
summary.tldr: GRADIENT constructs reinforcement learning curricula through optimal transport between task distributions, with conditional transfer guarantees and improved experimental performance.

title: Curriculum Reinforcement Learning using Optimal Transport via Gradual Domain Adaptation

abstract: Although Vision transformers (ViTs) have recently dominated many vision tasks, deploying ViT models on resource-limited devices remains a challenging problem. To address such a challenge, several methods have been proposed to compress ViTs. Most of them borrow experience in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and mainly focus on the spatial domain. However, the compression only in the spatial domain suffers from a dramatic performance drop without fine-tuning and is not robust to noise, as the noise in the spatial domain can easily confuse the pruning criteria, leading to some parameters/channels being pruned incorrectly. Inspired by recent findings that self-attention is a low-pass filter and low-frequency signals/components are more informative to ViTs, this paper proposes compressing ViTs with low-frequency components. Two metrics named low-frequency sensitivity (LFS) and low-frequency energy (LFE) are proposed for better channel pruning and token pruning. Additionally, a bottom-up cascade pruning scheme is applied to compress different dimensions jointly. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method could save 40% ～ 60% of the FLOPs in ViTs, thus significantly increasing the throughput on practical devices with less than 1% performance drop on ImageNet-1K.

paragraphs: Vision transformers can be costly to deploy on devices with limited resources. Existing compression approaches often select what to remove using spatial information, but the authors identify sensitivity to noise and substantial performance loss without fine-tuning as problems with this strategy. Their alternative uses low-frequency components to guide compression decisions.

The approach is motivated by findings that self-attention behaves as a low-pass filter and that low-frequency information is particularly informative for vision transformers. It introduces two measures, low-frequency sensitivity and low-frequency energy, to improve channel and token pruning. It also substantially improves throughput on practical devices. These results support frequency-informed pruning as an effective compression strategy in the evaluated setting. The computational savings and measured device throughput together connect the pruning method to its intended deployment benefit.
summary.tldr: Low-frequency-guided pruning reduces vision transformer computation by 40–60% with less than a 1% reported performance drop on ImageNet-1K.

title: VTC-LFC: Vision Transformer Compression with Low-Frequency Components

abstract: Progress in reinforcement learning (RL) research is often driven by the design of new, challenging environments---a costly undertaking requiring skills orthogonal to that of a typical machine learning researcher. The complexity of environment development has only increased with the rise of procedural-content generation (PCG) as the prevailing paradigm for producing varied environments capable of testing the robustness and generalization of RL agents. Moreover, existing environments often require complex build processes, making reproducing results difficult. To address these issues, we introduce GriddlyJS, a web-based Integrated Development Environment (IDE) based on the Griddly engine. GriddlyJS allows researchers to easily design and debug arbitrary, complex PCG grid-world environments, as well as visualize, evaluate, and record the performance of trained agent models. By connecting the RL workflow to the advanced functionality enabled by modern web standards, GriddlyJS allows publishing interactive agent-environment demos that reproduce experimental results directly to the web. To demonstrate the versatility of GriddlyJS, we use it to quickly develop a complex compositional puzzle-solving environment alongside arbitrary human-designed environment configurations and their solutions for use in a automatic curriculum learning and offline RL context. The GriddlyJS IDE is open source and freely available at https://griddly.ai.

paragraphs: Creating useful reinforcement-learning environments requires substantial engineering work beyond designing learning algorithms. Procedural generation adds further complexity because environments must produce varied situations for testing robustness and generalization. GriddlyJS addresses this development burden with a browser-based environment built on the Griddly engine.

The tool supports designing and debugging complex grid-world environments with procedural content. Researchers can also visualize, evaluate, and record trained agents within the same workflow. Its use of web capabilities makes it possible to publish interactive demonstrations that reproduce experimental results directly in a browser, addressing difficulties associated with complex environment build processes.

The contribution is an open-source environment-development and demonstration workflow, with the puzzle task illustrating its versatility. By connecting environment construction, agent inspection, and interactive publication, GriddlyJS aims to make the supporting infrastructure of reinforcement-learning research easier to create and share.
summary.tldr: GriddlyJS provides browser-based tools for building reinforcement-learning grid worlds, evaluating agents, and sharing interactive experimental demonstrations.

title: GriddlyJS: A Web IDE for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The online Frank-Wolfe (OFW) method has gained much popularity for online convex optimization due to its projection-free property. Previous studies show that OFW can attain an $O(T^{3/4})$ regret bound for convex losses and an $O(T^{2/3})$ regret bound for strongly convex losses. However, they assume that each gradient queried by OFW is revealed immediately, which may not hold in practice and limits the application of OFW. To address this limitation, we propose a delayed variant of OFW, which allows gradients to be delayed by arbitrary rounds. The main idea is to perform an update similar to OFW after receiving any delayed gradient, and play the latest decision for each round. Despite its simplicity, we prove that our delayed variant of OFW is able to achieve an $O(T^{3/4}+dT^{1/4})$ regret bound for convex losses and an $O(T^{2/3}+d\log T)$ regret bound for strongly convex losses, where $d$ is the maximum delay. This is quite surprising since under a relatively large amount of delay (e.g., $d=O(\sqrt{T})$ for convex losses and $d=O(T^{2/3}/\log T)$ for strongly convex losses), the delayed variant of OFW enjoys the same regret bound as that of the original OFW.

paragraphs: Online Frank–Wolfe is useful for sequential convex optimization because it avoids projection operations. Existing guarantees assumed that each requested gradient arrived immediately. This paper removes that timing requirement by allowing gradients to arrive after arbitrary numbers of rounds, addressing a setting where decisions must continue while some feedback remains unavailable.

The proposed algorithm performs a Frank–Wolfe-style update whenever a delayed gradient arrives and uses its latest decision in each round. Its regret bound is O(T^(3/4) + dT^(1/4)) for convex losses and O(T^(2/3) + d log T) for strongly convex losses, where T is the horizon and d is the maximum delay.

These bounds make the cost of delay explicit. For convex losses, delays of order √T still preserve the original regret order. For strongly convex losses, the corresponding threshold is order T^(2/3)/log T. The result shows that relatively substantial delays can be tolerated without changing the asymptotic regret rate, provided they stay within the stated ranges. A simple update rule therefore retains meaningful guarantees under delayed feedback.
summary.tldr: A delayed Online Frank–Wolfe variant preserves the original regret order for substantial, explicitly bounded feedback delays.

title: Online Frank-Wolfe with Arbitrary Delays

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is a critical task for ensuring the reliability and safety of deep neural networks in real-world scenarios. Different from most previous OOD detection methods that focus on designing OOD scores or introducing diverse outlier examples to retrain the model, we delve into the obstacle factors in OOD detection from the perspective of typicality and regard the feature's high-probability region of the deep model as the feature's typical set. We propose to rectify the feature into its typical set and calculate the OOD score with the typical features to achieve reliable uncertainty estimation. The feature rectification can be conducted as a plug-and-play module with various OOD scores. We evaluate the superiority of our method on both the commonly used benchmark (CIFAR) and the more challenging high-resolution benchmark with large label space (ImageNet). Notably, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods by up to 5.11% in the average FPR95 on the ImageNet benchmark.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input falls outside the data a model is expected to handle. This paper examines the internal features used to make that judgment. Its starting point is typicality: the authors identify a feature’s typical set with a high-probability region of the model’s feature distribution.

Their method rectifies features into these typical sets before computing an out-of-distribution score. This changes the representation supplied to the scoring procedure and is intended to improve uncertainty estimation. The rectification can be attached as a plug-and-play module to different scoring methods, giving it a role across multiple existing detection approaches.

Evaluations cover CIFAR and the higher-resolution ImageNet benchmark with its larger label space. On ImageNet, the paper reports improvements over state-of-the-art methods of up to 5.11% in average FPR95. The stated result supports feature rectification as a useful component of detection on these benchmarks; the maximum improvement should be understood as the reported best extent of the gain.
summary.tldr: Rectifying internal features into high-probability regions improves out-of-distribution detection with multiple scoring methods.

title: Boosting Out-of-distribution Detection with Typical Features

abstract: Recent advances in deep learning optimization showed that, with some a-posteriori information on fully-trained models, it is possible to match the same performance by simply training a subset of their parameters. Such a discovery has a broad impact from theory to applications, driving the research towards methods to identify the minimum subset of parameters to train without look-ahead information exploitation. However, the methods proposed do not match the state-of-the-art performance, and rely on unstructured sparsely connected models.In this work we shift our focus from the single parameters to the behavior of the whole neuron, exploiting the concept of neuronal equilibrium (NEq). When a neuron is in a configuration at equilibrium (meaning that it has learned a specific input-output relationship), we can halt its update; on the contrary, when a neuron is at non-equilibrium, we let its state evolve towards an equilibrium state, updating its parameters. The proposed approach has been tested on different state-of-the-art learning strategies and tasks, validating NEq and observing that the neuronal equilibrium depends on the specific learning setup.

paragraphs: Prior work suggests that training only some network parameters can match full-training performance when information from an already trained model is available. The harder question is how to decide what to train without that look-ahead information. This paper approaches the decision at the level of entire neurons.

The proposed criterion is neuronal equilibrium. A neuron is considered at equilibrium when it has learned a particular input-output relationship, and its updates can then be halted. A neuron that has not reached equilibrium continues to have its parameters updated. This makes the neuron's learned behavior the basis for deciding whether further change is needed.

The authors test the approach across different state-of-the-art learning strategies and tasks, reporting evidence that validates the equilibrium concept. They also observe that neuronal equilibrium depends on the learning setup. That finding matters for interpreting the method: whether a neuron should keep updating is connected to the particular training process, rather than being a fixed property shared across all uses of the neuron.
summary.tldr: The paper uses neuronal equilibrium to decide when to halt or continue neuron updates, finding that equilibrium depends on the learning setup.

title: To update or not to update? Neurons at equilibrium in deep models

abstract: Graph neural network (GNN) is a promising approach to learning and predicting physical phenomena described in boundary value problems, such as partial differential equations (PDEs) with boundary conditions. However, existing models inadequately treat boundary conditions essential for the reliable prediction of such problems. In addition, because of the locally connected nature of GNNs, it is difficult to accurately predict the state after a long time, where interaction between vertices tends to be global. We present our approach termed physics-embedded neural networks that considers boundary conditions and predicts the state after a long time using an implicit method. It is built based on an $\mathrm{E}(n)$-equivariant GNN, resulting in high generalization performance on various shapes. We demonstrate that our model learns flow phenomena in complex shapes and outperforms a well-optimized classical solver and a state-of-the-art machine learning model in speed-accuracy trade-off. Therefore, our model can be a useful standard for realizing reliable, fast, and accurate GNN-based PDE solvers. The code is available at https://github.com/yellowshippo/penn-neurips2022.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can learn physical behaviour described by partial differential equations, but reliable prediction requires handling boundary conditions properly. A second difficulty arises over long time intervals: physical interactions can become global even though graph networks typically exchange information locally. This paper addresses both issues in a learned PDE solver.

The proposed physics-embedded neural network incorporates boundary conditions and uses an implicit method to predict states farther into the future. It is built on an E(n)-equivariant graph neural network, connecting the architecture to geometric structure. The authors report that this design supports strong generalisation across different shapes, which matters for physical problems posed on varying computational domains.

Experiments show the model learning flow phenomena in complex geometries. In the reported comparisons, it offers a better balance of speed and accuracy than both a well-optimised classical solver and a state-of-the-art machine learning model. The result supports combining boundary-condition handling, implicit prediction, and geometric structure as a route toward reliable graph-based solvers in the tested flow settings.
summary.tldr: Physics-embedded graph networks combine boundary-condition handling and implicit prediction to improve the speed–accuracy tradeoff for learned flow simulation.

title: Physics-Embedded Neural Networks: Graph Neural PDE Solvers with Mixed Boundary Conditions

abstract: We study the problem of learning an adversarially robust predictor to test time attacks in the semi-supervised PAC model.We address the question of how many labeled and unlabeled examples are required to ensure learning.We show that having enough unlabeled data (the size of a labeled sample that a fully-supervised method would require),the labeled sample complexity can be arbitrarily smaller compared to previous works, and is sharply characterized by a different complexity measure. We prove nearly matching upper and lower bounds on this sample complexity.This shows that there is a significant benefit in semi-supervised robust learning even in the worst-case distribution-free model, and establishes a gap between supervised and semi-supervised label complexities which is known not to hold in standard non-robust PAC learning.

We prove nearly matching upper and lower bounds on this sample complexity.This shows that there is a significant benefit in semi-supervised robust learning even in the worst-case distribution-free model, and establishes a gap between supervised and semi-supervised label complexities which is known not to hold in standard non-robust PAC learning.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much labeled and unlabeled data is needed to learn a predictor that withstands adversarial attacks at test time. It studies this question in the semi-supervised PAC framework, where learning guarantees must hold across data distributions. The central issue is whether unlabeled examples can substantially reduce the need for labels when robustness is part of the learning objective.

The authors show that they can, provided enough unlabeled examples are available. The required unlabeled sample is as large as the labeled sample needed by a fully supervised method. Under that condition, the labeled sample requirement can be arbitrarily smaller than in previous work. A different complexity measure characterizes this requirement, with upper and lower bounds that nearly match.

The result establishes a separation between supervised and semi-supervised robust learning even under worst-case, distribution-free analysis. This matters because the corresponding separation does not hold in ordinary, non-robust PAC learning. The benefit is specifically a reduction in required labels under the stated unlabeled-data condition.
summary.tldr: With enough unlabeled data, adversarially robust learning can require arbitrarily fewer labels, with nearly matching theoretical bounds.

title: A Characterization of Semi-Supervised Adversarially Robust PAC Learnability

abstract: Graph-level anomaly detection aims to distinguish anomalous graphs in a graph dataset from normal graphs. Anomalous graphs represent a very few but essential patterns in the real world. The anomalous property of a graph may be referable to its anomalous attributes of particular nodes and anomalous substructures that refer to a subset of nodes and edges in the graph. In addition, due to the imbalance nature of anomaly problem, anomalous information will be diluted by normal graphs with overwhelming quantities. Various anomaly notions in the attributes and/or substructures and the imbalance nature together make detecting anomalous graphs a non-trivial task. In this paper, we propose a graph neural network for graph-level anomaly detection, namely iGAD. Specifically, an anomalous graph attribute-aware graph convolution and an anomalous graph substructure-aware deep Random Walk Kernel (deep RWK) are welded into a graph neural network to achieve the dual-discriminative ability on anomalous attributes and substructures. Deep RWK in iGAD makes up for the deficiency of graph convolution in distinguishing structural information caused by the simple neighborhood aggregation mechanism. Further, we propose a Point Mutual Information (PMI)-based loss function to target the problems caused by imbalance distributions. PMI-based loss function enables iGAD to capture essential correlation between input graphs and their anomalous/normal properties. We evaluate iGAD on four real-world graph datasets. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of iGAD on the graph-level anomaly detection task.

paragraphs: Detecting an anomalous graph requires recognizing unusual information that may appear in node attributes or in patterns of connected nodes and edges. The task becomes harder when normal graphs vastly outnumber anomalous ones, because rare signals can be diluted. This paper designs iGAD to address both the different forms of abnormality and the imbalance in their frequency.

The network combines an attribute-aware graph convolution with a deep Random Walk Kernel that focuses on anomalous substructures. The latter supplements the structural distinctions available through simple neighborhood aggregation. These components give the model complementary ways to distinguish graphs, covering unusual attributes as well as unusual arrangements of nodes and edges.

A loss based on point mutual information targets the imbalance problem by capturing associations between input graphs and their normal or anomalous status. Evaluations on four real-world graph datasets report superior anomaly-detection performance. The stated findings support combining specialized structural and attribute processing with an objective designed for rare anomalies, rather than treating representation and imbalance as unrelated concerns.
summary.tldr: iGAD combines attribute and substructure detection with an imbalance-aware loss to identify anomalous graphs.

title: Dual-discriminative Graph Neural Network for Imbalanced Graph-level Anomaly Detection

abstract: The recent progress in implicit 3D representation, i.e., Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs), has made accurate and photorealistic 3D reconstruction possible in a differentiable manner. This new representation can effectively convey the information of hundreds of high-resolution images in one compact format and allows photorealistic synthesis of novel views. In this work, using the variant of NeRF called Plenoxels, we create the first large-scale radiance fields datasets for perception tasks, called the PeRFception, which consists of two parts that incorporate both object-centric and scene-centric scans for classification and segmentation. It shows a significant memory compression rate (96.4\%) from the original dataset, while containing both 2D and 3D information in a unified form. We construct the classification and segmentation models that directly take this radiance fields format as input and also propose a novel augmentation technique to avoid overfitting on backgrounds of images. The code and data are publicly available in "https://postech-cvlab.github.io/PeRFception/".

The code and data are publicly available in "https://postech-cvlab.github.io/PeRFception/".

PeRFception explores using that representation directly for perception tasks. Instead of treating reconstructed scenes only as a way to render images, the paper makes radiance fields the input format for classification and segmentation.

Using Plenoxels, a variant of neural radiance fields, the authors construct large-scale datasets containing both object-centered and scene-centered scans. The format combines two-dimensional appearance and three-dimensional information in one representation. They report a 96.4% memory compression rate relative to the original dataset, demonstrating that this change in representation can substantially reduce storage requirements.

The authors build classification and segmentation models that consume the radiance fields directly. They also propose an augmentation technique intended to prevent models from overfitting to image backgrounds. The resulting contribution combines a data resource, a compact representation, and perception models built around that representation. It establishes a route for studying recognition and segmentation using reconstructed radiance fields, with the code and data made publicly available.
summary.tldr: PeRFception provides compact radiance-field datasets and models that use them directly for classification and segmentation.

title: PeRFception: Perception using Radiance Fields

abstract: We study the problem of rank aggregation where the goal is to obtain a global ranking by aggregating pair-wise comparisons of voters over a set of items. We consider an adversarial setting where the voters are partitioned into two sets. The first set votes in a stochastic manner according to the popular score-based Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) model for pairwise comparisons. The second set comprises malicious Byzantine voters trying to deteriorate the ranking. We consider a strongly-adversarial scenario where the Byzantine voters know the BTL scores, the votes of the good voters, the algorithm, and can collude with each other. We first show that the popular spectral ranking based Rank-Centrality algorithm, though optimal for the BTL model, does not perform well even when a small constant fraction of the voters are Byzantine.We introduce the Byzantine Spectral Ranking Algorithm (and a faster variant of it), which produces a reliable ranking when the number of good voters exceeds the number of Byzantine voters. We show that no algorithm can produce a satisfactory ranking with probability > 1/2 for all BTL weights when there are more Byzantine voters than good voters, showing that our algorithm works for all possible population fractions. We support our theoretical results with experimental results on synthetic and real datasets to demonstrate the failure of the Rank-Centrality algorithm under several adversarial scenarios and how the proposed Byzantine Spectral Ranking algorithm is robust in obtaining good rankings.

summary.tldr: Byzantine Spectral Ranking reliably aggregates adversarial pairwise votes when honest voters form a majority.

title: Byzantine Spectral Ranking

abstract: The usage of automated learning agents is becoming increasingly prevalent in many online economic applications such as online auctions and automated trading. Motivated by such applications, this paper is dedicated to fundamental modeling and analysis of the strategic situations that the users of automated learning agents are facing. We consider strategic settings where several users engage in a repeated online interaction, assisted by regret-minimizing learning agents that repeatedly play a "game" on their behalf. We propose to view the outcomes of the agents' dynamics as inducing a "meta-game" between the users. Our main focus is on whether users can benefit in this meta-game from "manipulating" their own agents by misreporting their parameters to them. We define a general framework to model and analyze these strategic interactions between users of learning agents for general games and analyze the equilibria induced between the users in three classes of games. We show that, generally, users have incentives to misreport their parameters to their own agents, and that such strategic user behavior can lead to very different outcomes than those anticipated by standard analysis.

paragraphs: When automated agents act for people in repeated economic interactions, the people themselves remain strategic participants. This paper asks whether a user can benefit by giving their own learning agent inaccurate parameters. The setting involves multiple users whose regret-minimizing agents repeatedly play a game on their behalf.

The authors treat the outcomes of the agents' learning dynamics as defining a second game among the users. In this meta-game, a user's choice includes what information to report to their agent, and the consequences depend on how the agents subsequently interact. This shifts attention from the agents' behavior alone to the incentives of the people configuring them.

The paper develops a general modeling framework and analyzes the resulting user equilibria in three classes of games. It shows that users generally have incentives to misreport their parameters, and that these strategic choices can substantially change outcomes relative to standard analysis. The finding makes user reporting behavior part of the economic system that needs to be analyzed.
summary.tldr: Users of regret-minimizing agents can have incentives to misreport their own parameters, changing the outcomes predicted by standard agent-level analysis.

title: How and Why to Manipulate Your Own Agent: On the Incentives of Users of Learning Agents

abstract: Historically, conditional random fields (CRFs) were popular tools in a variety of application areas from computer vision to natural language processing, but due to their higher computational cost and weaker practical performance, they have, in many situations, fallen out of favor and been replaced by end-to-end deep neural network (DNN) solutions. More recently, combined DNN-CRF approaches have been considered, but their speed and practical performance still falls short of the best performing pure DNN solutions. In this work, we present a generic combined approach in which a log-supermodular CRF acts as a regularizer to encourage similarity between outputs in a structured prediction task. We show that this combined approach is widely applicable, practical (it incurs only a moderate overhead on top of the base DNN solution) and, in some cases, it can rival carefully engineered pure DNN solutions for the same structured prediction task.

paragraphs: Structured prediction involves producing outputs whose parts are related, making their agreement useful information for a model. Conditional random fields provide a way to represent such relationships, but their computational cost and practical performance have often made standalone deep networks more attractive. Earlier combinations of the two have also struggled to match strong neural approaches.

This paper proposes a generic combination in which a log-supermodular conditional random field serves as a regularizer for a deep network. Its role is to encourage similarity between outputs within the structured prediction task. The approach therefore adds an explicit preference for coordinated predictions to the underlying neural solution.

The authors report that this combination applies broadly and adds only moderate computational overhead to the base network. In some cases, it can match carefully engineered approaches built entirely from deep networks. That qualification is central: the finding supports a practical way to improve generic frameworks, rather than establishing that adding this regularizer always beats specialized architectures. Its contribution is making structured output relationships useful at a manageable additional cost.
summary.tldr: A log-supermodular CRF regularizer encourages coordinated neural predictions with moderate overhead and can rival specialized deep networks in some cases.

title: Boosting the Performance of Generic Deep Neural Network Frameworks with Log-supermodular CRFs

abstract: Language model (LM) pre-training is useful in many language processing tasks. But can pre-trained LMs be further leveraged for more general machine learning problems? We propose an approach for using LMs to scaffold learning and generalization in general sequential decision-making problems. In this approach, goals and observations are represented as a sequence of embeddings, and a policy network initialized with a pre-trained LM predicts the next action. We demonstrate that this framework enables effective combinatorial generalization across different environments and supervisory modalities. We begin by assuming access to a set of expert demonstrations, and show that initializing policies with LMs and fine-tuning them via behavior cloning improves task completion rates by 43.6% in the VirtualHome environment. Next, we integrate an active data gathering procedure in which agents iteratively interact with the environment, relabel past "failed" experiences with new goals, and update their policies in a self-supervised loop. Active data gathering further improves combinatorial generalization, outperforming the best baseline by 25.1%. Finally, we explain these results by investigating three possible factors underlying the effectiveness of the LM-based policy. We find that sequential input representations (vs. fixed-dimensional feature vectors) and LM-based weight initialization are both important for generalization. Surprisingly, however, the format of the policy inputs encoding (e.g. as a natural language string vs. an arbitrary sequential encoding) has little influence. Together, these results suggest that language modeling induces representations that are useful for modeling not just language, but also goals and plans; these representations can aid learning and generalization even outside of language processing.

title: Pre-Trained Language Models for Interactive Decision-Making

abstract: In deep reinforcement learning (RL), data augmentation is widely considered as a tool to induce a set of useful priors about semantic consistency and improve sample efficiency and generalization performance. However, even when the prior is useful for generalization, distilling it to RL agent often interferes with RL training and degenerates sample efficiency. Meanwhile, the agent is forgetful of the prior due to the non-stationary nature of RL. These observations suggest two extreme schedules of distillation: (i) over the entire training; or (ii) only at the end. Hence, we devise a stand-alone network distillation method to inject the consistency prior at any time (even after RL), and a simple yet efficient framework to automatically schedule the distillation. Specifically, the proposed framework first focuses on mastering train environments regardless of generalization by adaptively deciding which {\it or no} augmentation to be used for the training. After this, we add the distillation to extract the remaining benefits for generalization from all the augmentations, which requires no additional new samples. In our experiments, we demonstrate the utility of the proposed framework, in particular, that considers postponing the augmentation to the end of RL training.
