paragraphs: Data augmentation encourages a reinforcement learning agent to treat certain transformed observations consistently. That can support generalization, but the paper observes that teaching this consistency during reinforcement learning can interfere with training and reduce sample efficiency. Because learning conditions change over time, an agent can also forget an earlier consistency prior.

The authors develop a separate network-distillation method that can inject the prior at different times, including after reinforcement learning finishes. Their scheduling framework first emphasizes success in the training environments. It adaptively chooses which augmentation to use, with the option to use none, rather than requiring a fixed augmentation throughout training.

Afterward, distillation draws remaining generalization benefits from all the augmentations without collecting additional samples. Experiments demonstrate the utility of this framework, particularly its ability to postpone augmentation until the end of reinforcement learning. The central implication is that when an agent learns an augmentation-induced prior matters alongside which augmentation is chosen: useful consistency information can still disrupt learning if introduced at an unsuitable time.
summary.tldr: Adaptive augmentation scheduling and later distillation help separate reinforcement learning progress from learning consistency priors for generalization.

title: Efficient Scheduling of Data Augmentation for Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The leap in performance in state-of-the-art computer vision methods is attributed to the development of deep neural networks. However it often comes at a computational price which may hinder their deployment. To alleviate this limitation, structured pruning is a well known technique which consists in removing channels, neurons or filters, and is commonly applied in order to produce more compact models. In most cases, the computations to remove are selected based on a relative importance criterion. At the same time, the need for explainable predictive models has risen tremendously and motivated the development of robust attribution methods that highlight the relative importance of pixels of an input image or feature map. In this work, we discuss the limitations of existing pruning heuristics, among which magnitude and gradient-based methods. We draw inspiration from attribution methods to design a novel integrated gradient pruning criterion, in which the relevance of each neuron is defined as the integral of the gradient variation on a path towards this neuron removal. Furthermore, We propose an entwined DNN pruning and fine-tuning flowchart to better preserve DNN accuracy while removing parameters. We show through extensive validation on several datasets, architectures as well as pruning scenarios that the proposed method, dubbed SInGE, significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art DNN pruning methods.

paragraphs: Deep vision networks can be costly to run, motivating structured pruning: removing whole neurons, channels, or filters to make a model smaller. The central decision is which components can be removed while preserving predictive accuracy. This paper examines limitations of common importance heuristics based on parameter magnitude or gradients and develops an alternative inspired by attribution methods.

SInGE measures a neuron’s relevance by integrating gradient variation along a path toward removing that neuron. This brings the attribution idea of examining a path of changes into the pruning decision. The criterion evaluates relevance in relation to the removal process, providing a different basis for selecting which computations to discard.

The authors also interleave pruning and fine-tuning so that parameter removal and accuracy preservation are handled together. Across multiple datasets, architectures, and pruning scenarios, they report significant improvements over existing leading pruning methods. The findings support using an attribution-inspired relevance measure together with an intertwined pruning and adaptation process to produce more compact networks while better preserving accuracy.
summary.tldr: SInGE combines an integrated-gradient neuron-relevance criterion with interleaved fine-tuning to improve structured network pruning.

title: SInGE: Sparsity via Integrated Gradients Estimation of Neuron Relevance

abstract: Recent studies have demonstrated that visual recognition models lack robustness to distribution shift. However, current work mainly considers model robustness to 2D image transformations, leaving viewpoint changes in the 3D world less explored. In general, viewpoint changes are prevalent in various real-world applications (e.g., autonomous driving), making it imperative to evaluate viewpoint robustness. In this paper, we propose a novel method called ViewFool to find adversarial viewpoints that mislead visual recognition models. By encoding real-world objects as neural radiance fields (NeRF), ViewFool characterizes a distribution of diverse adversarial viewpoints under an entropic regularizer, which helps to handle the fluctuations of the real camera pose and mitigate the reality gap between the real objects and their neural representations. Experiments validate that the common image classifiers are extremely vulnerable to the generated adversarial viewpoints, which also exhibit high cross-model transferability. Based on ViewFool, we introduce ImageNet-V, a new out-of-distribution dataset for benchmarking viewpoint robustness of image classifiers. Evaluation results on 40 classifiers with diverse architectures, objective functions, and data augmentations reveal a significant drop in model performance when tested on ImageNet-V, which provides a possibility to leverage ViewFool as an effective data augmentation strategy to improve viewpoint robustness.

Instead of producing only one problematic viewpoint, ViewFool characterizes a diverse distribution of them using an entropy-based regularizer. summary.tldr: ViewFool finds transferable adversarial camera viewpoints and introduces a benchmark exposing substantial viewpoint sensitivity across 40 classifiers.

title: ViewFool: Evaluating the Robustness of Visual Recognition to Adversarial Viewpoints

abstract: Algorithmic stability is an important notion that has proven powerful for deriving generalization bounds for practical algorithms. The last decade has witnessed an increasing number of stability bounds for different algorithms applied on different classes of loss functions. While these bounds have illuminated various properties of optimization algorithms, the analysis of each case typically required a different proof technique with significantly different mathematical tools. In this study, we make a novel connection between learning theory and applied probability and introduce a unified guideline for proving Wasserstein stability bounds for stochastic optimization algorithms. We illustrate our approach on stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and we obtain time-uniform stability bounds (i.e., the bound does not increase with the number of iterations) for strongly convex losses and non-convex losses with additive noise, where we recover similar results to the prior art or extend them to more general cases by using a single proof technique. Our approach is flexible and can be generalizable to other popular optimizers, as it mainly requires developing Lyapunov functions, which are often readily available in the literature. It also illustrates that ergodicity is an important component for obtaining time-uniform bounds -- which might not be achieved for convex or non-convex losses unless additional noise is injected to the iterates. Finally, we slightly stretch our analysis technique and prove time-uniform bounds for SGD under convex and non-convex losses (without additional additive noise), which, to our knowledge, is novel.

abstract: Timely outcome prediction is essential in healthcare to enable early detection and intervention of adverse events. However, in longitudinal follow-ups to patients' health status, cost-efficient acquisition of patient covariates is usually necessary due to the significant expense involved in screening and lab tests. To balance the timely and accurate outcome predictions with acquisition costs, an effective active sensing strategy is crucial. In this paper, we propose a novel risk-averse active sensing approach RAS that addresses the composite decision problem of when to conduct the acquisition and which measurements to make. Our approach decomposes the policy into two sub-policies: acquisition scheduler and feature selector, respectively. Moreover, we introduce a novel risk-aversion training strategy to focus on the underrepresented subgroup of high-risk patients for whom timely and accurate prediction of disease progression is of greater value. Our method outperforms baseline active sensing approaches in experiments with both synthetic and real-world datasets, and we illustrate the significance of our policy decomposition and the necessity of a risk-averse sensing policy through case studies.

paragraphs: Predicting a patient’s outcome early can support timely intervention, but repeated screening and laboratory measurements are expensive. Active sensing addresses this tension by deciding what information to collect and when. This paper focuses on balancing acquisition costs against prediction accuracy and timeliness during longitudinal patient follow-up.

The proposed approach, RAS, splits the decision into two sub-policies. An acquisition scheduler decides when to collect information, while a feature selector decides which measurements to obtain. A risk-averse training strategy gives attention to the underrepresented subgroup of high-risk patients, for whom accurate and timely prediction of disease progression has greater value.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show better performance than the compared active-sensing baselines. Case studies also illustrate the value of separating scheduling from feature selection and of explicitly considering high-risk patients. The contribution addresses both the structure of the sensing decision and the unequal importance of prediction quality across patient groups within a cost-constrained setting.
summary.tldr: RAS separates measurement timing from measurement selection and uses risk-averse training to prioritize timely predictions for underrepresented high-risk patients.

title: Risk-Averse Active Sensing for Timely Outcome Prediction under Cost Pressure

abstract: We first raise and tackle a ``time synchronization'' issue between the agent and the environment in non-stationary reinforcement learning (RL), a crucial factor hindering its real-world applications. In reality, environmental changes occur over wall-clock time ($t$) rather than episode progress ($k$), where wall-clock time signifies the actual elapsed time within the fixed duration $t \in [0, T]$. In existing works, at episode $k$, the agent rolls a trajectory and trains a policy before transitioning to episode $k+1$. In the context of the time-desynchronized environment, however, the agent at time $t_{k}$ allocates $\Delta t$ for trajectory generation and training, subsequently moves to the next episode at $t_{k+1}=t_{k}+\Delta t$. Despite a fixed total number of episodes ($K$), the agent accumulates different trajectories influenced by the choice of interaction times ($t_1,t_2,...,t_K$), significantly impacting the suboptimality gap of the policy. We propose a Proactively Synchronizing Tempo ($\texttt{ProST}$) framework that computes a suboptimal sequence {$t_1,t_2,...,t_K$} (= { $t_{1:K}$}) by minimizing an upper bound on its performance measure, i.e., the dynamic regret. Our main contribution is that we show that a suboptimal {$t_{1:K}$} trades-off between the policy training time (agent tempo) and how fast the environment changes (environment tempo). Theoretically, this work develops a suboptimal {$t_{1:K}$} as a function of the degree of the environment's non-stationarity while also achieving a sublinear dynamic regret. Our experimental evaluation on various high-dimensional non-stationary environments shows that the $\texttt{ProST}$ framework achieves a higher online return at suboptimal {$t_{1:K}$} than the existing methods.
originalAbstract: We first raise and tackle a ``time synchronization'' issue between the agent and the environment in non-stationary reinforcement learning (RL), a crucial factor hindering its real-world applications. In reality, environmental changes occur over wall-clock time ($t$) rather than episode progress ($k$), where wall-clock time signifies the actual elapsed time within the fixed duration $t \in [0, T]$. In existing works, at episode $k$, the agent rolls a trajectory and trains a policy before transitioning to episode $k+1$. In the context of the time-desynchronized environment, however, the agent at time $t_{k}$ allocates $\Delta t$ for trajectory generation and training, subsequently moves to the next episode at $t_{k+1}=t_{k}+\Delta t$. Despite a fixed total number of episodes ($K$), the agent accumulates different trajectories influenced by the choice of interaction times ($t_1,t_2,...,t_K$), significantly impacting the suboptimality gap of the policy. We propose a Proactively Synchronizing Tempo ($\texttt{ProST}$) framework that computes a suboptimal sequence {$t_1,t_2,...,t_K$} (= { $t_{1:K}$}) by minimizing an upper bound on its performance measure, i.e., the dynamic regret. Our main contribution is that we show that a suboptimal {$t_{1:K}$} trades-off between the policy training time (agent tempo) and how fast the environment changes (environment tempo). Theoretically, this work develops a suboptimal {$t_{1:K}$} as a function of the degree of the environment's non-stationarity while also achieving a sublinear dynamic regret. Our experimental evaluation on various high-dimensional non-stationary environments shows that the $\texttt{ProST}$ framework achieves a higher online return at suboptimal {$t_{1:K}$} than the existing methods.

paragraphs: In a changing environment, the world continues to evolve while a reinforcement-learning agent collects data and trains. This paper emphasizes that those changes occur in elapsed time, not according to episode number. Even with the same number of episodes, different interaction schedules can expose an agent to different trajectories and alter policy performance.

The Proactively Synchronizing Tempo framework, ProST, chooses interaction times by minimizing an upper bound on dynamic regret. Its schedule balances time spent training the policy against the speed of environmental change. The authors derive a suboptimal interaction sequence as a function of the environment’s degree of nonstationarity, rather than claiming to find the globally best schedule.

The analysis also establishes sublinear dynamic regret. In experiments across high-dimensional nonstationary environments, ProST achieves higher online return than existing methods at the derived schedules. The contribution makes timing an explicit part of learning: allocating additional training time can have different consequences depending on how much the environment changes before the agent interacts again.
summary.tldr: ProST adapts interaction timing to environmental change, balancing policy-training time with responsiveness and achieving higher reported online returns.

title: Tempo Adaptation in Non-stationary Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Diffusion-based planning has shown promising results in long-horizon, sparse-reward tasks by training trajectory diffusion models and conditioning the sampled trajectories using auxiliary guidance functions. However, due to their nature as generative models, diffusion models are not guaranteed to generate feasible plans, resulting in failed execution and precluding planners from being useful in safety-critical applications. In this work, we propose a novel approach to refine unreliable plans generated by diffusion models by providing refining guidance to error-prone plans. To this end, we suggest a new metric named restoration gap for evaluating the quality of individual plans generated by the diffusion model. A restoration gap is estimated by a gap predictor which produces restoration gap guidance to refine a diffusion planner. We additionally present an attribution map regularizer to prevent adversarial refining guidance that could be generated from the sub-optimal gap predictor, which enables further refinement of infeasible plans. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three different benchmarks in offline control settings that require long-horizon planning. We also illustrate that our approach presents explainability by presenting the attribution maps of the gap predictor and highlighting error-prone transitions, allowing for a deeper understanding of the generated plans.

paragraphs: Diffusion planners generate trajectories and guide them toward desired outcomes, which has shown promise for long tasks with sparse rewards. However, a generated trajectory may include transitions that cannot actually be executed. This paper addresses that reliability problem by detecting error-prone plans and supplying guidance intended to refine them.

The authors introduce a plan-quality metric called the restoration gap. A learned gap predictor estimates this quantity and produces guidance for the diffusion planner. Because an imperfect predictor can itself provide adversarial refining guidance, the method also includes an attribution-map regularizer intended to prevent that behavior and improve refinement of infeasible plans.

Experiments on three offline-control benchmarks requiring long-horizon planning demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The predictor's attribution maps also highlight transitions associated with errors, giving an interpretable view of which parts of a plan need attention. The contribution combines quality estimation, corrective guidance, and explanations of problematic transitions. It addresses the stated lack of feasibility guarantees through empirical refinement, without establishing that every resulting plan is feasible.
summary.tldr: A restoration-gap predictor guides diffusion planners away from infeasible trajectories, with attribution-based regularization and explanations of error-prone transitions.

title: Refining Diffusion Planner for Reliable Behavior Synthesis by Automatic Detection of Infeasible Plans

abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) is a challenging task in machine learning that involves finding a mathematical expression for a function based on its values. Recent advancements in SR have demonstrated the effectiveness of pre-trained transformer models in generating equations as sequences, leveraging large-scale pre-training on synthetic datasets and offering notable advantages in terms of inference time over classical Genetic Programming (GP) methods. However, these models primarily rely on supervised pre-training objectives borrowed from text generation and overlook equation discovery goals like accuracy and complexity. To address this, we propose TPSR, a Transformer-based Planning strategy for Symbolic Regression that incorporates Monte Carlo Tree Search planning algorithm into the transformer decoding process. Unlike conventional decoding strategies, TPSR enables the integration of non-differentiable equation verification feedback, such as fitting accuracy and complexity, as external sources of knowledge into the transformer equation generation process. Extensive experiments on various datasets show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, enhancing the model's fitting-complexity trade-off, extrapolation abilities, and robustness to noise.

paragraphs: Symbolic regression seeks a mathematical expression that explains observed function values. Pretrained Transformers can generate expressions as sequences, but their supervised training objectives do not directly capture every goal of equation discovery. In particular, producing a likely sequence does not directly optimize the balance between fitting the observations and keeping the equation simple.

TPSR adds Monte Carlo Tree Search to the Transformer’s decoding process. This planning procedure allows equation generation to incorporate external verification feedback, including fit quality and expression complexity. Because that feedback need not be differentiable, the search can use criteria that are not readily expressed as an ordinary gradient-based generation objective.

Across the evaluated datasets, the authors report improvements over state-of-the-art methods in the fit–complexity tradeoff, extrapolation, and robustness to noise. The findings indicate that planning during generation can help align a pretrained equation model with the goals of symbolic regression. The contribution centers on guiding the decoding process with evaluations of the mathematical candidates it produces.
summary.tldr: TPSR guides Transformer equation generation with tree search and verification feedback to improve fit, simplicity, extrapolation, and noise robustness.

title: Transformer-based Planning for Symbolic Regression

abstract: The task of point cloud segmentation, comprising semantic, instance, and panoptic segmentation, has been mainly tackled by designing task-specific network architectures, which often lack the flexibility to generalize across tasks, thus resulting in a fragmented research landscape. In this paper, we introduce ProtoSEG, a prototype-based model that unifies semantic, instance, and panoptic segmentation tasks. Our approach treats these three homogeneous tasks as a classification problem with different levels of granularity. By leveraging a Transformer architecture, we extract point embeddings to optimize prototype-class distances and dynamically learn class prototypes to accommodate the end tasks. Our prototypical design enjoys simplicity and transparency, powerful representational learning, and ad-hoc explainability. Empirical results demonstrate that ProtoSEG outperforms concurrent well-known specialized architectures on 3D point cloud benchmarks, achieving 72.3%, 76.4% and 74.2% mIoU for semantic segmentation on S3DIS, ScanNet V2 and SemanticKITTI, 66.8% mCov and 51.2% mAP for instance segmentation on S3DIS and ScanNet V2, 62.4% PQ for panoptic segmentation on SemanticKITTI, validating the strength of our concept and the effectiveness of our algorithm. The code and models are available at https://github.com/zyqin19/PROTOSEG.

paragraphs: Point-cloud segmentation includes assigning semantic categories, separating individual instances, and combining these goals in panoptic segmentation. These tasks have often used separate architectures, making methods less flexible across tasks. ProtoSEG unifies them by treating segmentation as classification at different levels of granularity.

The model uses a Transformer to extract representations for individual points and dynamically learns class prototypes suited to the end task. It optimizes distances between these representations and prototypes, giving the different segmentation problems a shared computational structure. The prototype design also provides a transparent way to relate point assignments to learned class representatives.

Experiments show ProtoSEG outperforming concurrent specialized architectures on three-dimensional point-cloud benchmarks. Semantic segmentation results span S3DIS, ScanNet V2, and SemanticKITTI; instance results cover S3DIS and ScanNet V2; and panoptic results include SemanticKITTI. The reported performance supports the central claim that a common prototype-based formulation can be competitive across all three tasks. Its significance is the combination of a simpler shared design with strong task-specific results, reducing the need to treat each segmentation setting as an entirely separate architecture problem.
summary.tldr: ProtoSEG unifies semantic, instance, and panoptic point-cloud segmentation through learned prototypes and point-level classification.

title: Unified 3D Segmenter As Prototypical Classifiers

abstract: We study multi-task representation learning for the problem of pure exploration in bilinear bandits. In bilinear bandits, an action takes theform of a pair of arms from two different entity types and the reward is a bilinear function of the known feature vectors of the arms. In the \textit{multi-task bilinear bandit problem}, we aim to find optimal actions for multiple tasks that share a common low-dimensional linear representation. The objective is to leverage this characteristic to expedite the process of identifying the best pair of arms for all tasks. We propose the algorithm GOBLIN that uses an experimental design approach to optimize sample allocations for learning the global representation as well as minimize the number of samples needed to identify the optimal pair of arms in individual tasks. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to give sample complexity analysis for pure exploration in bilinear bandits with shared representation. Our results demonstrate that by learning the shared representation across tasks, we achieve significantly improved sample complexity compared to the traditional approach of solving tasks independently.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to identify the best action for several related bilinear bandit tasks using fewer observations. Each action selects a pair of arms from two entity types, and its reward depends bilinearly on their known feature vectors. The pure-exploration objective is to discover the best pair for each task.

The tasks are assumed to share a low-dimensional linear representation. The proposed GOBLIN algorithm uses experimental design to decide how to allocate samples, addressing two connected needs: learning the common representation and identifying optimal pairs within individual tasks. Observations therefore contribute both to shared understanding and to resolving each task's own choices.

The authors provide a sample-complexity analysis for this shared-representation setting, describing how many samples the identification process requires. Their results show significant improvements over solving the tasks independently. The benefit rests on the shared structure: learning a useful representation across tasks reduces the amount of separate exploration needed to find their respective best actions.
summary.tldr: GOBLIN exploits a shared low-dimensional representation to identify optimal arm pairs across bilinear bandit tasks with fewer samples.

title: Multi-task Representation Learning for Pure Exploration in Bilinear Bandits

abstract: Feature bagging is a well-established ensembling method which aims to reduceprediction variance by combining predictions of many estimators trained on subsetsor projections of features. Here, we develop a theory of feature-bagging in noisyleast-squares ridge ensembles and simplify the resulting learning curves in the specialcase of equicorrelated data. Using analytical learning curves, we demonstratethat subsampling shifts the double-descent peak of a linear predictor. This leadsus to introduce heterogeneous feature ensembling, with estimators built on varyingnumbers of feature dimensions, as a computationally efficient method to mitigatedouble-descent. Then, we compare the performance of a feature-subsamplingensemble to a single linear predictor, describing a trade-off between noise amplificationdue to subsampling and noise reduction due to ensembling. Our qualitativeinsights carry over to linear classifiers applied to image classification tasks withrealistic datasets constructed using a state-of-the-art deep learning feature map.

paragraphs: Feature bagging combines predictors trained using different subsets or projections of input features to reduce prediction variance. This paper develops a theory for that strategy in noisy least-squares ridge ensembles. It derives learning curves and simplifies them for equicorrelated data, a special case with a shared correlation structure.

The analysis shows that feature subsampling moves the double-descent peak of a linear predictor. That observation motivates ensembles whose members use different numbers of feature dimensions. Varying those sizes provides a computationally efficient way to mitigate double descent, because the members do not all place their error peak at the same point.

The theory also compares a feature-subsampled ensemble with a single linear predictor. It identifies competing effects: subsampling can amplify noise, while combining predictors can reduce it. The authors find that these qualitative insights also apply to linear image classifiers using features from a modern deep learning model. The results explain both a reason to diversify feature counts and why ensembling benefits depend on the balance of noise effects.
summary.tldr: Learning-curve analysis shows how varying feature counts across ridge predictors can mitigate double descent while balancing competing noise effects.

title: Learning Curves for Noisy Heterogeneous Feature-Subsampled Ridge Ensembles

abstract: For speaker recognition, it is difficult to extract an accurate speaker representation from speech because of its mixture of speaker traits and content. This paper proposes a disentanglement framework that simultaneously models speaker traits and content variability in speech. It is realized with the use of three Gaussian inference layers, each consisting of a learnable transition model that extracts distinct speech components. Notably, a strengthened transition model is specifically designed to model complex speech dynamics. We also propose a self-supervision method to dynamically disentangle content without the use of labels other than speaker identities. The efficacy of the proposed framework is validated via experiments conducted on the VoxCeleb and SITW datasets with 9.56\% and 8.24\% average reductions in EER and minDCF, respectively. Since neither additional model training nor data is specifically needed, it is easily applicable in practical use.

paragraphs: Speaker recognition must identify a person from speech that also varies with what they say. Those two sources of variation are mixed in the signal, making it difficult to extract a representation focused on the speaker. This paper addresses that problem by explicitly modeling both speaker traits and changing speech content.

The proposed framework uses three Gaussian inference layers, each containing a learnable transition model that extracts distinct speech components. A strengthened transition model handles more complex speech dynamics. A self-supervision method then dynamically separates content using only speaker-identity labels, avoiding the need for additional labels describing what was spoken.

Experiments on VoxCeleb and SITW report average reductions of 9.56% in equal error rate and 8.24% in minimum detection cost. These are improvements in the reported recognition measures, rather than percentage-point claims. The authors also state that no additional model training or data is specifically needed. The practical contribution is a way to improve speaker representations by accounting for content variability within the recognition framework.
summary.tldr: A self-supervised disentanglement framework separates speaker traits from speech content and improves reported speaker-recognition measures.

title: Disentangling Voice and Content with Self-Supervision for Speaker Recognition

abstract: With the growth of model and data sizes, a broad effort has been made to design pruning techniques that reduce the resource demand of deep learning pipelines, while retaining model performance. In order to reduce both inference and training costs, a prominent line of work uses low-rank matrix factorizations to represent the network weights. Although able to retain accuracy, we observe that low-rank methods tend to compromise model robustness against adversarial perturbations. By modeling robustness in terms of the condition number of the neural network, we argue that this loss of robustness is due to the exploding singular values of the low-rank weight matrices. Thus, we introduce a robust low-rank training algorithm that maintains the network's weights on the low-rank matrix manifold while simultaneously enforcing approximate orthonormal constraints. The resulting model reduces both training and inference costs while ensuring well-conditioning and thus better adversarial robustness, without compromising model accuracy. This is shown by extensive numerical evidence and by our main approximation theorem that shows the computed robust low-rank network well-approximates the ideal full model, provided a highly performing low-rank sub-network exists.

paragraphs: Low-rank weight factorizations can reduce neural-network training and inference costs, but may weaken resistance to adversarial perturbations. This paper models robustness through network conditioning and links the loss of robustness to growing singular values in low-rank weight matrices.

The proposed training algorithm keeps weights on a low-rank matrix manifold while enforcing approximate orthonormal constraints. The intention is to retain computational savings without allowing poor conditioning to undermine the model’s sensitivity to input perturbations.

Numerical experiments support improved robustness without sacrificing accuracy. An approximation theorem shows that the computed low-rank network approximates the ideal full model when a sufficiently strong low-rank subnetwork exists. That existence condition is essential: the theorem does not promise that every full model admits an equally capable compressed version. The abstract gives no specific compression ratios, attack budgets, or numerical accuracy results.
summary.tldr: Approximate orthonormal constraints improve the robustness of low-rank neural-network training.

title: Robust low-rank training via approximate orthonormal constraints

abstract: We propose an interpretable model to uncover the behavioral patterns of human movements by analyzing their trajectories. Our approach is based on the belief that human actions are driven by intentions and are influenced by environmental factors such as spatial relationships with surrounding objects. To model this, we use a set of spatial-temporal logic rules that include intention variables as principles. These rules are automatically discovered and used to capture the dynamics of human actions. To learn the model parameters and rule content, we design an EM learning algorithm that treats the unknown rule content as a latent variable. In the E-step, we evaluate the posterior over the latent rule content, and in the M-step, we optimize the rule generator and model parameters by maximizing the expected log-likelihood. Our model has wide-ranging applications in areas such as sports analytics, robotics, and autonomous cars. We demonstrate the model's superior interpretability and prediction performance on both pedestrian and NBA basketball player datasets, achieving promising results.

paragraphs: This paper seeks to explain human movement by discovering behavioral rules from trajectories. Its modeling premise is that actions reflect intentions and are influenced by environmental factors, including spatial relationships with nearby objects. The goal is to capture movement dynamics in an interpretable form that also supports prediction.

The model uses spatial-temporal logic rules containing intention variables. Rather than requiring the rule content to be supplied in advance, it learns that content as a latent variable. An expectation-maximization algorithm alternates between estimating a posterior over possible rule content and updating the rule generator and model parameters to maximize the expected log-likelihood. This connects learning the rules with fitting the movement model.

Experiments on pedestrian trajectories and NBA basketball player data show superior interpretability and predictive performance in the reported evaluations. The results support discovering structured explanations alongside movement predictions. Sports analytics, robotics, and autonomous vehicles are identified as application areas; the empirical demonstrations described in the abstract concern pedestrians and basketball players.
summary.tldr: An interpretable trajectory model learns spatial-temporal rules involving intentions to explain and predict human movement.

title: Discovering Intrinsic Spatial-Temporal Logic Rules to Explain Human Actions

abstract: This paper presents IB-POMCP, a novel algorithm for online planning under partial observability. Our approach enhances the decision-making process by using estimations of the world belief's entropy to guide a tree search process and surpass the limitations of planning in scenarios with sparse reward configurations. By performing what we denominate as an *information-guided planning process*, the algorithm, which incorporates a novel I-UCB function, shows significant improvements in reward and reasoning time compared to state-of-the-art baselines in several benchmark scenarios, along with theoretical convergence guarantees.

By performing what we denominate as an *information-guided planning process*, the algorithm, which incorporates a novel I-UCB function, shows significant improvements in reward and reasoning time compared to state-of-the-art baselines in several benchmark scenarios, along with theoretical convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: IB-POMCP addresses online planning when an agent cannot directly observe the complete state of its environment. The planner works with a belief about the world, reflecting uncertainty about what is happening. The paper focuses on improving decisions in this setting, especially when rewards are sparse and therefore provide limited guidance during planning.

The proposed approach uses estimates of the belief’s entropy to guide tree search. Entropy summarizes uncertainty, so the search can use information about the agent’s knowledge in addition to the available reward signal. A new function called I-UCB forms part of this information-guided planning process. The central design choice is to make uncertainty relevant to how the planner directs its search.

The authors report significant improvements in both reward and reasoning time over state-of-the-art baselines across several benchmark scenarios. They also provide theoretical convergence guarantees. Together, these results support information-guided search as a useful approach to partially observable planning, with empirical gains addressing both decision quality and the computation spent reaching a decision.
summary.tldr: IB-POMCP guides planning with belief uncertainty, improving reported rewards and reasoning time in partially observable benchmark scenarios.

title: Information-guided Planning: An Online Approach for Partially Observable Problems

abstract: Spectral clustering has gained popularity for clustering non-convex data due to its simplicity and effectiveness. It is essential to construct a similarity graph using a high-quality affinity measure that models the local neighborhood relations among the data samples. However, incomplete data can lead to inaccurate affinity measures, resulting in degraded clustering performance. To address these issues, we propose an imputation-free framework with two novel approaches to improve spectral clustering on incomplete data. Firstly, we introduce a new kernel correction method that enhances the quality of the kernel matrix estimated on incomplete data with a theoretical guarantee, benefiting classical spectral clustering on pre-defined kernels. Secondly, we develop a series of affinity learning methods that equip the self-expressive framework with $\ell_p$-norm to construct an intrinsic affinity matrix with an adaptive extension. Our methods outperform existing data imputation and distance calibration techniques on benchmark datasets, offering a promising solution to spectral clustering on incomplete data in various real-world applications.

paragraphs: Spectral clustering groups samples using a graph whose connections describe their similarity. Its success depends on those connections accurately representing local relationships. Missing entries can distort the estimated similarities, so even an otherwise effective clustering procedure may receive a misleading graph. This paper addresses the similarity construction stage without first filling in missing data.

The framework offers two approaches. The first corrects a kernel matrix estimated from incomplete observations, with a theoretical guarantee for the correction. This supports classical spectral clustering methods that begin with a predefined kernel. The second learns affinities through a self-expressive framework equipped with an lp norm, and includes an adaptive extension.

Both approaches target the relationships used for clustering directly. This matters because the desired output is a useful affinity structure, rather than necessarily a completed dataset. On benchmark datasets, the proposed methods outperform existing imputation and distance-calibration techniques. Those results support improving the similarity representation itself as an effective route to spectral clustering when some measurements are unavailable.
summary.tldr: Kernel correction and affinity learning improve spectral clustering on incomplete data without imputing missing entries.

title: Boosting Spectral Clustering on Incomplete Data via Kernel Correction and Affinity Learning

abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of representing high-fidelity volumetric videos with low storage cost. Some recent feature grid-based methods have shown superior performance of fast learning implicit neural representations from input 2D images. However, such explicit representations easily lead to large model sizes when modeling dynamic scenes. To solve this problem, our key idea is reducing the spatial and temporal redundancy of feature grids, which intrinsically exist due to the self-similarity of scenes. To this end, we propose a novel neural representation, named dynamic codebook, which first merges similar features for the model compression and then compensates for the potential decline in rendering quality by a set of dynamic codes. Experiments on the NHR and DyNeRF datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art rendering quality, while being able to achieve more storage efficiency. The source code is available at https://github.com/zju3dv/compact_vv.

Some recent feature grid-based methods have shown superior performance of fast learning implicit neural representations from input 2D images. However, such explicit representations easily lead to large model sizes when modeling dynamic scenes. To solve this problem, our key idea is reducing the spatial and temporal redundancy of feature grids, which intrinsically exist due to the self-similarity of scenes. To this end, we propose a novel neural representation, named dynamic codebook, which first merges similar features for the model compression and then compensates for the potential decline in rendering quality by a set of dynamic codes. Experiments on the NHR and DyNeRF datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art rendering quality, while being able to achieve more storage efficiency. The source code is available at https://github.com/zju3dv/compact_vv.

paragraphs: Representing a changing three-dimensional scene at high visual quality can require substantial storage. Feature-grid methods can learn neural scene representations quickly from two-dimensional images, but their explicit grids can become large for dynamic scenes. This paper targets that storage problem by exploiting repeated or similar features across both space and time.

The proposed representation, called a dynamic codebook, first merges similar features to compress the model. Sharing features can reduce rendering quality, so the representation also includes dynamic codes that compensate for this potential loss. The two parts address complementary needs: the merged features remove redundancy, while the additional codes help preserve the distinctions needed for high-quality rendering.

Experiments on the NHR and DyNeRF datasets report state-of-the-art rendering quality alongside improved storage efficiency. The stated result shows that reducing the redundancy of feature grids can be compatible with strong visual fidelity on those datasets. The contribution is therefore a representation that treats compression and quality preservation together, rather than considering model size only after constructing a dynamic scene.
summary.tldr: Dynamic codebooks compress repeated scene features and compensate with dynamic codes, achieving strong volumetric-video rendering quality with lower storage costs.

title: Compact Neural Volumetric Video Representations with Dynamic Codebooks

abstract: Large language models (LLMs), typically designed as a function of next-word prediction, have excelled across extensive NLP tasks. Despite the generality, next-word prediction is often not an efficient formulation for many of the tasks, demanding an extreme scale of model parameters (10s or 100s of billions) and sometimes yielding suboptimal performance.In practice, it is often desirable to build more efficient models---despite being less versatile, they still apply to a substantial subset of problems, delivering on par or even superior performance with much smaller model sizes.In this paper, we propose text alignment as an efficient unified model for a wide range of crucial tasks involving text entailment, similarity, question answering (and answerability), factual consistency, and so forth. Given a pair of texts, the model measures the degree of alignment between their information. We instantiate an alignment model through lightweight finetuning of RoBERTa (355M parameters) using 5.9M examples from 28 datasets. Despite its compact size, extensive experiments show the model's efficiency and strong performance: (1) On over 20 datasets of aforementioned diverse tasks, the model matches or surpasses FLAN-T5 models that have around 2x or 10x more parameters; the single unified model also outperforms task-specific models finetuned on individual datasets; (2) When applied to evaluate factual consistency of language generation on 23 datasets, our model improves over various baselines, including the much larger GPT-3.5 (ChatGPT) and sometimes even GPT-4; (3) The lightweight model can also serve as an add-on component for LLMs such as GPT-3.5 in question answering tasks, improving the average exact match (EM) score by 17.94 and F1 score by 15.05 through identifying unanswerable questions.

paragraphs: Many language tasks involve judging the relationship between two texts rather than generating a continuation. This paper proposes text alignment as a shared formulation for entailment, similarity, question answering, answerability, and factual consistency. The model measures how closely the information in a pair of texts aligns.

The authors fine-tune a 355-million-parameter RoBERTa model using 5.9 million examples from 28 datasets. Across more than 20 evaluation datasets, the unified model matches or exceeds FLAN-T5 models with roughly two or ten times as many parameters. It also outperforms models fine-tuned separately on individual task datasets.

On factual-consistency evaluation across 23 datasets, it improves over several baselines, including GPT-3.5 and sometimes GPT-4. As an add-on to language models for question answering, identifying unanswerable questions improves average exact match by 17.94 and F1 by 15.05 in the reported experiments. The findings show that a less versatile but broadly shared comparison task can support strong performance with a much smaller model.
summary.tldr: A compact text-alignment model handles diverse language-evaluation tasks and often matches or exceeds much larger models in reported comparisons.

title: Text Alignment Is An Efficient Unified Model for Massive NLP Tasks

abstract: High-quality preference datasets are essential for training reward models that can effectively guide large language models (LLMs) in generating high-quality responses aligned with human preferences.As LLMs become stronger and better aligned, permissively licensed preference datasets, such as Open Assistant, HH-RLHF, and HelpSteer need to be updated to remain effective for reward modeling.Methods that distil preference data from proprietary LLMs such as GPT-4 have restrictions on commercial usage imposed by model providers.To improve upon both generated responses and attribute labeling quality, we release HelpSteer2, a permissively licensed preference dataset (CC-BY-4.0). Using a powerful Nemotron-4-340B base model trained on HelpSteer2, we are able to achieve the SOTA score (92.0%) on Reward-Bench's primary dataset, outperforming currently listed open and proprietary models, as of June 12th, 2024.Notably, HelpSteer2 consists of only ten thousand response pairs, an order of magnitude fewer than existing preference datasets (e.g., HH-RLHF), which makes it highly efficient for training reward models. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that reward models trained with HelpSteer2 are effective in aligning LLMs. Additionally, we propose SteerLM 2.0, a model alignment approach that can effectively make use of the rich multi-attribute score predicted by our reward models. HelpSteer2 is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/HelpSteer2 and code is available at https://github.com/NVIDIA/NeMo-Aligner

paragraphs: Reward models help guide language models toward responses that match human preferences, making the quality of their training data consequential. HelpSteer2 addresses the need for updated preference data as language models improve. It also offers a permissive CC-BY-4.0 license, addressing usage restrictions associated with some preference datasets distilled from proprietary models.

The dataset contains ten thousand response pairs and emphasizes improvements in both generated responses and attribute labeling. A reward model based on Nemotron-4-340B and trained with HelpSteer2 achieves 92.0% on Reward-Bench’s primary dataset. The paper reports that this exceeded the listed open and proprietary models as of June 12, 2024. That result belongs to the particular model-and-dataset combination and the stated comparison date.

Despite being an order of magnitude smaller than datasets such as HH-RLHF, HelpSteer2 supports effective reward-model training in the reported experiments. The authors also show that its reward models help align language models and introduce SteerLM 2.0 to use their multiple attribute scores. Together, the contributions connect compact preference data with practical alignment methods.
summary.tldr: HelpSteer2 provides ten thousand permissively licensed response pairs that support strong reward modeling and multi-attribute language-model alignment.

title: HelpSteer 2: Open-source dataset for training top-performing reward models

abstract: Vector Symbolic Architectures (VSAs) are one approach to developing Neuro-symbolic AI, where two vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$ are 'bound' together to produce a new vector in the same space. VSAs support the commutativity and associativity of this binding operation, along with an inverse operation, allowing one to construct symbolic-style manipulations over real-valued vectors. Most VSAs were developed before deep learning and automatic differentiation became popular and instead focused on efficacy in hand-designed systems. In this work, we introduce the Hadamard-derived linear Binding (HLB), which is designed to have favorable computational efficiency, and efficacy in classic VSA tasks, and perform well in differentiable systems.

paragraphs: Vector Symbolic Architectures provide a way to perform symbolic operations using real-valued vectors. Their central operation is binding: combining two vectors into another vector of the same dimensionality. This lets a system represent combinations of information without making the representation longer every time something is added. The paper places this approach within the broader effort to connect neural computation with symbolic manipulation.

The algebraic properties of binding matter because they determine which manipulations the representation supports. The abstract describes commutativity, associativity, and an inverse operation, which provide structure for combining and recovering information. However, many existing architectures originated in systems whose operations were designed by hand, before automatic differentiation became a routine part of neural-network development.

The paper introduces Hadamard-derived linear Binding, or HLB, to address that design context. Its stated goals combine computational efficiency, effectiveness on established vector-symbolic tasks, and suitability for differentiable systems. The contribution is a binding architecture designed with both symbolic operations and modern neural learning in mind.
summary.tldr: HLB introduces a vector-binding architecture designed for efficient symbolic operations and use in differentiable learning systems.

title: A Walsh Hadamard Derived Linear Vector Symbolic Architecture

abstract: Neural algorithmic reasoning is an emerging area of machine learning that focuses on building neural networks capable of solving complex algorithmic tasks. Recent advancements predominantly follow the standard supervised learning paradigm -- feeding an individual problem instance into the network each time and training it to approximate the execution steps of a classical algorithm. We challenge this mode and propose a novel open-book learning framework. In this framework, whether during training or testing, the network can access and utilize all instances in the training dataset when reasoning for a given instance.Empirical evaluation is conducted on the challenging CLRS Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark, which consists of 30 diverse algorithmic tasks. Our open-book learning framework exhibits a significant enhancement in neural reasoning capabilities. Further, we notice that there is recent literature suggesting that multi-task training on CLRS can improve the reasoning accuracy of certain tasks, implying intrinsic connections between different algorithmic tasks. We delve into this direction via the open-book framework. When the network reasons for a specific task, we enable it to aggregate information from training instances of other tasks in an attention-based manner. We show that this open-book attention mechanism offers insights into the inherent relationships among various tasks in the benchmark and provides a robust tool for interpretable multi-task training.

paragraphs: Neural algorithmic reasoning trains networks to perform algorithmic tasks, often by approximating the execution steps of a classical algorithm. The standard setup processes one problem instance at a time. This paper introduces an open-book alternative in which a network can consult all training instances while reasoning about a particular problem.

That access is available during both training and testing. The framework is evaluated on the CLRS Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark, containing 30 diverse tasks, where it produces a significant reported improvement in reasoning capability. The central change is to make training examples available as a resource during reasoning itself, expanding the information the network can use for an individual instance.

The framework thus combines improved reported reasoning with a way to examine cross-task information use.
summary.tldr: Open-book neural reasoning lets networks consult training examples during inference, improving CLRS performance and revealing cross-task relationships.

title: Open-Book Neural Algorithmic Reasoning

abstract: We introduce camera ray matching (CRAYM) into the joint optimization of camera poses and neural fields from multi-view images. The optimized field, referred to as a feature volume, can be “probed” by the camera rays for novel view synthesis (NVS) and 3D geometry reconstruction. One key reason for matching camera rays, instead of pixels as in prior works, is that the camera rays can be parameterized by the feature volume to carry both geometric and photometric information. Multi-view consistencies involving the camera rays and scene rendering can be naturally integrated into the joint optimization and network training, to impose physically meaningful constraints to improve the final quality of both the geometric reconstruction and photorealistic rendering. We formulate our per-ray optimization and matched ray coherence by focusing on camera rays passing through keypoints in the input images to elevate both the efficiency and accuracy of scene correspondences. Accumulated ray features along the feature volume provide a means to discount the coherence constraint amid erroneous ray matching. We demonstrate the effectiveness of CRAYM for both NVS and geometry reconstruction, over dense- or sparse-view settings, with qualitative and quantitative comparisons to state-of-the-art alternatives.

paragraphs: CRAYM jointly optimizes camera poses and a neural scene representation from multiple images. The resulting feature volume supports both rendering new viewpoints and reconstructing three-dimensional geometry. Its central choice is to match camera rays across views, using the feature volume to give those rays information about scene geometry and appearance.

This representation lets the method combine consistency between rays with consistency in rendered images during optimization and training. The intended benefit is to impose physically meaningful constraints on both reconstruction and rendering. CRAYM concentrates its per-ray calculations and matching constraints on rays through image keypoints, improving the efficiency and accuracy of identifying scene correspondences. Features accumulated along rays also allow the method to reduce the influence of a coherence constraint when the associated ray match is erroneous.

The authors demonstrate the method on novel-view synthesis and geometry reconstruction using both dense and sparse sets of views. Their evaluation includes qualitative and quantitative comparisons with state-of-the-art alternatives. The stated contribution is a shared geometric and photometric basis for improving camera estimation and scene modeling together.
summary.tldr: CRAYM matches camera rays carrying geometric and appearance information to jointly improve camera poses and neural scene reconstruction.

title: CRAYM: Neural Field Optimization via Camera RAY Matching

abstract: We consider learning a sparse model from linear measurements taken by a network of agents. Different from existing decentralized methods designed based on the LASSO regression with explicit $\ell_1$ norm regularization, we exploit the implicit regularization of decentralized optimization method applied to an over-parameterized nonconvex least squares formulation without penalization. Our first result shows that despite nonconvexity, if the network connectivity is good, the well-known decentralized gradient descent algorithm (DGD) with small initialization and early stopping can compute the statistically optimal solution. Sufficient conditions on the initialization scale, choice of step size, network connectivity, and stopping time are further provided to achieve convergence. Our result recovers the convergence rate of gradient descent in the centralized setting, showing its tightness. Based on the analysis of DGD, we further propose a communication-efficient version, termed T-DGD, by truncating the iterates before transmission. In the high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regime, we show that T-DGD achieves comparable statistical accuracy to DGD, while the communication cost is logarithmic in the number of parameters. Numerical results are provided to validate the effectiveness of DGD and T-DGD for sparse learning through implicit regularization.

paragraphs: The paper studies sparse regression when linear measurements are distributed across a network of agents. A sparse model uses relatively few active parameters. Existing decentralized approaches commonly encourage sparsity through an explicit LASSO penalty; this work investigates whether the optimization process itself can produce an appropriately sparse solution.

The authors apply decentralized gradient descent to an over-parameterized, nonconvex least-squares formulation without a penalty. With good network connectivity, small initialization, and early stopping, they show that the method can reach statistically optimal accuracy. They also give sufficient conditions governing initialization, step size, connectivity, and stopping time, and recover the centralized gradient-descent convergence rate.

Numerical results support both methods. The guarantees tie the benefits of implicit regularization and reduced communication to specific optimization, network, and signal conditions.
summary.tldr: Under sufficient conditions, decentralized gradient descent learns sparse models without explicit penalties, with a truncated variant reducing communication at high signal-to-noise ratios.

title: Implicit Regularization of Decentralized Gradient Descent for Sparse Regression

abstract: This paper studies first-order policy optimization for robust average cost Markov decision processes (MDPs). Specifically, we focus on ergodic Markov chains. For robust average cost MDPs, the goal is to optimize the worst-case average cost over an uncertainty set of transition kernels. We first develop a sub-gradient of the robust average cost. Based on the sub-gradient, a robust policy mirror descent approach is further proposed. To characterize its iteration complexity, we develop a lower bound on the difference of robust average cost between two policies and further show that the robust average cost satisfies the PL-condition. We then show that with increasing step size, our robust policy mirror descent achieves a linear convergence rate in the optimality gap, and with constant step size, our algorithm converges to an $\epsilon$-optimal policy with an iteration complexity of $\mathcal{O}(1/\epsilon)$. The convergence rate of our algorithm matches with the best convergence rate of policy-based algorithms for robust MDPs. Moreover, our algorithm is the first algorithm that converges to the global optimum with general uncertainty sets for robust average cost MDPs. We provide simulation results to demonstrate the performance of our algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper studies decision-making when the environment's transition rules are uncertain and performance is measured by long-run average cost. The objective is to choose a policy with the best worst-case cost across an uncertainty set of transition models. The analysis focuses on ergodic Markov chains, an explicit condition on the processes being studied.

The authors derive a subgradient of robust average cost and use it to build a robust policy mirror-descent algorithm. They also establish a bound comparing the costs of two policies and show that the objective satisfies the PL condition. These theoretical properties support convergence analysis even though the optimization problem involves uncertain dynamics.

With increasing step sizes, the method achieves linear convergence in the optimality gap. With a constant step size, it reaches an epsilon-optimal policy in order 1/epsilon iterations. The authors report a rate matching the best policy-based robust-MDP rates and claim the first global-optimum convergence result for general uncertainty sets in this average-cost setting. Simulations demonstrate the algorithm's performance alongside the theoretical guarantees.
summary.tldr: Robust policy mirror descent obtains global convergence guarantees for average-cost MDPs with general uncertainty sets in the ergodic setting.

title: Policy Optimization for Robust Average Reward MDPs

abstract: Recent advancements in 2D/3D generative techniques have facilitated the generation of dynamic 3D objects from monocular videos. Previous methods mainly rely on the implicit neural radiance fields (NeRF) or explicit Gaussian Splatting as the underlying representation, and struggle to achieve satisfactory spatial-temporal consistency and surface appearance. Drawing inspiration from modern 3D animation pipelines, we introduce DreamMesh4D, a novel framework combining mesh representation with geometric skinning technique to generate high-quality 4D object from a monocular video. Instead of utilizing classical texture map for appearance, we bind Gaussian splats to triangle face of mesh for differentiable optimization of both the texture and mesh vertices. In particular, DreamMesh4D begins with a coarse mesh obtained through an image-to-3D generation procedure. Sparse points are then uniformly sampled across the mesh surface, and are used to build a deformation graph to drive the motion of the 3D object for the sake of computational efficiency and providing additional constraint. For each step, transformations of sparse control points are predicted using a deformation network, and the mesh vertices as well as the surface Gaussians are deformed via a novel geometric skinning algorithm. The skinning algorithm is a hybrid approach combining LBS (linear blending skinning) and DQS (dual-quaternion skinning), mitigating drawbacks associated with both approaches. The static surface Gaussians and mesh vertices as well as the dynamic deformation network are learned via reference view photometric loss, score distillation loss as well as other regularization losses in a two-stage manner. Extensive experiments demonstrate superior performance of our method in terms of both rendering quality and spatial-temporal consistency. Furthermore, our method is compatible with modern graphic pipelines, showcasing its potential in the 3D gaming and film industry.

Earlier approaches using neural radiance fields or Gaussian splatting struggle with surface appearance and consistency across space and time. The proposed framework draws on animation techniques by combining a mesh surface with a mechanism for deforming that surface.

The method begins with a coarse mesh generated from an image. Gaussian splats are attached to its triangular faces, allowing appearance and vertex positions to be optimized together. Sparse control points sampled across the surface form a deformation graph. A network predicts their transformations, which then drive the mesh and attached Gaussians through a skinning method combining linear blending and dual-quaternion approaches.

This sparse control structure provides constraints while supporting computational efficiency. Training proceeds in two stages using reference-view image matching, score distillation, and regularization losses. Experiments show superior rendering quality and spatial-temporal consistency. Compatibility with modern graphics pipelines also gives the approach potential for game and film applications, where an animated surface representation can fit existing production workflows.
summary.tldr: DreamMesh4D combines meshes, surface-bound Gaussian splats, and sparse motion controls to generate visually consistent animated 3D objects from monocular video.

title: DreamMesh4D: Video-to-4D Generation with Sparse-Controlled Gaussian-Mesh Hybrid Representation

abstract: The flexible and generalized nature of large language models has allowed for their application in a wide array of language-based domains.Much like their human contemporaries, these models are capable of engaging in discussions and debates as a means of improving answer quality.We first take a theoretical approach to analyzing debate and provide a framework through which debate can be mathematically examined.Building on this framework, we provide several theoretical results for multi-agent debate.In particular, we demonstrate that similar model capabilities, or similar model responses, can result in static debate dynamics where the debate procedure simply converges to the majority opinion. When this majority opinion is the result of a common misconception (ingrained in the models through shared training data) debate is likely to converge to answers associated with that common misconception.Using insights from our theoretical results we then propose three interventions which improve the efficacy of debate. For each intervention, we provide theoretical results demonstrating how debate is improved.We also demonstrate that these interventions result in better performance on four common benchmark tasks.

When this majority opinion is the result of a common misconception (ingrained in the models through shared training data) debate is likely to converge to answers associated with that common misconception.Using insights from our theoretical results we then propose three interventions which improve the efficacy of debate. paragraphs: Having several language models debate an answer offers a possible route to improving answer quality. This paper develops a mathematical framework for analyzing that process and identifying when discussion may fail to produce useful revisions. Its focus is on the dynamics of agreement among models, including how their capabilities and starting responses shape the outcome.

The theoretical results show that similar capabilities or similar responses can lead to static debate dynamics that settle on the majority opinion. If shared training data has embedded a common misconception, that majority can favor an incorrect answer. Under those circumstances, debate is likely to reinforce the misconception rather than resolve it.

Using these insights, the authors propose three interventions intended to improve debate. They provide theoretical results for each intervention and report better performance on four benchmark tasks. The contribution therefore combines an account of a possible failure mechanism with supported ways to improve the process, emphasizing that agreement among participants can reflect shared error as well as useful deliberation.
summary.tldr: The paper explains how multi-model debate can reinforce shared misconceptions and proposes three interventions supported by theory and benchmark improvements.

title: Multi-LLM Debate: Framework, Principals, and Interventions

abstract: Recent advances in text-to-image generation have enabled the creation of high-quality images with diverse applications. However, accurately describing desired visual attributes can be challenging, especially for non-experts in art and photography. An intuitive solution involves adopting favorable attributes from source images. Current methods attempt to distill identity and style from source images. However, "style" is a broad concept that includes texture, color, and artistic elements, but does not cover other important attributes like lighting and dynamics. Additionally, a simplified "style" adaptation prevents combining multiple attributes from different sources into one generated image. In this work, we formulate a more effective approach to decompose the aesthetics of a picture into specific visual attributes, letting users apply characteristics like lighting, texture, and dynamics from different images. To achieve this goal, we constructed the first fine-grained visual attributes dataset (FiVA) to the best of our knowledge. This FiVA dataset features a well-organized taxonomy for visual attributes and includes 1 M high-quality generated images with visual attribute annotations. Leveraging this dataset, we propose a fine-grained visual attributes adaptation framework (FiVA-Adapter) , which decouples and adapts visual attributes from one or more source images into a generated one. This approach enhances user-friendly customization, allowing users to selectively apply desired attributes to create images that meet their unique preferences and specific content requirements.

title: FiVA: Fine-grained Visual Attribute Dataset for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models

abstract: Program synthesis with language models (LMs) has unlocked a large set of reasoning abilities; code-tuned LMs have proven adept at generating programs that solve a wide variety of algorithmic symbolic manipulation tasks (e.g. word concatenation). However, not all reasoning tasks are easily expressible as code, e.g. tasks involving commonsense reasoning, moral decision-making, and sarcasm understanding. Our goal is to extend a LM’s program synthesis skills to such tasks and evaluate the results via pseudo-programs, namely Python programs where some leaf function calls are left undefined. To that end, we propose, Code Generation and Emulated EXecution (COGEX). COGEX works by (1) training LMs to generate pseudo-programs and (2) teaching them to emulate their generated program’s execution, including those leaf functions, allowing the LM’s knowledge to fill in the execution gaps; and (3) using them to search over many programs to find an optimal one. To adapt the COGEX model to a new task, we introduce a method for performing program search to find a single program whose pseudo-execution yields optimal performance when applied to all the instances of a given dataset. We show that our approach yields large improvements compared to standard in-context learning approaches on a battery of tasks, both algorithmic and soft reasoning. This result thus demonstrates that code synthesis can be applied to a much broader class of problems than previously considered.

The authors report large improvements over standard in-context learning on both algorithmic and softer reasoning tasks. These findings support extending code synthesis beyond problems with fully specified symbolic operations, using learned execution to connect program structure with less formal judgments.
summary.tldr: COGEX combines pseudo-program generation, learned execution, and program search to improve algorithmic and less formal reasoning.

title: Learning to Reason via Program Generation, Emulation, and Search

abstract: Large language model systems face significant security risks from maliciously crafted messages that aim to overwrite the system's original instructions or leak private data. To study this problem, we organized a capture-the-flag competition at IEEE SaTML 2024, where the flag is a secret string in the LLM system prompt. The competition was organized in two phases. In the first phase, teams developed defenses to prevent the model from leaking the secret. During the second phase, teams were challenged to extract the secrets hidden for defenses proposed by the other teams. This report summarizes the main insights from the competition. Notably, we found that all defenses were bypassed at least once, highlighting the difficulty of designing a successful defense and the necessity for additional research to protect LLM systems. To foster future research in this direction, we compiled a dataset with over 137k multi-turn attack chats and open-sourced the platform.

paragraphs: Language model systems can receive malicious messages designed to override their instructions or expose private information. This paper studies that risk through a capture-the-flag competition in which the protected information was a secret string placed in the model's system prompt. Successfully extracting that string provided a concrete test of whether a defense held up.

The competition had two phases. Teams first developed defenses intended to stop the model from revealing its secret. They then attacked defenses created by other teams, trying to recover the hidden strings. This arrangement exposed defenses to adversarial conversations devised by competing participants, making the exercise a direct examination of their behavior under attack.

Every defense in the competition was bypassed at least once. That finding demonstrates the difficulty of protecting secrets in the tested systems; it does not establish that every possible defense must fail. The authors also release the platform and a dataset containing more than 137,000 multi-turn attack conversations, providing material for studying attacks and developing further defenses.
summary.tldr: A secret-extraction competition bypassed every submitted defense at least once and produced over 137,000 attack conversations for further research.

title: Dataset and Lessons Learned from the 2024 SaTML LLM Capture-the-Flag Competition

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) targeting different deployment scales and sizes are currently produced by training each variant from scratch; this is extremely compute-intensive. In this paper, we investigate if pruning an existing LLM and then re-training it with a fraction <3% of the original training data can be a suitable alternative to repeated, full retraining. To this end, we develop a set of practical and effective **compression best practices** for LLMs that combine depth, width, attention and MLP pruning with knowledge distillation-based retraining; we arrive at these best practices through a detailed empirical exploration of pruning strategies for each axis, methods to combine axes, distillation strategies, and search techniques for arriving at optimal compressed architectures. We use this guide to compress the Nemotron-4 family of LLMs by a factor of 2-4x, and compare their performance to similarly-sized models on a variety of language modeling tasks. On these tasks, we perform better than Nemotron-3 8B and LLaMa2 7B using **up to 40x** fewer training tokens}, on par with Mistral 7B and Gemma 7B using **up to 85x fewer tokens** and slightly worse than LLaMa3 8B using **up to 159x fewer tokens**. Our models also compare favorably to state-of-the-art compression techniques from the literature.
