paragraphs: Producing language models at several sizes usually means paying for several training runs from scratch. This paper investigates a different route: remove parts of an existing model, then retrain the smaller model using less than three percent of the original training data. Knowledge distillation guides that retraining using the larger model.

The authors empirically examine pruning along several dimensions: depth, width, attention, and multilayer perceptron components. They also investigate how to combine these choices, select compressed architectures, and apply distillation. The resulting practical guidance is used to shrink models in the Nemotron-4 family by factors of two to four.

On the evaluated language tasks, the compressed models outperform Nemotron-3 8B and LLaMa2 7B with up to forty times fewer training tokens. They match Mistral 7B and Gemma 7B with up to eighty-five times fewer tokens, while slightly trailing LLaMa3 8B with up to 159 times fewer tokens. These comparisons support compression and limited retraining as a promising way to derive smaller models from an already trained foundation.
summary.tldr: Pruning and distillation produce compact Nemotron-4 models that compete with similarly sized models using substantially fewer retraining tokens.

title: Compact Language Models via Pruning and Knowledge Distillation

abstract: Conventional wisdom holds that autoregressive models for image generation are typically accompanied by vector-quantized tokens. We observe that while a discrete-valued space can facilitate representing a categorical distribution, it is not a necessity for autoregressive modeling. In this work, we propose to model the per-token probability distribution using a diffusion procedure, which allows us to apply autoregressive models in a continuous-valued space. Rather than using categorical cross-entropy loss, we define a Diffusion Loss function to model the per-token probability. This approach eliminates the need for discrete-valued tokenizers. We evaluate its effectiveness across a wide range of cases, including standard autoregressive models and generalized masked autoregressive (MAR) variants. By removing vector quantization, our image generator achieves strong results while enjoying the speed advantage of sequence modeling. We hope this work will motivate the use of autoregressive generation in other continuous-valued domains and applications. Code is available at [https://github.com/LTH14/mar](https://github.com/LTH14/mar).

paragraphs: Autoregressive image generators commonly represent images using discrete tokens produced through vector quantization. That representation makes it convenient to predict a categorical distribution over the next token. This paper separates that convenient choice from the underlying idea of autoregressive generation: a model can predict successive image tokens without requiring their values to be discrete.

The proposed method uses a diffusion procedure to represent each token’s probability distribution in a continuous space. A Diffusion Loss replaces the categorical cross-entropy objective ordinarily used for discrete predictions. This changes how the model learns a token’s distribution and eliminates the need for a tokenizer that converts image information into discrete values.

The authors evaluate the approach with standard autoregressive models and generalized masked autoregressive variants. They report strong image-generation results while retaining the speed advantage of sequence modeling. The contribution is therefore a way to combine continuous token representations with autoregressive generation. Applying the same idea to other continuous-valued domains is presented as a direction the work could encourage, rather than an established experimental result.
summary.tldr: A diffusion-based token loss enables autoregressive image generation with continuous tokens, removing the need for vector quantization.

title: Autoregressive Image Generation without Vector Quantization

abstract: Recent advancements in generative models have significantly enhanced their capacity for image generation, enabling a wide range of applications such as image editing, completion and video editing. A specialized area within generative modeling is layout-to-image (L2I) generation, where predefined layouts of objects guide the generative process. In this study, we introduce a novel regional cross-attention module tailored to enrich layout-to-image generation. This module notably improves the representation of layout regions, particularly in scenarios where existing methods struggle with highly complex and detailed textual descriptions. Moreover, while current open-vocabulary L2I methods are trained in an open-set setting, their evaluations often occur in closed-set environments. To bridge this gap, we propose two metrics to assess L2I performance in open-vocabulary scenarios. Additionally, we conduct a comprehensive user study to validate the consistency of these metrics with human preferences.

paragraphs: Layout-to-image generation creates pictures from predefined arrangements of objects. When those objects have detailed textual descriptions, the model must represent both the requested placement and the rich content associated with each region. This paper introduces a regional cross-attention module intended to improve that regional representation.

The authors report that the module is particularly helpful for complex descriptions that existing methods struggle to handle. Its purpose is to strengthen how the generation process represents individual layout regions. This connects the method directly to a demanding part of the task: translating detailed descriptions into appropriately represented parts of an image.

The paper also identifies a mismatch between training and evaluation. Open-vocabulary systems are trained in an open-set setting but often tested in closed-set environments. The authors propose two metrics for assessing open-vocabulary layout-to-image generation and conduct a comprehensive user study to validate their consistency with human preferences. The work thus addresses both generation quality and whether evaluation reflects the broader conditions these systems are designed to handle.
summary.tldr: The paper improves regional modeling for detailed layout-to-image generation and introduces open-vocabulary evaluation metrics checked against human preferences.

title: Rethinking The Training And Evaluation of Rich-Context Layout-to-Image Generation

abstract: Dimension reduction (DR) is an important and widely studied technique in exploratory data analysis. However, traditional DR methods are not applicable to datasets with with a contrastive structure, where data are split into a foreground group of interest (case or treatment group), and a background group (control group). This type of data, common in biomedical studies, necessitates contrastive dimension reduction (CDR) methods to effectively capture information unique to or enriched in the foreground group relative to the background group. Despite the development of various CDR methods, two critical questions remain underexplored: when should these methods be applied, and how can the information unique to the foreground group be quantified? In this work, we address these gaps by proposing a hypothesis test to determine the existence of contrastive information, and introducing a contrastive dimension estimator (CDE) to quantify the unique components in the foreground group. We provide theoretical support for our methods and validate their effectiveness through extensive simulated, semi-simulated, and real experiments involving images, gene expressions, protein expressions, and medical sensors, demonstrating their ability to identify the unique information in the foreground group.

paragraphs: Some datasets contain a foreground group of interest and a background group used for comparison, such as treatment and control groups. The analytical goal is to find information that is specific to, or more prominent in, the foreground. A representation of overall variation does not directly answer that comparative question, motivating contrastive dimension reduction.

This paper addresses two decisions that arise before interpreting such a representation. First, the authors propose a hypothesis test for whether contrastive information exists. Second, they introduce a contrastive dimension estimator to estimate how many components capture information unique to the foreground. These tools distinguish evidence for a contrastive signal from the question of how much structure that signal contains.

The authors provide theoretical support and evaluate the methods using simulated, semi-simulated, and real data. The applications include images, gene expression, protein expression, and medical sensors. The reported results support the methods' ability to identify foreground-specific information across these settings, giving analysts a more principled basis for deciding when contrastive analysis is useful and how many dimensions to retain.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces a test for foreground-specific information and an estimator of its dimensionality to guide contrastive dimension reduction.

title: Contrastive dimension reduction: when and how?

abstract: We introduce a multi-winner reconfiguration model to examine how to transition between subsets of alternatives (aka. committees) through a sequence of minor yet impactful modifications, called reconfiguration path. We analyze this model under four approval-based voting rules: Chamberlin-Courant (CC), Proportional Approval Voting (PAV), Approval Voting (AV), and Satisfaction Approval Voting (SAV). The problem exhibits computational intractability for CC and PAV, and polynomial solvability for AV and SAV. We provide a detailed multivariate complexity analysis for CC and PAV, demonstrating that although the problem remains challenging in many scenarios, there are specific cases that allow for efficient parameterized algorithms.

paragraphs: Multi-winner selection chooses a subset of alternatives, called a committee. This paper studies the process of moving between committees through a sequence of small changes. It introduces a reconfiguration model in which those intermediate modifications form a path, making the transition between selections an object of computational study in its own right.

The authors examine four approval-based voting rules: Chamberlin-Courant, Proportional Approval Voting, Approval Voting, and Satisfaction Approval Voting. The complexity differs sharply by rule. Reconfiguration is computationally intractable for the first two, while the latter two admit polynomial-time solutions. Thus, the choice of voting rule affects the difficulty of computing a transition as well as defining how committees are evaluated.

For the two difficult rules, the paper provides a multivariate complexity analysis that examines how different problem parameters affect tractability. Many scenarios remain challenging, but some admit efficient parameterized algorithms. This refines the broad hardness result by identifying cases where additional structure makes computation manageable, helping distinguish general difficulty from more favorable settings.
summary.tldr: The difficulty of transitioning between committees through small changes depends strongly on the approval-based voting rule.

title: Multi-Winner Reconfiguration

abstract: We present a novel method, Contextual goal-Oriented Data Augmentation (CODA), which uses commonly available unlabeled trajectories and context-goal pairs to solve Contextual Goal-Oriented (CGO) problems. By carefully constructing an action-augmented MDP that is equivalent to the original MDP, CODA creates a fully labeled transition dataset under training contexts without additional approximation error. We conduct a novel theoretical analysis to demonstrate CODA's capability to solve CGO problems in the offline data setup. Empirical results also showcase the effectiveness of CODA, which outperforms other baseline methods across various context-goal relationships of CGO problem. This approach offers a promising direction to solving CGO problems using offline datasets.

paragraphs: The paper considers goal-oriented decision problems in which the relevant goal depends on context, using data that has already been collected. Its method, Contextual goal-Oriented Data Augmentation, or CODA, starts from unlabeled trajectories together with context-goal pairs. The central task is to turn these available information sources into data suitable for learning contextual decisions.

CODA constructs an action-augmented Markov decision process that is equivalent to the original decision process. Through this construction, it produces a fully labeled transition dataset for the training contexts without introducing additional approximation error. The equivalence matters because the data transformation is supported by a relationship to the original problem, rather than merely producing labels for a different decision task.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis of CODA's ability to solve these problems in an offline setting. Experiments also show that it outperforms baseline methods across different relationships between contexts and goals. The stated contribution is a principled way to make unlabeled trajectories useful for contextual goal-oriented learning, supported by both an error-preserving construction and empirical comparisons.
summary.tldr: CODA transforms unlabeled trajectories and context-goal pairs into labeled offline training data through an equivalent action-augmented decision process.

title: How to Solve Contextual Goal-Oriented Problems with Offline Datasets?

abstract: Learning the unknown causal parameters of a linear structural causal model is a fundamental task in causal analysis. The task, known as the problem of identification, asks to estimate the parameters of the model from acombination of assumptions on the graphical structure of the model and observational data, represented as a non-causal covariance matrix.In this paper, we give a new sound and complete algorithm for generic identification which runs in polynomial space. By a standard simulation result, namely $\mathsf{PSPACE} \subseteq \mathsf{EXP}$,this algorithm has exponential running time which vastly improves the state-of-the-art double exponential time method using a Gröbner basis approach. The paper also presents evidence that parameter identification is computationally hard in general. In particular, we prove, that the taskasking whether, for a given feasible correlation matrix, there are exactly one or two or more parameter sets explaining the observed matrix, is hard for $\forall \mathbb{R}$, the co-class of the existential theory of the reals. In particular, this problem is $\mathsf{coNP}$-hard.To our best knowledge, this is the first hardness result for some notion of identifiability.

paragraphs: Identification asks whether a causal model’s unknown parameters can be determined from observational data together with assumptions about its graphical structure. For linear structural causal models, the observations are represented by a covariance matrix. This paper studies the computational difficulty of deciding identification, rather than assuming that observational associations uniquely determine causal parameters.

The authors provide a sound and complete algorithm for generic identification that uses polynomial space. A standard complexity result gives an exponential-time simulation, improving substantially on the previous doubly exponential method based on Gröbner bases. This establishes a better computational upper bound for the generic identification problem.

The paper also proves hardness for a distinct question about a given feasible correlation matrix: whether exactly one parameter set, or multiple parameter sets, can explain it. That problem is hard for the universal theory of the reals and, consequently, coNP-hard. Together, the results improve the known algorithmic guarantee while showing that identification still includes computationally hard cases.
summary.tldr: A polynomial-space algorithm improves generic causal identification bounds, while a related uniqueness problem is proved computationally hard.

title: On the Complexity of Identification in Linear Structural Causal Models

abstract: Recent advancements in models linking natural language with human motions have shown significant promise in motion generation and editing based on instructional text. Motivated by applications in sports coaching and motor skill learning, we investigate the inverse problem: generating corrective instructional text, leveraging motion editing and generation models. We introduce a novel approach that, given a user’s current motion (source) and the desired motion (target), generates text instructions to guide the user towards achieving the target motion. We leverage large language models to generate corrective texts and utilize existing motion generation and editing frameworks to compile datasets of triplets (source motion, target motion, and corrective text). Using this data, we propose a new motion-language model for generating corrective instructions. We present both qualitative and quantitative results across a diverse range of applications that largely improve upon baselines. Our approach demonstrates its effectiveness in instructional scenarios, offering text-based guidance to correct and enhance user performance.

paragraphs: Motion generation and editing systems use written instructions to produce or alter human movement. CigTime investigates the reverse task: given someone's current movement and a desired movement, produce instructions explaining how to move toward the target. Sports coaching and motor skill learning motivate this focus on corrective guidance.

The approach uses large language models to create corrective text and existing motion generation and editing frameworks to assemble training examples. Each example connects three elements: a source motion, a target motion, and an instruction describing the correction. These triplets provide supervision for a new motion-language model that generates instructions from the two motions.

This formulation matters because its output describes a change between movements rather than merely describing a movement in isolation. The authors report qualitative and quantitative results across diverse applications, with substantial improvements over baselines. Their findings support the approach's effectiveness in the instructional scenarios examined, where text provides guidance for correcting performance toward a specified target.
summary.tldr: CigTime learns to generate corrective instructions by connecting a person's current motion, a target motion, and text describing the change.

title: CigTime: Corrective Instruction Generation Through Inverse Motion Editing

abstract: Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search is a key component in many modern machine learning pipelines; recent use cases include retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and vector databases. Clustering-based ANN algorithms, that use score computation methods based on product quantization (PQ), are often used in industrial-scale applications due to their scalability and suitability for distributed and disk-based implementations. However, they have slower query times than the leading graph-based ANN algorithms. In this work, we propose a new supervised score computation method based on the observation that inner product approximation is a multivariate (multi-output) regression problem that can be solved efficiently by reduced-rank regression. Our experiments show that on modern high-dimensional data sets, the proposed reduced-rank regression (RRR) method is superior to PQ in both query latency and memory usage. We also introduce LoRANN, a clustering-based ANN library that leverages the proposed score computation method. LoRANN is competitive with the leading graph-based algorithms and outperforms the state-of-the-art GPU ANN methods on high-dimensional data sets.

paragraphs: Approximate nearest-neighbor search retrieves vectors similar to a query and supports applications such as vector databases and retrieval-augmented generation. Clustering-based search methods scale well and suit distributed or disk-based systems, but methods using product quantization for scoring have slower queries than leading graph-based alternatives. This paper targets that scoring step.

The authors recast inner-product approximation as a supervised regression problem with multiple outputs. Reduced-rank regression then supplies an efficient way to estimate those scores. This changes how candidate similarities are computed while retaining a clustering-based search organization. The proposed scoring method is incorporated into the LoRANN search library.

On the high-dimensional datasets studied, reduced-rank regression improves both query latency and memory usage relative to product quantization. LoRANN is also competitive with leading graph-based algorithms and outperforms the compared state-of-the-art GPU search methods on high-dimensional data. These results show that improving the scoring mechanism can make clustering-based search substantially more competitive in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: LoRANN uses reduced-rank regression for similarity scoring, improving clustering-based nearest-neighbor search on high-dimensional datasets.

title: LoRANN: Low-Rank Matrix Factorization for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search

abstract: Inspired by the success of foundation models in applications such as ChatGPT, as graph data has been ubiquitous, one can envision the far-reaching impacts that can be brought by Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) with broader applications in the areas such as scientific research, social network analysis, drug discovery, and e-commerce. Despite the significant progress of pre-trained graph neural networks, there haven’t been GFMs that can achieve desired performance on various graph-learning-related tasks. Building GFMs may rely on a vocabulary that encodes transferable patterns shared among different tasks and domains. Unlike image and text, defining such transferable patterns for graphs remains an open question. In this paper, we aim to bridge this gap by rethinking the transferable patterns on graphs as computation trees -- i.e., tree structures derived from the message-passing process. Based on this insight, we propose a cross-task, cross-domain graph foundation model named GFT, short for Graph Foundation model with transferable Tree vocabulary. By treating computation trees as tokens within the transferable vocabulary, GFT improves model generalization and reduces the risk of negative transfer. The theoretical analyses and extensive experimental studies have demonstrated the transferability of computation trees and shown the effectiveness of GFT across diverse tasks and domains in graph learning. The open source code and data are available at https://github.com/Zehong-Wang/GFT.

paragraphs: A graph foundation model needs patterns that remain useful when the task or application domain changes. The paper identifies the choice of a transferable vocabulary as a central obstacle: graphs do not come with an obvious equivalent of reusable text tokens. GFT proposes computation trees as the units from which such a vocabulary can be built.

These trees are derived from the message-passing process used to exchange information across a graph. By treating the resulting structures as tokens, GFT represents graphs through patterns associated with how information is gathered and combined. The intended benefit is a shared representation that helps transfer across tasks and domains while reducing negative transfer, where knowledge carried from one setting harms another.

The paper provides theoretical analyses and extensive experiments supporting the transferability of computation trees and the effectiveness of GFT across diverse graph-learning settings. Its contribution is therefore both a model and a proposal for what a reusable graph vocabulary should contain. The reported findings support computation trees as useful transferable patterns without establishing them as the only possible foundation for graph models.
summary.tldr: GFT uses computation trees from graph message passing as reusable tokens to improve transfer across graph-learning tasks and domains.

title: GFT: Graph Foundation Model with Transferable Tree Vocabulary

abstract: Image Signal Processors (ISPs) convert raw sensor signals into digital images, which significantly influence the image quality and the performance of downstream computer vision tasks. Designing ISP pipeline and tuning ISP parameters are two key steps for building an imaging and vision system. To find optimal ISP configurations, recent works use deep neural networks as a proxy to search for ISP parameters or ISP pipelines. However, these methods are primarily designed to maximize the image quality, which are sub-optimal in the performance of high-level computer vision tasks such as detection, recognition, and tracking. Moreover, after training, the learned ISP pipelines are mostly fixed at the inference time, whose performance degrades in dynamic scenes. To jointly optimize ISP structures and parameters, we propose AdaptiveISP, a task-driven and scene-adaptive ISP. One key observation is that for the majority of input images, only a few processing modules are needed to improve the performance of downstream recognition tasks, and only a few inputs require more processing. Based on this, AdaptiveISP utilizes deep reinforcement learning to automatically generate an optimal ISP pipeline and the associated ISP parameters to maximize the detection performance. Experimental results show that AdaptiveISP not only surpasses the prior state-of-the-art methods for object detection but also dynamically manages the trade-off between detection performance and computational cost, especially suitable for scenes with large dynamic range variations.Project website: https://openimaginglab.github.io/AdaptiveISP/.

paragraphs: An image signal processor turns raw camera measurements into an image. Its processing choices affect both visual quality and how well an object detector works. AdaptiveISP addresses a mismatch in existing approaches: optimizing images to look good does not necessarily produce the best inputs for detection, and a fixed processing pipeline can struggle as scenes change.

The method learns to choose both the processing modules and their parameters for each input. It uses deep reinforcement learning with detection performance as the objective. Its design follows the observation that most images need only a few processing steps, while a smaller number benefit from more extensive processing.

The reported experiments show better object detection than prior state-of-the-art approaches, together with dynamic control over the balance between detection performance and computation. This makes the contribution more than another parameter-tuning method: it adapts the amount and structure of image processing to the scene. The abstract particularly highlights scenes with large variations in dynamic range.
summary.tldr: AdaptiveISP learns scene-dependent image-processing pipelines that improve object detection while adjusting computational cost.

title: AdaptiveISP: Learning an Adaptive Image Signal Processor for Object Detection

abstract: We investigate algorithmic collective action in transformer-based recommender systems. Our use case is a collective of fans aiming to promote the visibility of an underrepresented artist by strategically placing one of their songs in the existing playlists they control. We introduce two easily implementable strategies to select the position at which to insert the song and boost recommendations at test time. The strategies exploit statistical properties of the learner to leverage discontinuities in the recommendations, and the long-tail nature of song distributions. We evaluate the efficacy of our strategies using a publicly available recommender system model released by a major music streaming platform. Our findings reveal that even small collectives (controlling less than 0.01\% of the training data) can achieve up to $40\times$ more test time recommendations than songs with similar training set occurrences, on average. Focusing on the externalities of the strategy, we find that the recommendations of other songs are largely preserved, and the newly gained recommendations are distributed across various artists. Together, our findings demonstrate how carefully designed collective action strategies can be effective while not necessarily being adversarial.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether music fans can collectively increase an underrepresented artist’s visibility by changing playlists they already control. The intervention is specific: insert one of the artist’s songs at a strategically chosen position. The researchers introduce two simple placement strategies for influencing a transformer-based recommender trained on those playlists.

The strategies use statistical properties of the recommendation model, including abrupt changes in which songs get recommended and the uneven distribution of song popularity. This makes placement an additional source of influence beyond merely adding more occurrences of a song. The experiments use a publicly released recommendation model from a major streaming platform.

In the reported evaluation, groups controlling less than 0.01% of the training data could obtain up to 40 times as many recommendations, on average, as songs with similar training frequencies. Recommendations for other songs were largely preserved, and gains extended across different artists. These findings suggest that carefully coordinated participation can influence recommendations without necessarily functioning as an adversarial intervention.
summary.tldr: Small groups of fans can strategically position songs in playlists to substantially increase recommendations while largely preserving recommendations for other songs.

title: Algorithmic Collective Action in Recommender Systems: Promoting Songs by Reordering Playlists

abstract: Deep Neural Collapse (DNC) refers to the surprisingly rigid structure of the data representations in the final layers of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). Though the phenomenon has been measured in a variety of settings, its emergence is typically explained via data-agnostic approaches, such as the unconstrained features model. In this work, we introduce a data-dependent setting where DNC forms due to feature learning through the average gradient outer product (AGOP). The AGOP is defined with respect to a learned predictor and is equal to the uncentered covariance matrix of its input-output gradients averaged over the training dataset. Deep Recursive Feature Machines are a method that constructs a neural network by iteratively mapping the data with the AGOP and applying an untrained random feature map. We demonstrate theoretically and empirically that DNC occurs in Deep Recursive Feature Machines as a consequence of the projection with the AGOP matrix computed at each layer. We then provide evidence that this mechanism holds for neural networks more generally. We show that the right singular vectors and values of the weights can be responsible for the majority of within-class variability collapse for DNNs trained in the feature learning regime. As observed in recent work, this singular structure is highly correlated with that of the AGOP.

paragraphs: Deep neural collapse describes the unusually rigid organization of representations found in the final layers of trained networks. Many explanations treat those representations without explicitly incorporating the training data. This paper develops a data-dependent mechanism based on the average gradient outer product, or AGOP, which summarizes input-output gradient structure across the training set.

The authors study Deep Recursive Feature Machines, which repeatedly transform data using the AGOP and then apply an untrained random feature map. They show both theoretically and empirically that neural collapse arises in these models from the AGOP projection at each layer. This supplies a concrete feature-learning process through which the observed representation structure can emerge.

The paper also presents evidence that the mechanism extends to neural networks more broadly. In networks trained in the feature-learning regime, weight singular vectors and singular values can account for most of the collapse in variation within classes. Their strong relationship with AGOP structure supports the proposed explanation, while the broader-network claim remains evidence-based rather than a universal theorem.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes an AGOP-based mechanism for neural collapse in Deep Recursive Feature Machines and finds supporting evidence in broader neural networks.

title: Average gradient outer product as a mechanism for deep neural collapse

abstract: We introduce Exo2Ego-V, a novel exocentric-to-egocentric diffusion-based video generation method for daily-life skilled human activities where sparse 4-view exocentric viewpoints are configured 360° around the scene. This task is particularly challenging due to the significant variations between exocentric and egocentric viewpoints and high complexity of dynamic motions and real-world daily-life environments. To address these challenges, we first propose a new diffusion-based multi-view exocentric encoder to extract the dense multi-scale features from multi-view exocentric videos as the appearance conditions for egocentric video generation. Then, we design an exocentric-to-egocentric view translation prior to provide spatially aligned egocentric features as a concatenation guidance for the input of egocentric video diffusion model. Finally, we introduce the temporal attention layers into our egocentric video diffusion pipeline to improve the temporal consistency cross egocentric frames. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Exo2Ego-V significantly outperforms SOTA approaches on 5 categories from the Ego-Exo4D dataset with an average of 35% in terms of LPIPS. Our code and model will be made available on https://github.com/showlab/Exo2Ego-V.

paragraphs: Exo2Ego-V generates a first-person video from external recordings of someone performing a skilled everyday activity. Its input uses four viewpoints arranged around the scene. The task is challenging because the desired viewpoint differs substantially from the cameras' views, while both the person and the surrounding scene can change over time.

The method combines three components in a diffusion-based video system. A multi-view encoder extracts appearance information at several scales from the external videos. A view-translation prior supplies features spatially aligned with the desired first-person view. Temporal attention layers then help maintain consistency between generated frames. These components address appearance, viewpoint alignment, and continuity across time.

Experiments cover five categories from Ego-Exo4D. The authors report that Exo2Ego-V surpasses state-of-the-art approaches, with an average improvement of 35% in LPIPS. This supports the effectiveness of combining information from multiple external views with explicit guidance for the first-person viewpoint and temporal processing. The reported result concerns this four-view setup and the evaluated activity categories.
summary.tldr: Exo2Ego-V combines four external video views, viewpoint guidance, and temporal attention to generate first-person activity videos.

title: Exocentric-to-Egocentric Video Generation

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated notable potential in conducting complex tasks and are increasingly utilized in various financial applications. However, high-quality sequential financial investment decision-making remains challenging. These tasks require multiple interactions with a volatile environment for every decision, demanding sufficient intelligence to maximize returns and manage risks. Although LLMs have been used to develop agent systems that surpass human teams and yield impressive investment returns, opportunities to enhance multi-source information synthesis and optimize decision-making outcomes through timely experience refinement remain unexplored. Here, we introduce FinCon, an LLM-based multi-agent framework tailored for diverse financial tasks. Inspired by effective real-world investment firm organizational structures, FinCon utilizes a manager-analyst communication hierarchy. This structure allows for synchronized cross-functional agent collaboration towards unified goals through natural language interactions and equips each agent with greater memory capacity than humans. Additionally, a risk-control component in FinCon enhances decision quality by episodically initiating a self-critiquing mechanism to update systematic investment beliefs. The conceptualized beliefs serve as verbal reinforcement for the future agent’s behavior and can be selectively propagated to the appropriate node that requires knowledge updates. This feature significantly improves performance while reducing unnecessary peer-to-peer communication costs. Moreover, FinCon demonstrates strong generalization capabilities in various financial tasks, including stock trading and portfolio management.

paragraphs: Financial investment decisions unfold over time, requiring repeated interpretation of information and adjustment to a volatile environment. FinCon organizes LLM agents around this problem using a manager-analyst hierarchy inspired by investment firms. Agents communicate in natural language and coordinate their different responsibilities toward shared objectives, helping combine information from multiple sources.

A risk-control component periodically triggers self-critique. The system uses that reflection to update its investment beliefs, expressing lessons as concepts that can guide later behavior. These verbal updates can be sent selectively to the agents that need them. This makes experience refinement part of the decision process while reducing unnecessary communication among peers.

The paper reports that this mechanism improves performance and that FinCon generalizes across financial tasks, including stock trading and portfolio management. Its central contribution is the combination of hierarchical collaboration and targeted revision of investment beliefs. The stated results support using structured communication and experience-based language feedback to improve sequential decision-making within the evaluated financial applications.
summary.tldr: FinCon coordinates financial LLM agents through a manager-analyst hierarchy and targeted belief updates derived from periodic self-critique.

title: FinCon: A Synthesized LLM Multi-Agent System with Conceptual Verbal Reinforcement for Enhanced Financial Decision Making

abstract: We propose estimating Gaussian graphical models (GGMs) that are fair with respect to sensitive nodal attributes. Many real-world models exhibit unfair discriminatory behavior due to biases in data. Such discrimination is known to be exacerbated when data is equipped with pairwise relationships encoded in a graph. Additionally, the effect of biased data on graphical models is largely underexplored. We thus introduce fairness for graphical models in the form of two bias metrics to promote balance in statistical similarities across nodal groups with different sensitive attributes. Leveraging these metrics, we present Fair GLASSO, a regularized graphical lasso approach to obtain sparse Gaussian precision matrices with unbiased statistical dependencies across groups. We also propose an efficient proximal gradient algorithm to obtain the estimates. Theoretically, we express the tradeoff between fair and accurate estimated precision matrices. Critically, this includes demonstrating when accuracy can be preserved in the presence of a fairness regularizer. On top of this, we study the complexity of Fair GLASSO and demonstrate that our algorithm enjoys a fast convergence rate. Our empirical validation includes synthetic and real-world simulations that illustrate the value and effectiveness of our proposed optimization problem and iterative algorithm.

paragraphs: Fair GLASSO addresses fairness in Gaussian graphical models, where a graph represents statistical relationships among variables. The paper focuses on sensitive attributes associated with nodes and on imbalances between groups. It introduces two bias measures that encourage balance in statistical similarities across those groups, making the intended notion of fairness part of the model-estimation problem.

The method adds fairness regularization to graphical lasso, which estimates sparse Gaussian precision matrices. These matrices describe the dependency structure the model learns. An efficient proximal gradient algorithm computes the estimates. By incorporating the proposed bias measures into estimation, the method makes group balance an explicit objective alongside the accuracy and sparsity of the resulting graphical model.

The theoretical analysis describes the tradeoff between fairness and estimation accuracy, including conditions under which adding fairness regularization can preserve accuracy. It also analyzes computational complexity and establishes fast convergence for the algorithm. Synthetic and real-world simulations support the approach’s effectiveness. The fairness claim is tied to the proposed statistical measures, and accuracy preservation is a conditional result.
summary.tldr: Fair GLASSO adds group-balance penalties to sparse Gaussian graphical-model estimation and analyzes when fairness improvements can preserve accuracy.

title: Fair GLASSO: Estimating Fair Graphical Models with Unbiased Statistical Behavior

paragraphs: Sequential decision-making can be approached by generating trajectories conditioned on what a user wants. Existing return-conditioned diffusion approaches depend on well-defined reward functions, which require human effort and can be difficult to specify across multiple tasks. This paper instead considers preferences as the information used to guide behavior.

The proposed framework learns representations aligned with preference labels across tasks. Those representations become conditions for a diffusion model’s generation process. This connects preference learning with trajectory generation: the model receives a learned encoding of the desired preference, rather than relying only on a target return supplied by a reward function.

The authors identify a consistency problem in conventional classifier-free guidance: generated trajectories may not agree with their conditions. They introduce an auxiliary regularization objective aimed at strengthening that connection. The supplied abstract ends while describing its mutual-information objective, so it provides no completed formulation or experimental findings. The supported contribution is the proposed combination of multi-task preference representations, conditional diffusion, and regularization addressing condition–trajectory consistency.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes preference-conditioned diffusion with auxiliary regularization to better align generated trajectories with preferences across tasks.

title: Regularized Conditional Diffusion Model for Multi-Task Preference Alignment

abstract: This paper introduces a human-in-the-loop computer vision framework that uses generative AI to propose micro-scale design interventions in public space and support more continuous, local participation. Using Grounding DINO and a curated subset of the ADE20K dataset as a proxy for the urban built environment, the system detects urban objects and builds co-occurrence embeddings that reveal common spatial configurations. From this analysis, the user receives five statistically likely complements to a chosen anchor object. A vision language model then reasons over the scene image and the selected pair to suggest a third object that completes a more complex urban tactic. The workflow keeps people in control of selection and refinement and aims to move beyond top-down master planning by grounding choices in everyday patterns and lived experience.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a recommendation workflow for small design interventions in public spaces. It combines computer vision with human selection so that suggestions can reflect the objects already present in a scene. The broader aim is to support ongoing, local participation in urban design through choices grounded in everyday spatial patterns.

The system uses Grounding DINO and a curated subset of ADE20K as a proxy for the urban built environment. Detected objects are used to build co-occurrence embeddings that capture common configurations. After a user chooses an anchor object, the system recommends five statistically likely complementary objects.

A vision-language model then considers the scene image and the selected pair to propose a third object, developing a more complex intervention. People retain control over selection and refinement throughout the process. The method combines statistical familiarity with scene-based reasoning: common combinations provide initial options, and contextual interpretation extends the chosen arrangement. Its intended contribution is participatory design support for localized public-space decisions.
summary.tldr: A human-guided urban design workflow combines object co-occurrence patterns and vision-language reasoning to suggest small public-space interventions.

title: Scene-Aware Urban Design: A Human–AI Recommendation Framework Using Co-Occurrence Embeddings and Vision-Language Models

abstract: AI-generated images have become pervasive, raising critical concerns around content authenticity, intellectual property, and the spread of misinformation. Invisible watermarks offer a promising solution for identifying AI-generated images, preserving content provenance without degrading visual quality. However, their real-world robustness remains uncertain due to the lack of standardized evaluation protocols and large-scale stress testing. To bridge this gap, we organized “Erasing the Invisible,” a NeurIPS 2024 competition and newly established benchmark designed to systematically stress testing the resilience of watermarking techniques. The competition introduced two attack tracks—Black-box and Beige-box—that simulate practical scenarios with varying levels of attacker knowledge on watermarks, providing a comprehensive assessment of watermark robustness. The competition attracted significant global participation, with 2,722 submissions from 298 teams. Through a rigorous evaluation pipeline featuring real-time feedback and human-verified final rankings, participants developed and demonstrated new attack strategies that revealed critical vulnerabilities in state-of-the-art watermarking methods. On average, the top-5 teams in both tracks could remove watermarks from $\geq$ 89% of the images while preserving high visual quality, setting strong baselines for future research on watermark attacks and defenses. abstract: Federated clustering (FC) aims to discover global cluster structures across decentralized clients without sharing raw data, making privacy preservation a fundamental requirement. There are two critical challenges: (1) privacy leakage during collaboration, and (2) robustness degradation due to aggregation of proxy information from non-independent and identically distributed (Non-IID) local data, leading to inaccurate or inconsistent global clustering. Existing solutions typically rely on model-specific local proxies, which are sensitive to data heterogeneity and inherit inductive biases from their centralized counterparts, thus limiting robustness and generality. We propose Omni Federated Clustering (OmniFC), a unified and model-agnostic framework. Leveraging Lagrange coded computing, our method enables clients to share only encoded data, allowing exact reconstruction of the global distance matrix—a fundamental representation of sample relationships—without leaking private information, even under client collusion. This construction is naturally resilient to Non-IID data distributions. This approach decouples FC from model-specific proxies, providing a unified extension mechanism applicable to diverse centralized clustering methods. Theoretical analysis confirms both reconstruction fidelity and privacy guarantees, while comprehensive experiments demonstrate OmniFC's superior robustness, effectiveness, and generality across various benchmarks compared to state-of-the-art methods. Code will be released.

The paper argues that these proxies can become unreliable when clients have different data distributions, while collaboration also creates opportunities for privacy leakage.

OmniFC replaces model-specific proxy aggregation with reconstruction of the global distance matrix, which represents relationships between samples. It uses Lagrange coded computing so clients share encoded data. The authors establish exact reconstruction and privacy guarantees, including protection under client collusion. This construction is described as naturally resilient to differences in the clients’ data distributions.

That provides a unified way to extend diverse centralized clustering methods to distributed data. Theoretical analysis supports reconstruction fidelity and privacy, while benchmark experiments report stronger robustness, effectiveness, and generality than state-of-the-art alternatives. The central contribution is preserving global sample relationships without relying on heterogeneous local model summaries.
summary.tldr: OmniFC uses encoded client data to reconstruct global distances exactly, enabling privacy-preserving clustering across heterogeneous clients.

title: OmniFC: Rethinking Federated Clustering via Lossless and Secure Distance Reconstruction

abstract: The unusual properties of in-context learning (ICL) have prompted investigations into the internal mechanisms of large language models. Prior work typically focuses on either special attention heads or task vectors at specific layers, but lacks a unified framework linking these components to the evolution of hidden states across layers that ultimately produce the model’s output. In this paper, we propose such a framework for ICL in classification tasks by analyzing two geometric factors that govern performance: the separability and alignment of query hidden states. A fine-grained analysis of layer-wise dynamics reveals a striking two-stage mechanism—separability emerges in early layers, while alignment develops in later layers. Ablation studies further show that Previous Token Heads drive separability, while Induction Heads and task vectors enhance alignment. Our findings thus bridge the gap between attention heads and task vectors, offering a unified account of ICL’s underlying mechanisms.

The layer-by-layer analysis reveals a two-stage pattern, with separability emerging early and alignment developing later. This gives an account of how changes in hidden-state geometry relate to performance across the model’s depth, bringing previously separate mechanisms into a shared description.

Ablation studies associate Previous Token Heads with driving separability, while Induction Heads and task vectors improve alignment. These findings assign different roles to the components within the same overall process. The resulting explanation links attention heads, task vectors, and hidden-state evolution for the classification setting studied, offering a unified account of how these internal mechanisms contribute to in-context learning.
summary.tldr: The paper links attention heads and task vectors through a two-stage pattern of early separability and later alignment in classification representations.

title: Unifying Attention Heads and Task Vectors via Hidden State Geometry in In-Context Learning

abstract: Availability attacks, or unlearnable examples, are defensive techniques that allow data owners to modify their datasets in ways that prevent unauthorized machine learning models from learning effectively while maintaining the data's intended functionality. It has led to the release of popular black-box tools (e.g., APIs) for users to upload personal data and receive protected counterparts. In this work, we show that such black-box protections can be substantially compromised if a small set of unprotected in-distribution data is available. Specifically, we propose a novel threat model of protection leakage, where an adversary can (1) easily acquire (unprotected, protected) pairs by querying the black-box protections with a small unprotected dataset; and (2) train a diffusion bridge model to build a mapping between unprotected and protected data. This mapping, termed BridgePure, can effectively remove the protection from any previously unseen data within the same distribution. BridgePure demonstrates superior purification performance on classification and style mimicry tasks, exposing critical vulnerabilities in black-box data protection. We suggest that practitioners implement multi-level countermeasures to mitigate such risks.

paragraphs: Some data-protection systems modify examples so that unauthorized models struggle to learn from them while the data retain their intended use. Black-box services make such protection available without exposing how it works. This paper investigates whether hiding the protection mechanism is sufficient when an adversary possesses a small amount of unprotected data from the same distribution.

The proposed threat model is protection leakage. An adversary submits those unprotected examples to the protection service, obtaining matched original and protected pairs. BridgePure uses these pairs to train a diffusion bridge model that learns a mapping between the two forms of data. The learned mapping can then remove protection from previously unseen examples within that same distribution.

Experiments on classification and style mimicry tasks report superior purification performance, showing that limited paired data can substantially compromise the studied protections. The shared-distribution condition is central to the stated threat. The findings motivate the authors' recommendation for multiple levels of countermeasures, because black-box access can itself provide examples that reveal how to reverse protection.
summary.tldr: BridgePure shows that a small set of paired examples can enable removal of black-box data protection from unseen data in the same distribution.

title: BridgePure: Limited Protection Leakage Can Break Black-Box Data Protection

abstract: Recently, slow-thinking systems like GPT-o1 and DeepSeek-R1 have demonstrated great potential in solving challenging problems through explicit reflection. They significantly outperform the best fast-thinking models, such as GPT-4o, on various math and science benchmarks. However, their multimodal reasoning capabilities remain on par with fast-thinking models. For instance, GPT-o1's performance on benchmarks like MathVista, MathVerse, and MathVision is similar to fast-thinking models. In this paper, we aim to enhance the slow-thinking capabilities of vision-language models using reinforcement learning (without relying on distillation) to advance the state of the art. First, we adapt the GRPO algorithm with a novel technique called Selective Sample Replay (SSR) to address the vanishing advantages problem. While this approach yields strong performance, the resulting RL-trained models exhibit limited self-reflection or self-verification. To further encourage slow-thinking, we introduce Forced Rethinking, which appends a rethinking trigger token to the end of rollouts in RL training, explicitly enforcing a self-reflection reasoning step. By combining these two techniques, our model, VL-Rethinker, advances state-of-the-art scores on MathVista, MathVerse to achieve 80.4%, 63.5% respectively. VL-Rethinker also achieves open-source SoTA on multi-disciplinary benchmarks such as MathVision, MMMU-Pro, EMMA, and MEGA-Bench, narrowing the gap with OpenAI-o1. We conduct comprehensive ablations and analysis to provide insights into the effectiveness of our approach.

abstract: Distinguishing cause and effect from bivariate observational data is a foundational problem in many disciplines, but challenging without additional assumptions. Additive noise models (ANMs) are widely used to enable sample-efficient bivariate causal discovery. However, conventional ANM-based methods fail when unobserved mediators corrupt the causal relationship between variables. This paper makes three key contributions: first, we rigorously characterize why standard ANM approaches break down in the presence of unmeasured mediators. Second, we demonstrate that prior solutions for hidden mediation are brittle in finite sample settings, limiting their practical utility. To address these gaps, we propose Bivariate Denoising Diffusion (BiDD) for causal discovery, a method designed to handle latent noise introduced by unmeasured mediators. Unlike prior methods that infer directionality through mean squared error loss comparisons, our approach introduces a novel independence test statistic: during the noising and denoising processes for each variable, we condition on the other variable as input and evaluate the independence of the predicted noise relative to this input. We prove asymptotic consistency of BiDD under the ANM, and conjecture that it performs well under hidden mediation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate consistent performance, outperforming existing methods in mediator-corrupted settings while maintaining strong performance in mediator-free settings.

paragraphs: Inferring which of two observed variables causes the other requires assumptions. Additive noise models provide one useful foundation, but unobserved mediating variables can disrupt their usual causal tests. This paper characterizes why conventional methods fail in that situation and shows that earlier approaches to hidden mediation can be fragile when only finite samples are available.

Bivariate Denoising Diffusion, or BiDD, compares the two possible directions using a new independence statistic. For each variable, its noising and denoising process is conditioned on the other variable. The method then evaluates whether the predicted noise is independent of that conditioning input. This replaces the mean-squared-error comparisons used by prior approaches with a test centered on noise independence.

The theoretical and empirical claims have different scopes. The authors prove asymptotic consistency under the additive noise model, while good performance with hidden mediation is a conjecture. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data support that conjecture: BiDD outperforms existing methods in mediator-corrupted settings and retains strong performance without mediators. These findings do not extend the stated consistency proof to hidden mediation.
summary.tldr: BiDD uses diffusion-based noise-independence tests for causal direction, with consistency under additive noise models and empirical support under hidden mediation.

title: When Additive Noise Meets Unobserved Mediators: Bivariate Denoising Diffusion for Causal Discovery

abstract: In modern theoretical analyses of neural networks, the infinite-width limit is often invoked to justify Gaussian approximations of neuron preactivations (e.g., via neural network Gaussian processes or Tensor Programs). However, these Gaussian-based asymptotic theories have so far been unable to capture the behavior of attention layers, except under special regimes such as infinitely many heads or tailored scaling schemes. In this paper, leveraging the Tensor Programs framework, we rigorously identify the infinite-width limit distribution of variables within a single attention layer under realistic architectural dimensionality and standard $1/\sqrt{n}$-scaling with $n$ dimensionality. We derive the exact form of this limit law without resorting to infinite-head approximations or tailored scalings, demonstrating that it departs fundamentally from Gaussianity. This limiting distribution exhibits non-Gaussianity from a hierarchical structure, being Gaussian conditional on the random similarity scores. Numerical experiments validate our theoretical predictions, confirming the effectiveness of our theory at finite width and accurate description of finite-head attentions. Beyond characterizing a standalone attention layer, our findings lay the groundwork for developing a unified theory of deep Transformer architectures in the infinite-width regime.

Attention has resisted that treatment under ordinary architectural choices, with earlier Gaussian descriptions requiring special scaling or infinitely many attention heads. This paper uses Tensor Programs to characterize the limiting distribution inside a single attention layer under standard inverse-square-root scaling.

The derived distribution is fundamentally non-Gaussian overall, but its structure is more specific than that label alone suggests. Conditional on the random similarity scores used by attention, the distribution is Gaussian. The randomness in those scores creates a hierarchy that changes the unconditional distribution. This distinction explains why a simple Gaussian approximation misses part of attention’s behavior.

Numerical experiments support the theoretical predictions and show that the description is useful at finite width and with finitely many heads. The result establishes an exact limiting law for the studied single layer without the special regimes previously needed. It also offers groundwork for a broader theory of deep Transformers, rather than already providing that complete theory.
summary.tldr: A single attention layer has a non-Gaussian infinite-width limit under standard scaling, although it is Gaussian conditional on random similarity scores.

title: Infinite-Width Limit of a Single Attention Layer: Analysis via Tensor Programs

abstract: Recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have enabled the development of mobile agents that can understand visual inputs and follow user instructions, unlocking new possibilities for automating complex tasks on mobile devices. However, applying these models to real-world mobile scenarios remains a significant challenge due to the long-horizon task execution, difficulty in error recovery, and the cold-start problem in unfamiliar environments. To address these challenges, we propose MobileUse, a GUI agent designed for robust and adaptive mobile task execution. To improve resilience in long-horizon tasks and dynamic environments, we introduce a hierarchical reflection architecture that enables the agent to self-monitor, detect, and recover from errors across multiple temporal scales—ranging from individual actions to overall task completion—while maintaining efficiency through a Reflection-on-Demand strategy. To tackle cold-start issues, we further introduce a proactive exploration module, which enriches the agent’s understanding of the environment through self-planned exploration. Evaluations on the AndroidWorld and AndroidLab benchmarks demonstrate that MobileUse establishes new state-of-the-art performance, achieving success rates of 62.9% and 44.2%, respectively. To facilitate real-world applications, we release an out-of-the-box toolkit for automated task execution on physical mobile devices, which is available at https://github.com/MadeAgents/mobile-use.

MobileUse addresses these challenges with a graphical-interface agent built around monitoring its own progress. title: MobileUse: A Hierarchical Reflection-Driven GUI Agent for Autonomous Mobile Operation

abstract: We study the problem of estimating the average treatment effect (ATE) in adaptive experiments where treatment can only be encouraged—rather than directly assigned—via a binary instrumental variable. Building on semiparametric efficiency theory, we derive the efficiency bound for ATE estimation under arbitrary, history-dependent instrument-assignment policies, and show it is minimized by a variance-aware allocation rule that balances outcome noise and compliance variability. Leveraging this insight, we introduce AMRIV—an **A**daptive, **M**ultiply-**R**obust estimator for **I**nstrumental-**V**ariable settings with variance-optimal assignment. AMRIV pairs (i) an online policy that adaptively approximates the optimal allocation with (ii) a sequential, influence-function–based estimator that attains the semiparametric efficiency bound while retaining multiply-robust consistency. We establish asymptotic normality, explicit convergence rates, and anytime-valid asymptotic confidence sequences that enable sequential inference. Finally, we demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our approach through empirical studies, showing that adaptive instrument assignment, when combined with the AMRIV estimator, yields improved efficiency and robustness compared to existing baselines.

This creates a gap between the assigned encouragement and actual treatment. The paper studies average treatment-effect estimation in this setting when a binary instrument supplies the encouragement and its assignment can adapt to the experiment’s history.

The authors derive a semiparametric efficiency bound, describing the achievable statistical precision within their framework. They show that a variance-aware assignment rule minimizes this bound by balancing outcome noise with variability in compliance. summary.tldr: AMRIV jointly adapts treatment encouragement and effect estimation to improve statistical efficiency when participants may not comply.

title: Efficient Adaptive Experimentation with Noncompliance

abstract: Despite the significant progress in diffusion prior-based image restoration for real-world scenarios, most existing methods apply uniform processing to the entire image, lacking the capability to perform region-customized image restoration according to user preferences. In this work, we propose a new framework, namely InstructRestore, to perform region-adjustable image restoration following human instructions. To achieve this, we first develop a data generation engine to produce training triplets, each consisting of a high-quality image, the target region description, and the corresponding region mask. With this engine and careful data screening, we construct a comprehensive dataset comprising 536,945 triplets to support the training and evaluation of this task. We then examine how to integrate the low-quality image features under the ControlNet architecture to adjust the degree of image details enhancement. Consequently, we develop a ControlNet-like model to identify the target region and allocate different integration scales to the target and surrounding regions, enabling region-customized image restoration that aligns with user instructions. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed InstructRestore approach enables effective human-instructed image restoration, including restoration with controllable bokeh blur effects and region-specific restoration with continuous intensity control. Our work advances the investigation of interactive image restoration and enhancement techniques. Data, code, and models are publicly available at https://github.com/shuaizhengliu/InstructRestore.git.

The authors build a data-generation engine and screen its outputs to produce 536,945 training and evaluation triplets. Each contains a high-quality image, a description of a target region, and a corresponding mask. They then study how incorporating low-quality image features within a ControlNet architecture affects the strength of detail enhancement.

The resulting ControlNet-like model identifies the requested region and uses different feature-integration scales for that region and its surroundings. Experiments demonstrate instruction-guided restoration with adjustable bokeh blur and continuous control over regional restoration intensity. The contribution combines a dataset for learning where instructions apply with a mechanism for controlling how strongly those areas are restored, supporting more interactive image enhancement.
summary.tldr: InstructRestore follows region descriptions to apply different restoration strengths across an image, including controllable background blur.

title: InstructRestore: Region-Customized Image Restoration with Human Instructions

abstract: Stereo Depth Estimation in real-world environments poses significant challenges due to dynamic domain shifts, sparse or unreliable supervision, and the high cost of acquiring dense ground-truth labels. While recent Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) methods offer promising solutions, most rely on static target domain assumptions and input-invariant adaptation strategies, limiting their effectiveness under continual shifts. In this paper, we propose RobIA, a novel Robust, Instance-Aware framework for Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA) in stereo depth estimation. RobIA integrates two key components: (1) Attend-and-Excite Mixture-of-Experts (AttEx-MoE), a parameter-efficient module that dynamically routes input to frozen experts via lightweight self-attention mechanism tailored to epipolar geometry, and (2) Robust AdaptBN Teacher, a PEFT-based teacher model that provides dense pseudo-supervision by complementing sparse handcrafted labels. This strategy enables input-specific flexibility, broad supervision coverage, improving generalization under domain shift. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RobIA achieves superior adaptation performance across dynamic target domains while maintaining computational efficiency.

paragraphs: RobIA adapts stereo depth estimation as the operating environment keeps changing. Stereo models face shifting visual conditions and limited reliable depth supervision, while dense ground-truth labels are expensive to obtain. The paper targets continual test-time adaptation, where an approach must respond to ongoing changes rather than assume one fixed target domain.

Its first component, AttEx-MoE, routes each input to frozen experts using a lightweight attention mechanism designed around stereo geometry. This provides input-specific adaptation with relatively few adjustable parameters. The second component, Robust AdaptBN Teacher, uses parameter-efficient adaptation to produce dense pseudo-labels that complement sparse handcrafted labels.

These components address different needs: routing provides flexibility for individual inputs, and the teacher broadens the coverage of supervision available during adaptation. Experiments across dynamic target domains report superior adaptation performance while maintaining computational efficiency. The findings support combining instance-aware computation with denser teacher-provided supervision when a stereo system must keep adapting to changing conditions.
summary.tldr: RobIA combines input-specific expert routing with dense teacher supervision to adapt stereo depth models efficiently across continually changing domains.

title: RobIA: Robust Instance-aware Continual Test-time Adaptation for Deep Stereo

abstract: Accurately modeling pedestrian intention and understanding driver decision-making processes are critical for the development of safe and socially aware autonomous driving systems. However, existing datasets primarily emphasize observable behavior, offering limited insight into the underlying causal reasoning that informs human interpretation and response during traffic interactions. To address this gap, we introduce PSI, a benchmark dataset that captures the dynamic evolution of pedestrian crossing intentions from the driver’s perspective, enriched with human-annotated textual explanations that reflect the reasoning behind intention estimation and driving decision making. These annotations offer a unique foundation for developing and benchmarking models that combine predictive performance with interpretable and human-aligned reasoning. PSI supports standardized tasks and evaluation protocols across multiple dimensions, including pedestrian intention prediction, driver decision modeling, reasoning generation, and trajectory forecasting and more. By enabling causal and interpretable evaluation, PSI advances research toward autonomous systems that can reason, act, and explain in alignment with human cognitive processes.

paragraphs: Predicting pedestrian behavior requires interpreting how a traffic interaction develops, as well as observing movement. PSI addresses a gap in datasets that emphasize visible behavior but provide little information about the reasoning behind a driver’s interpretation and response. It focuses on pedestrian crossing intentions as understood from the driver’s perspective.

The benchmark records how those intentions evolve and adds human-written explanations of intention estimates and driving decisions. These annotations let researchers study both a model’s prediction and its account of the reasoning behind that prediction. Standardized tasks and evaluation protocols cover intention prediction, driver decision modeling, reasoning generation, trajectory forecasting, and related capabilities.

The main contribution is an evaluation resource that connects traffic predictions with human interpretations and explanations. It supports research on systems whose decisions can be assessed for predictive quality and alignment with human reasoning. The abstract presents PSI as a foundation for causal and interpretable evaluation, rather than reporting that a particular autonomous driving system has already achieved human-aligned reasoning or improved road safety.
summary.tldr: PSI benchmarks evolving pedestrian intentions and driver responses using human explanations alongside standardized prediction and reasoning tasks.

title: PSI: A Benchmark for Human Interpretation and Response in Traffic Interactions

abstract: Are there any conditions under which a generative model’s outputs are guaranteed not to infringe the copyrights of its training data? This is the question of "provable copyright protection" first posed by Vyas, Kakade, and Barak [ICML 2023]. They define _near access-freeness (NAF)_ and propose it as sufficient for protection. This paper revisits the question and establishes new foundations for provable copyright protection---foundations that are firmer both technically and legally. First, we show that NAF alone does not prevent infringement. In fact, NAF models can enable verbatim copying, a blatant failure of copy protection that we dub being _tainted_. Then, we introduce our _blameless copy protection framework_ for defining meaningful guarantees, and instantiate it with _clean-room copy protection_. Clean-room copy protection allows a user to control their risk of copying by behaving in a way that is unlikely to copy in a counterfactual "clean-room setting." Finally, we formalize a common intuition about differential privacy and copyright by proving that DP implies clean-room copy protection when the dataset is _golden_, a copyright deduplication requirement.

paragraphs: The paper asks what formal conditions could protect generative-model users against copying copyrighted training material. It revisits near access-freeness, a previously proposed sufficient condition, and shows that this condition alone does not prevent infringement. In particular, models satisfying it can still enable verbatim copying, which the authors describe as a tainted model.

To develop more meaningful guarantees, the authors introduce a blameless copy protection framework and a specific version called clean-room copy protection. This version relates a user's copying risk to their behavior in a hypothetical clean-room setting. A user can control that risk by behaving in a way that would be unlikely to produce copying in that counterfactual setting.

The paper also establishes a conditional connection to differential privacy: it implies clean-room copy protection when the dataset meets the authors' golden requirement for copyright deduplication. That dataset condition is essential to the stated result. The contribution replaces an insufficient guarantee with a framework that explicitly accounts for user behavior and the conditions under which privacy can provide copying protection.
summary.tldr: The paper exposes a flaw in an earlier copyright-protection condition and develops a clean-room guarantee that differential privacy satisfies under a deduplication requirement.

title: Blameless Users in a Clean Room: Defining Copyright Protection for Generative Models

abstract: Humanoid robots are promising to acquire various skills by imitating human behaviors. However, existing algorithms are only capable of tracking smooth, low-speed human motions, even with delicate reward and curriculum design. This paper presents a physics-based humanoid control framework, aiming to master highly-dynamic human behaviors such as Kungfu and dancing through multi-steps motion processing and adaptive motion tracking. For motion processing, we design a pipeline to extract, filter out, correct, and retarget motions, while ensuring compliance with physical constraints to the maximum extent. For motion imitation, we formulate a bi-level optimization problem to dynamically adjust the tracking accuracy tolerance based on the current tracking error, creating an adaptive curriculum mechanism. We further construct an asymmetric actor-critic framework for policy training. In experiments, we train whole-body control policies to imitate a set of highly dynamic motions. Our method achieves significantly lower tracking errors than existing approaches and is successfully deployed on the Unitree G1 robot, demonstrating stable and expressive behaviors. The project page is https://kungfubot.github.io.
