paragraphs: KungfuBot tackles humanoid imitation of rapid, demanding human movements such as Kungfu and dancing. These motions create challenges beyond tracking smooth, slow demonstrations. The framework addresses both the preparation of human motion data and the way a robot learns to follow that motion under physical constraints.

Its processing pipeline extracts motions, filters unsuitable material, corrects motions, and retargets them to the robot while seeking the greatest possible physical compatibility. During learning, a bi-level optimization procedure adjusts the allowed tracking error according to the policy's current performance. This creates an adaptive curriculum: tracking demands change as the robot learns. Policy training also uses an asymmetric actor-critic framework.

In experiments with a collection of highly dynamic motions, the resulting whole-body policies achieve substantially lower tracking errors than existing approaches. The researchers also deploy the controller on a Unitree G1 robot, where it produces stable and expressive behavior. These results connect improvements in motion tracking to demonstrated physical execution, supporting the combination of careful motion preparation and adaptive training.
summary.tldr: KungfuBot combines motion processing and adaptive tracking to learn dynamic humanoid skills and demonstrate them on a Unitree G1.

title: KungfuBot: Physics-Based Humanoid Whole-Body Control for Learning Highly-Dynamic Skills

abstract: Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning (FSCIL) challenges models to sequentially learn new classes from minimal examples without forgetting prior knowledge, a task complicated by the stability-plasticity dilemma and data scarcity. Current FSCIL methods often struggle with generalization due to their reliance on limited datasets. While diffusion models offer a path for data augmentation, their direct application can lead to semantic misalignment or ineffective guidance. This paper introduces Diffusion-Classifier Synergy (DCS), a novel framework that establishes a mutual boosting loop between diffusion model and FSCIL classifier. DCS utilizes a reward-aligned learning strategy, where a dynamic, multi-faceted reward function derived from the classifier's state directs the diffusion model. This reward system operates at two levels: the feature level ensures semantic coherence and diversity using prototype-anchored maximum mean discrepancy and dimension-wise variance matching, while the logits level promotes exploratory image generation and enhances inter-class discriminability through confidence recalibration and cross-session confusion-aware mechanisms. This co-evolutionary process, where generated images refine the classifier and an improved classifier state yields better reward signals, demonstrably achieves state-of-the-art performance on FSCIL benchmarks, significantly enhancing both knowledge retention and new class learning.

paragraphs: Few-shot class-incremental learning requires a classifier to learn new categories from very few examples while retaining earlier categories. Synthetic images could expand the training data, but a diffusion model may generate examples that are semantically misaligned or insufficiently useful. DCS makes image generation responsive to the classifier’s current learning needs.

The framework establishes a feedback loop between generator and classifier. Rewards derived from the classifier guide the diffusion model, and generated images then help train the classifier. Feature-level rewards encourage semantic agreement and diversity through prototype-anchored distribution comparison and dimension-wise variance matching. Output-score rewards encourage exploration and better class separation through confidence recalibration and mechanisms that account for confusion across learning sessions.

As the classifier improves, its updated state supplies new reward signals for generation. The paper reports state-of-the-art performance on the evaluated benchmarks, with gains in both retaining old knowledge and learning new classes. The findings support adapting augmentation to an evolving classifier, rather than treating synthetic data production as a fixed preliminary step.
summary.tldr: DCS couples a diffusion generator and incremental classifier in a reward-guided feedback loop that improves old-class retention and new-class learning.

title: Diffusion-Classifier Synergy: Reward-Aligned Learning via Mutual Boosting Loop for FSCIL

abstract: In recent years, face-based deep-learning gaze estimation methods have achieved significant advancements. However, while face images provide supplementary information beneficial for gaze inference, the substantial extraneous information they contain also increases the risk of overfitting during model training and compromises generalization capability. To alleviate this problem, we propose the 3DPE-Gaze framework, explicitly modeling 3D facial priors for feature decoupling and generalized gaze estimation. The 3DPE-Gaze framework consists of two core modules: the 3D Geometric Prior Module (3DGP) incorporating the FLAME model to parameterize facial structures and gaze-irrelevant facial appearances while extracting gaze features; the Semantic Concept Alignment Module (SCAM) separates gaze-related and unrelated concepts through CLIP-guided contrastive learning. Finally, the 3DPE-Gaze framework combines 3D facial landmark as prior for generalized gaze estimation. Experimental results show that 3DPE-Gaze outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on four major cross-domain tasks, with particularly outstanding performance in challenging scenarios such as lighting variations, extreme head poses, and glasses occlusion.

paragraphs: Estimating gaze from a face image requires separating useful visual cues from facial details that do not indicate where someone is looking. Those extra details can encourage a model to overfit its training data, weakening performance in new settings. 3DPE-Gaze addresses this problem by explicitly separating gaze information using facial geometry and semantic concepts.

Its geometric module uses the FLAME face model to parameterize facial structure and appearance unrelated to gaze while extracting gaze features. A second module uses CLIP-guided contrastive learning to distinguish concepts relevant to gaze from irrelevant ones. The framework also incorporates three-dimensional facial landmarks as prior information, giving the estimator an explicit geometric reference.

The authors report that 3DPE-Gaze outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on four cross-domain tasks. They highlight performance under lighting changes, extreme head orientations, and occlusion from glasses. These findings suggest that organizing face information around geometry and relevance can improve transfer across conditions, addressing the risk that a model learns incidental appearance patterns instead of useful gaze cues.
summary.tldr: 3DPE-Gaze separates gaze-relevant information from distracting facial appearance using 3D geometry and semantic alignment.

title: 3DPE-Gaze:Unlocking the Potential of 3D Facial Priors for Generalized Gaze Estimation

abstract: Real-world datasets typically exhibit long-tailed (LT) distributions, where a few head classes dominate and many tail classes are severely underrepresented. While recent work shows that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like LoRA and AdaptFormer preserve tail-class performance on foundation models such as CLIP, we find that they do so at the cost of head-class accuracy. We identify the head-tail ratio, the proportion of head to tail classes, as a crucial but overlooked factor influencing this trade-off. Through controlled experiments on CIFAR100 with varying imbalance ratio ($\rho$) and head-tail ratio ($\eta$), we show that PEFT excels in tail-heavy scenarios but degrades in more balanced and head-heavy distributions. To overcome these limitations, we propose LT-Soups, a two-stage model soups framework designed to generalize across diverse LT regimes. In the first stage, LT-Soups averages models fine-tuned on balanced subsets to reduce head-class bias; in the second, it fine-tunes only the classifier on the full dataset to restore head-class accuracy. Experiments across six benchmark datasets show that LT-Soups achieves superior trade-offs compared to both PEFT and traditional model soups across a wide range of imbalance regimes.

paragraphs: LT-Soups addresses classification datasets where some classes have many examples and others have very few. The paper finds that parameter-efficient adaptation methods can preserve performance on rare tail classes while sacrificing accuracy on common head classes. It identifies the proportion of head classes to tail classes as a crucial factor in this trade-off, alongside the severity of sample imbalance.

Controlled CIFAR100 experiments vary both factors. They show that parameter-efficient methods work particularly well in tail-heavy settings but degrade in more balanced or head-heavy distributions. The findings make the dataset's class composition part of the adaptation decision. They also support separating the creation of less biased representations from the final adjustment of the classifier to the full training distribution.
summary.tldr: LT-Soups averages models trained on balanced subsets, then adjusts the classifier to improve accuracy trade-offs between common and rare classes.

title: LT-Soups: Bridging Head and Tail Classes via Subsampled Model Soups

abstract: Heterogeneous Federated Learning (HtFL) enables collaborative learning across clients with diverse model architectures and non-IID data distributions, which are prevalent in real-world edge computing applications. Existing HtFL approaches typically employ proxy datasets to facilitate knowledge sharing or implement coarse-grained model-level knowledge transfer. However, such approaches not only elevate risks of user privacy leakage but also lead to the loss of fine-grained model-specific knowledge, ultimately creating barriers to effective knowledge sharing. To address these challenges, we propose FedFree, a novel data-free and model-free HtFL framework featuring two key innovations. First, FedFree introduces a reverse layer-wise knowledge transfer mechanism that aggregates heterogeneous client models into a global model solely using Gaussian-based pseudo data, eliminating reliance on proxy datasets. Second, it leverages Knowledge Gain Entropy (KGE) to guide targeted layer-wise knowledge alignment, ensuring that each client receives the most relevant global updates tailored to its specific architecture. We provide rigorous theoretical convergence guarantees for FedFree and conduct extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. Results demonstrate that FedFree achieves substantial performance gains, with relative accuracy improving up to 46.3% over state-of-the-art baselines. The framework consistently excels under highly heterogeneous model/data distributions and in large scale settings.

paragraphs: Federated learning becomes harder when participating clients use different model architectures and have differently distributed data. Existing approaches often share knowledge through proxy datasets or transfer information at the level of entire models. The authors argue that these choices can create privacy risks or discard useful details specific to individual models.

FedFree organizes knowledge exchange layer by layer. A reverse transfer mechanism combines information from heterogeneous clients into a global model using Gaussian-based pseudo data, removing reliance on proxy datasets. A measure called Knowledge Gain Entropy then guides which global knowledge should be aligned with each client’s layers. This targets updates to the client’s architecture instead of treating every model as an interchangeable recipient.

The paper provides theoretical convergence guarantees and evaluates the framework on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. It reports relative accuracy gains of up to 46.3% over the compared state-of-the-art baselines, alongside strong results under substantial model and data heterogeneity and at larger scale. The central contribution is a more targeted route for sharing knowledge across structurally different participants.
summary.tldr: FedFree uses synthetic pseudo data and targeted layer alignment to share knowledge among federated clients with different models and data distributions.

title: FedFree: Breaking Knowledge-sharing Barriers through Layer-wise Alignment in Heterogeneous Federated Learning

abstract: Recently, equivariant neural networks for policy learning have shown promising improvements in sample efficiency and generalization, however, their wide adoption faces substantial barriers due to implementation complexity. Equivariant architectures typically require specialized mathematical formulations and custom network design, posing significant challenges when integrating with modern policy frameworks like diffusion-based models. In this paper, we explore a number of straightforward and practical approaches to incorporate symmetry benefits into diffusion policies without the overhead of full equivariant designs. Specifically, we investigate (i) invariant representations via relative trajectory actions and eye-in-hand perception, (ii) integrating equivariant vision encoders, and (iii) symmetric feature extraction with pretrained encoders using Frame Averaging. We first prove that combining eye-in-hand perception with relative or delta action parameterization yields inherent SE(3)-invariance, thus improving policy generalization. We then perform a systematic experimental study on those design choices for integrating symmetry in diffusion policies, and conclude that an invariant representation with equivariant feature extraction significantly improves the policy performance. Our method achieves performance on par with or exceeding fully equivariant architectures while greatly simplifying implementation.

paragraphs: Robot policies can benefit from recognizing when a situation has changed only by a rotation or translation. Networks built to respect these symmetries have shown improvements in data efficiency and generalization, but their specialized mathematics and architecture make them difficult to integrate into diffusion policies. This paper studies simpler ways to obtain those benefits.

The authors investigate three design choices: representing actions relative to the robot’s trajectory while using a camera attached to its hand, incorporating equivariant vision encoders, and extracting symmetric features from pretrained encoders through Frame Averaging. They prove that combining eye-in-hand perception with relative or delta actions produces SE(3) invariance, meaning invariance to three-dimensional rotations and translations.

Their experimental study finds that combining an invariant representation with equivariant feature extraction substantially improves policy performance. The resulting approach matches or exceeds fully equivariant architectures in the reported comparisons while simplifying implementation. The contribution is both a mathematical justification for particular representation choices and practical evidence that symmetry can help without requiring a fully specialized policy architecture.
summary.tldr: Careful perception, action, and feature representations bring symmetry benefits to diffusion policies with substantially simpler implementation.

title: A Practical Guide for Incorporating Symmetry in Diffusion Policy

abstract: Networks have been extensively used and have provided novel insights across a wide variety of research areas. However, many real-world systems are, in fact, a ``network of networks'', or a multilayer network, which interact as components of a larger multimodal system. A major difficulty in this multilayer framework is the estimation of interlayer edges or connections. In this work, we propose a new estimation method, called multilayer sparse + low-rank inverse covariance estimation (multiSLICE), which estimates the interlayer edges. multiSLICE bridges latent variable Gaussian graphical methods with multilayer networks, offering a flexible framework for modeling processes with irregular sampling and heterogeneous graph structures. We develop an effective algorithm to compute the estimator. We also establish theoretical conditions for the recoverability of the joint space, analyze how inter-layer interactions influence joint parameter estimation, and provide theoretical bounds on their relationships. Finally, we rigorously evaluate our method on both simulated and multimodal neuroimaging data, demonstrating improvements over state-of-the-art approaches. Finally, all the relevant R code implementing the method in the article is available on [GitHub](https://github.com/mondrus96/multiSLICE).

paragraphs: Many complex systems contain several interacting networks. Studying each network separately can miss the connections through which these components influence one another. This paper introduces multiSLICE, a method for estimating those connections between layers. Its central goal is to recover relationships across a larger system while accommodating differences in the networks that compose it.

The method combines latent-variable Gaussian graphical modeling with a multilayer network representation. Its inverse covariance estimator uses sparse and low-rank structure, bringing these modeling ideas together in a framework that can handle irregular sampling and heterogeneous graph structures. The authors also develop an algorithm for computing the estimator, making the statistical formulation usable in practice.

The theoretical analysis establishes conditions under which the joint space can be recovered and bounds relationships between interlayer interactions and joint parameter estimation. These are conditional recovery results. Evaluations on simulated data and multimodal neuroimaging data report improvements over leading alternatives, supporting the value of explicitly modeling connections between networks.
summary.tldr: multiSLICE estimates connections between interacting networks, with conditional recovery theory and improved results on simulated and neuroimaging data.

title: A Latent Multilayer Graphical Model For Complex, Interdependent Systems

abstract: Scaling laws are typically fit using a family of models with a narrow range of frozen hyperparameter choices. In this work we study scaling laws using multiple architectural shapes and hyperparameter choices, highlighting their impact on resulting prescriptions. As a primary artifact of our research, we release the Gemstones: an open-source scaling law dataset, consisting of over 4000 checkpoints from transformers with up to 2 billion parameters and diverse architectural shapes; including ablations over learning rate and cooldown. Our checkpoints enable more complex studies of scaling, such as analyzing the relationship between width and depth. By examining our model suite, we find that the prescriptions of scaling laws can be highly sensitive to the experimental design process and the specific model checkpoints used during fitting.

paragraphs: Scaling laws turn measurements from trained models into prescriptions about how to scale future models. Those prescriptions are often fitted using model families with a narrow set of fixed hyperparameters. Gemstones examines how expanding the architectural and training choices changes the conclusions that such fits produce.

The main artifact is an open-source dataset containing more than 4,000 transformer checkpoints, with models reaching two billion parameters. The suite varies architectural shape and includes ablations of learning rate and cooldown. This variety supports questions that a narrowly configured model family cannot explore as directly, including the relationship between network width and depth.

Analysis of the suite finds that scaling prescriptions can be highly sensitive to experimental design and to the particular checkpoints included in fitting. The finding makes the selection of training runs part of interpreting a scaling result. Gemstones contributes both evidence for this sensitivity and a broader collection of checkpoints for studying how architectural and hyperparameter choices affect scaling conclusions.
summary.tldr: Gemstones provides over 4,000 diverse transformer checkpoints and shows that scaling-law prescriptions can depend strongly on experimental design.

title: Gemstones: A Model Suite for Multi-Faceted Scaling Laws

abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) show great promise, their tendencies to hallucinate pose significant risks in high-stakes domains like finance, especially when used for regulatory reporting and decision-making. Existing hallucination detection benchmarks fail to capture the complexities of financial benchmarks, which require high numerical precision, nuanced understanding of the language of finance, and ability to handle long-context documents. To address this, we introduce PHANTOM, a novel benchmark dataset for evaluating hallucination detection in long-context financial QA. Our approach first generates a seed dataset of high-quality "query-answer-document (chunk)" triplets, with either hallucinated or correct answers - that are validated by human annotators and subsequently expanded to capture various context lengths and information placements. We demonstrate how PHANTOM allows fair comparison of hallucination detection models and provides insights into LLM performance, offering a valuable resource for improving hallucination detection in financial applications. Further, our benchmarking results highlight the severe challenges out-of-the-box models face in detecting real-world hallucinations on long context data, and establish some promising directions towards alleviating these challenges, by fine-tuning open-source LLMs using PHANTOM.

paragraphs: PHANTOM evaluates whether models can detect hallucinated answers in financial question answering over long documents. This setting combines several demands: precise numbers, specialized financial language, and evidence that may be difficult to locate within a large context. The benchmark is designed to capture these demands together in hallucination-detection evaluation.

Construction begins with a seed collection linking a question, an answer, and a document chunk. Answers may be correct or hallucinated, and human annotators validate the examples. The collection is then expanded to vary context length and the placement of relevant information. Those variations let the benchmark examine detection when the surrounding material and evidence location change.

The reported evaluations show that out-of-the-box models face severe difficulties detecting real-world hallucinations in long contexts. Fine-tuning open-source language models on PHANTOM provides promising directions for improvement. The contribution is therefore both a comparison resource and evidence that financial hallucination detection requires attention to document structure, context length, and domain-specific accuracy.
summary.tldr: PHANTOM benchmarks hallucination detection in long financial documents and finds substantial challenges for out-of-the-box models.

title: PHANTOM: A Benchmark for Hallucination Detection in Financial Long-Context QA

abstract: Behavioral cloning is a simple yet effective technique for learning sequential decision-making from demonstrations. Recently, it has gained prominence as the core of foundation models for the physical world, where achieving generalization requires countless demonstrations of a multitude of tasks. Typically, a human expert with full information on the task demonstrates a (nearly) optimal behavior. In this paper, we propose to hide some of the task's information from the demonstrator. This ``blindfolded'' expert is compelled to employ non-trivial *exploration* to solve the task. We show that cloning the blindfolded expert generalizes better to unseen tasks than its fully-informed counterpart. We conduct experiments of real-world robot peg insertion tasks with (limited) human demonstrations, alongside videogames from the Procgen benchmark. Additionally, we support our findings with theoretical analysis, which confirms that the generalization error scales with $\sqrt{I/m}$, where $I$ measures the amount of task information available to the demonstrator, and $m$ is the number of demonstrated tasks. Both theory and practice indicate that cloning blindfolded experts generalizes better with fewer demonstrated tasks. Project page with videos and code: [https://sites.google.com/view/blindfoldedexperts/home](https://sites.google.com/view/blindfoldedexperts/home)

paragraphs: Behavioral cloning learns decision-making by copying demonstrations. Usually, the demonstrator already knows the task well and shows nearly optimal behavior. This paper asks whether withholding some task information can produce more useful demonstrations for generalization. An expert who lacks that information must explore to discover how to complete the task.

The resulting demonstrations include behavior for dealing with uncertainty, which a learner can then imitate. The authors compare cloning these partially informed experts with cloning fully informed experts in real robot peg insertion tasks and Procgen videogames. Their experiments show better generalization to unseen tasks from the blindfolded demonstrations, including settings with limited human demonstrations.

The theoretical analysis supports the empirical pattern: generalization error scales with the square root of I divided by m, where I measures task information available to the demonstrator and m counts demonstrated tasks. Within that analysis, reducing available task information improves the scaling. Together, the results indicate that demonstration design can reduce the number of demonstrated tasks needed for effective generalization.
summary.tldr: Cloning experts who must explore because some task information is hidden improves generalization in the studied robotic and videogame settings.

title: Blindfolded Experts Generalize Better: Insights from Robotic Manipulation and Videogames

abstract: In this paper, we study the generalization properties of online learning based stochastic methods for supervised learning problems where the loss function is dependent on more than one training sample (e.g., metric learning, ranking). We present a generic decoupling technique that enables us to provide Rademacher complexity-based generalization error bounds. Our bounds are in general tighter than those obtained by Wang et al. (COLT 2012) for the same problem. Using our decoupling technique, we are further able to obtain fast convergence rates for strongly con-vex pairwise loss functions. We are also able to analyze a class of memory efficient on-line learning algorithms for pairwise learning problems that use only a bounded subset of past training samples to update the hypothesis at each step. Finally, in order to complement our generalization bounds, we propose a novel memory efficient online learning algorithm for higher order learning problems with bounded regret guarantees.

Finally, in order to complement our generalization bounds, we propose a novel memory efficient online learning algorithm for higher order learning problems with bounded regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Some supervised learning objectives evaluate relationships among examples instead of assigning a separate loss to each example. Ranking and metric learning are examples of this setting. The paper studies how well online stochastic learning methods for such objectives generalize beyond the training data, with particular attention to losses involving pairs of samples.

The authors introduce a general decoupling technique that enables error bounds based on Rademacher complexity, a measure used to characterize the flexibility of a hypothesis class. Their bounds are generally tighter than earlier bounds for the same problem. For strongly convex pairwise losses, the technique also yields fast convergence rates.

The analysis extends to memory-efficient online methods that update using only a bounded subset of previously observed examples. The authors additionally propose an algorithm for higher-order learning problems with bounded regret guarantees. Together, these contributions connect generalization analysis, favorable convergence under strong convexity, and limited-memory learning, addressing both predictive reliability and the storage demands of online relational objectives.
summary.tldr: A decoupling technique strengthens generalization analysis for pairwise online learning and supports guarantees for memory-efficient algorithms.

title: On the Generalization Ability of Online Learning Algorithms for Pairwise Loss Functions

abstract: We consider the problem of Bayesian learning on sensitive datasets and present two simple but somewhat surprising results that connect Bayesian learning to “differential privacy”, a cryptographic approach to protect individual-level privacy while permitting database-level utility. Specifically, we show that under standard assumptions, getting one sample from a posterior distribution is differentially private “for free”; and this sample as a statistical estimator is often consistent, near optimal, and computationally tractable. Similarly but separately, we show that a recent line of work that use stochastic gradient for Hybrid Monte Carlo (HMC) sampling also preserve differentially privacy with minor or no modifications of the algorithmic procedure at all, these observations lead to an “anytime” algorithm for Bayesian learning under privacy constraint. We demonstrate that it performs much better than the state-of-the-art differential private methods on synthetic and real datasets.

Similarly but separately, we show that a recent line of work that use stochastic gradient for Hybrid Monte Carlo (HMC) sampling also preserve differentially privacy with minor or no modifications of the algorithmic procedure at all, these observations lead to an “anytime” algorithm for Bayesian learning under privacy constraint. paragraphs: Bayesian learning on sensitive data must balance statistical usefulness with protection for individuals. This paper connects Bayesian sampling to differential privacy, which permits aggregate learning while controlling individual-level privacy exposure. Its first result shows that, under standard assumptions, drawing one sample from a posterior distribution already provides a differential-privacy guarantee.

The same sample can serve as a statistical estimator. The authors state that it is often consistent, near optimal, and computationally tractable, linking privacy to useful estimation rather than treating privacy as an entirely separate processing step. The qualification about assumptions and the focus on one posterior draw are part of the stated result.

A separate result concerns stochastic-gradient methods for Hybrid Monte Carlo sampling. The authors show that these methods can preserve differential privacy with minor or no procedural changes, leading to an anytime Bayesian-learning algorithm under a privacy constraint. On synthetic and real datasets, the resulting approach substantially outperforms the compared state-of-the-art private methods. The work identifies sampling randomness as a source of both statistical computation and privacy protection.
summary.tldr: Under stated assumptions, posterior sampling provides differential privacy, and stochastic-gradient Monte Carlo supports practical private Bayesian learning.

title: Privacy for Free: Posterior Sampling and Stochastic Gradient Monte Carlo

abstract: Matrix eigen-decomposition is a classic and long-standing problem that plays a fundamental role in scientific computing and machine learning. Despite some existing algorithms for this inherently non-convex problem, the study remains inadequate for the need of large data nowadays. To address this gap, we propose a Doubly Stochastic Riemannian Gradient EIGenSolver, DSRG-EIGS, where the double stochasticity comes from the generalization of the stochastic Euclidean gradient ascent and the stochastic Euclidean coordinate ascent to Riemannian manifolds. As a result, it induces a greatly reduced complexity per iteration, enables the algorithm to completely avoid the matrix inversion, and consequently makes it well-suited to large-scale applications. We theoretically analyze its convergence properties and empirically validate it on real-world datasets. Encouraging experimental results demonstrate its advantages over the deterministic counterparts.

paragraphs: Matrix eigen-decomposition is a core operation in scientific computing and machine learning, but large datasets create demands that existing methods do not adequately address. This paper approaches the inherently nonconvex problem through optimization on Riemannian manifolds. It introduces DSRG-EIGS, an eigensolver designed to reduce the computational burden of each optimization iteration.

The method combines two sources of randomness. It generalizes stochastic Euclidean gradient ascent and stochastic Euclidean coordinate ascent to the Riemannian setting. This combination is the basis of its description as doubly stochastic. According to the authors, it substantially reduces per-iteration complexity and avoids matrix inversion entirely, two properties that make the method suitable for large-scale applications.

The authors theoretically analyze convergence and evaluate the solver on real-world datasets. They report encouraging advantages over deterministic counterparts. The significance is both algorithmic and empirical: the method changes how work is allocated within each iteration, and the experiments support the usefulness of that change. The reported comparisons establish benefits in the evaluated settings rather than a universal advantage for every matrix.
summary.tldr: A doubly stochastic Riemannian eigensolver lowers per-iteration cost, avoids matrix inversion, and shows advantages over deterministic methods.

title: Matrix Eigen-decomposition via Doubly Stochastic Riemannian Optimization

abstract: We consider empirical risk minimization of linear predictors with convex loss functions. Such problems can be reformulated as convex-concave saddle point problems and solved by primal-dual first-order algorithms. However, primal-dual algorithms often require explicit strongly convex regularization in order to obtain fast linear convergence, and the required dual proximal mapping may not admit closed-form or efficient solution. In this paper, we develop both batch and randomized primal-dual algorithms that can exploit strong convexity from data adaptively and are capable of achieving linear convergence even without regularization. We also present dual-free variants of adaptive primal-dual algorithms that do not need the dual proximal mapping, which are especially suitable for logistic regression.

However, primal-dual algorithms often require explicit strongly convex regularization in order to obtain fast linear convergence, and the required dual proximal mapping may not admit closed-form or efficient solution. In this paper, we develop both batch and randomized primal-dual algorithms that can exploit strong convexity from data adaptively and are capable of achieving linear convergence even without regularization. paragraphs: The paper studies fitting linear predictors by minimizing empirical risk with convex losses. These objectives can be rewritten as saddle point problems and addressed with primal-dual first-order algorithms. Such algorithms often rely on an explicitly strongly convex regularizer to obtain linear convergence, a rate at which optimization error decreases geometrically.

The authors develop batch and randomized algorithms that adaptively exploit strong convexity arising from the data. This allows them to achieve linear convergence even without regularization when the relevant curvature is available. The distinction matters because useful curvature can already be present in the learning objective, rather than needing to be introduced through an additional penalty.

A second contribution addresses the dual proximal mapping, an update operation that may lack a simple formula or an efficient solution. The proposed dual-free variants avoid requiring that operation and are described as particularly suitable for logistic regression. Together, the contributions target both the source of fast convergence and a computational obstacle within primal-dual updates.
summary.tldr: Adaptive primal-dual algorithms use strong convexity supplied by data to enable linear convergence, with dual-free variants suited to logistic regression.

title: Exploiting Strong Convexity from Data with Primal-Dual First-Order Algorithms

abstract: Finding a dataset of minimal cardinality to characterize the optimal parameters of a model is of paramount importance in machine learning and distributed optimization over a network. This paper investigates the compressibility of large datasets. More specifically, we propose a framework that jointly learns the input-output mapping as well as the most representative samples of the dataset (sufficient dataset). Our analytical results show that the cardinality of the sufficient dataset increases sub-linearly with respect to the original dataset size. Numerical evaluations of real datasets reveal a large compressibility, up to 95%, without a noticeable drop in the learnability performance, measured by the generalization error.

This paper investigates the compressibility of large datasets. More specifically, we propose a framework that jointly learns the input-output mapping as well as the most representative samples of the dataset (sufficient dataset). Our analytical results show that the cardinality of the sufficient dataset increases sub-linearly with respect to the original dataset size. Numerical evaluations of real datasets reveal a large compressibility, up to 95%, without a noticeable drop in the learnability performance, measured by the generalization error.

paragraphs: A large dataset may contain more examples than are needed to characterize a model's optimal parameters. This paper investigates that form of compressibility: how much of a dataset can be represented by a smaller collection of informative samples. The question matters for machine learning and for optimization distributed across a network.

The proposed framework learns two things jointly: the mapping from inputs to outputs and the samples that most effectively represent the dataset. The authors call this selected collection a sufficient dataset. Their analysis shows that its size grows sublinearly with the size of the original dataset, meaning the required collection grows more slowly than the full data under their analytical result.

Numerical evaluations on real datasets report compression of up to 95% without a noticeable deterioration in generalization error. That figure describes the reported evaluations rather than a guaranteed reduction for every dataset. The findings support treating sample selection as part of learning itself, with the possibility of retaining predictive performance using substantially fewer examples.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning a predictor and representative samples yields sublinear sufficient-dataset growth and substantial compression in the reported evaluations.

title: Learning and Data Selection in Big Datasets

abstract: Hyperbolic space is a geometry that is known to be well-suited for representation learning of data with an underlying hierarchical structure. In this paper, we present a novel hyperbolic distribution called hyperbolic wrapped distribution, a wrapped normal distribution on hyperbolic space whose density can be evaluated analytically and differentiated with respect to the parameters. Our distribution enables the gradient-based learning of the probabilistic models on hyperbolic space that could never have been considered before. Also, we can sample from this hyperbolic probability distribution without resorting to auxiliary means like rejection sampling. As applications of our distribution, we develop a hyperbolic-analog of variational autoencoder and a method of probabilistic word embedding on hyperbolic space. We demonstrate the efficacy of our distribution on various datasets including MNIST, Atari 2600 Breakout, and WordNet.

paragraphs: Hyperbolic space is useful for representing data with hierarchical structure, but probabilistic learning also requires distributions that can be evaluated and optimized in that geometry. This paper introduces a wrapped normal distribution on hyperbolic space to supply those computational ingredients. Its contribution concerns both the geometry of representations and the tractability of learning probability models over them.

The proposed distribution has a density that can be evaluated analytically and differentiated with respect to its parameters. These properties make it suitable for gradient-based learning. The authors also provide sampling without auxiliary procedures such as rejection sampling. Together, evaluation, differentiation, and sampling give probabilistic models practical ways to use the hyperbolic distribution during learning.

The paper develops two applications: a hyperbolic version of a variational autoencoder and probabilistic word embeddings in hyperbolic space. It demonstrates the distribution’s effectiveness on datasets including MNIST, Atari 2600 Breakout, and WordNet. These applications show how the same distribution can support different learning tasks while retaining the geometry intended to represent hierarchical relationships.
summary.tldr: A tractable wrapped normal distribution makes gradient-based probabilistic learning possible in hyperbolic space.

title: A Wrapped Normal Distribution on Hyperbolic Space for Gradient-Based Learning

abstract: Mesh models are a promising approach for encoding the structure of 3D objects. Current mesh reconstruction systems predict uniformly distributed vertex locations of a predetermined graph through a series of graph convolutions, leading to compromises with respect to performance or resolution. In this paper, we argue that the graph representation of geometric objects allows for additional structure, which should be leveraged for enhanced reconstruction. Thus, we propose a system which properly benefits from the advantages of the geometric structure of graph-encoded objects by introducing (1) a graph convolutional update preserving vertex information; (2) an adaptive splitting heuristic allowing detail to emerge; and (3) a training objective operating both on the local surfaces defined by vertices as well as the global structure defined by the mesh. Our proposed method is evaluated on the task of 3D object reconstruction from images with the ShapeNet dataset, where we demonstrate state of the art performance, both visually and numerically, while having far smaller space requirements by generating adaptive meshes.

paragraphs: A mesh describes a three-dimensional object through connected vertices that define surfaces. Existing reconstruction systems described in this paper predict positions for vertices in a predetermined graph, with vertices distributed uniformly. That design creates compromises between reconstruction performance and resolution. GEOMetrics instead uses the geometric meaning of the graph to guide how the object is represented and learned.

The system combines three changes. A revised graph convolution preserves vertex information during updates. An adaptive splitting heuristic allows additional detail to emerge in the mesh. A training objective accounts for both the local surfaces formed by nearby vertices and the global structure of the whole object. Together, these components make geometry relevant to the updates, the mesh resolution, and the learning objective.

The authors evaluate reconstruction from images using ShapeNet and report state-of-the-art performance in both visual and numerical assessments. They also report substantially smaller space requirements through adaptive meshes. The result supports allocating mesh detail adaptively, while considering local and global shape, as a useful approach to improving reconstruction quality and representation efficiency.
summary.tldr: GEOMetrics combines geometry-aware graph updates, adaptive mesh refinement, and local-and-global training objectives to improve 3D reconstruction.

title: GEOMetrics: Exploiting Geometric Structure for Graph-Encoded Objects

abstract: Producing probabilistic forecasts for large collections of similar and/or dependent time series is a practically highly relevant, yet challenging task. Classical time series models fail to capture complex patterns in the data and multivariate techniques struggle to scale to large problem sizes, but their reliance on strong structural assumptions makes them data-efficient and allows them to provide estimates of uncertainty. The converse is true for models based on deep neural networks, which can learn complex patterns and dependencies given enough data. In this paper, we propose a hybrid model that incorporates the benefits of both approaches. Our new method is data-driven and scalable via a latent, global, deep component. It also handles uncertainty through a local classical model. We provide both theoretical and empirical evidence for the soundness of our approach through a necessary and sufficient decomposition of exchangeable time series into a global and a local part and extensive experiments. Our experiments demonstrate the advantages of our model both in term of data efficiency and computational complexity.

paragraphs: Forecasting many related time series requires learning shared patterns while also describing uncertainty. This paper combines two approaches with complementary strengths. Classical models use strong structural assumptions to work efficiently with limited data and estimate uncertainty, while deep neural networks can learn complex patterns and dependencies when sufficient data are available.

The proposed hybrid assigns shared structure to a latent global component built with deep learning. A local classical model handles uncertainty. This division gives the method a way to learn across a large collection of series while retaining a local modeling component, rather than asking a single type of model to provide every capability.

The theoretical analysis supplies a necessary and sufficient decomposition of exchangeable time series into global and local parts. That exchangeability setting is central to the stated decomposition. Experiments additionally show advantages in data efficiency and computational complexity. Together, the theory and experiments support the proposed combination as a scalable approach to probabilistic forecasting for collections of related series.
summary.tldr: Deep Factors combines a global deep model with local classical models to forecast related time series and represent uncertainty.

title: Deep Factors for Forecasting

abstract: Bayesian nonparametric models provide a principled way to automatically adapt the complexity of a model to the amount of the data available, but computation in such models is difficult. Amortized variational approximations are appealing because of their computational efficiency, but current methods rely on a fixed finite truncation of the infinite model. This truncation level can be difficult to set, and also interacts poorly with amortized methods due to the over-pruning problem. Instead, we propose a new variational approximation, based on a method from statistical physics called Russian roulette sampling. This allows the variational distribution to adapt its complexity during inference, without relying on a fixed truncation level, and while still obtaining an unbiased estimate of the gradient of the original variational objective. We demonstrate this method on infinite sized variational auto-encoders using a Beta-Bernoulli (Indian buffet process) prior.

paragraphs: Bayesian nonparametric models allow model complexity to adapt to the amount of available data, but inference is computationally difficult. Efficient amortized variational methods commonly impose a fixed finite cutoff on an infinite model. Choosing that cutoff is challenging, and its interaction with amortized inference can lead to over-pruning.

This paper replaces the fixed truncation with a variational approximation based on Russian roulette sampling, a method originating in statistical physics. The resulting variational distribution can change its complexity during inference. Crucially, the procedure still produces an unbiased estimate of the gradient of the original variational objective, keeping the gradient target tied to that objective.

The authors demonstrate the method with infinite-sized variational autoencoders using a Beta-Bernoulli, or Indian buffet process, prior. The contribution combines adaptive inference complexity with unbiased gradient estimation, addressing a tension between computational efficiency and the flexibility of an infinite model. The unbiasedness claim concerns the gradient estimator; the inference procedure remains a variational approximation.
summary.tldr: Russian roulette sampling lets variational inference adapt model complexity without fixed truncation while preserving unbiased estimates of the original objective's gradient.

title: Variational Russian Roulette for Deep Bayesian Nonparametrics

abstract: Normalization is known to help the optimization of deep neural networks. Curiously, different architectures require specialized normalization methods. In this paper, we study what normalization is effective for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). First, we adapt and evaluate the existing methods from other domains to GNNs. Faster convergence is achieved with InstanceNorm compared to BatchNorm and LayerNorm. We provide an explanation by showing that InstanceNorm serves as a preconditioner for GNNs, but such preconditioning effect is weaker with BatchNorm due to the heavy batch noise in graph datasets. Second, we show that the shift operation in InstanceNorm results in an expressiveness degradation of GNNs for highly regular graphs. We address this issue by proposing GraphNorm with a learnable shift. Empirically, GNNs with GraphNorm converge faster compared to GNNs using other normalization. GraphNorm also improves the generalization of GNNs, achieving better performance on graph classification benchmarks.
originalAbstract: Normalization is known to help the optimization of deep neural networks. Curiously, different architectures require specialized normalization methods. In this paper, we study what normalization is effective for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). First, we adapt and evaluate the existing methods from other domains to GNNs. Faster convergence is achieved with InstanceNorm compared to BatchNorm and LayerNorm. We provide an explanation by showing that InstanceNorm serves as a preconditioner for GNNs, but such preconditioning effect is weaker with BatchNorm due to the heavy batch noise in graph datasets. Second, we show that the shift operation in InstanceNorm results in an expressiveness degradation of GNNs for highly regular graphs. We address this issue by proposing GraphNorm with a learnable shift. Empirically, GNNs with GraphNorm converge faster compared to GNNs using other normalization. GraphNorm also improves the generalization of GNNs, achieving better performance on graph classification benchmarks.

paragraphs: Normalization can make neural networks easier to optimize, but methods that work well for one architecture may not transfer directly to another. This paper investigates normalization specifically for graph neural networks. It begins by adapting existing techniques and comparing how they affect training convergence.

InstanceNorm converges faster than BatchNorm and LayerNorm in the reported evaluation. The authors explain this through a preconditioning effect: normalization changes the optimization problem in a helpful way. BatchNorm provides a weaker version of that effect because graph datasets introduce substantial batch noise. However, InstanceNorm has its own problem: its shift operation reduces expressiveness for highly regular graphs.

GraphNorm addresses that expressiveness issue by making the shift learnable. This preserves the motivation for normalization while allowing the model to adjust an operation that could otherwise discard useful distinctions. Empirically, graph neural networks using GraphNorm converge faster than those using other normalization methods and perform better on graph classification benchmarks, indicating benefits for both training and generalization.
summary.tldr: GraphNorm uses a learnable shift to address InstanceNorm’s expressiveness problem and empirically improves graph-network convergence and classification performance.

title: GraphNorm: A Principled Approach to Accelerating Graph Neural Network Training

abstract: In this paper, we introduce a new perspective on training deep neural networks capable of state-of-the-art performance without the need for the expensive over-parameterization by proposing the concept of In-Time Over-Parameterization (ITOP) in sparse training. By starting from a random sparse network and continuously exploring sparse connectivities during training, we can perform an Over-Parameterization over the course of training, closing the gap in the expressibility between sparse training and dense training. We further use ITOP to understand the underlying mechanism of Dynamic Sparse Training (DST) and discover that the benefits of DST come from its ability to consider across time all possible parameters when searching for the optimal sparse connectivity. As long as sufficient parameters have been reliably explored, DST can outperform the dense neural network by a large margin. We present a series of experiments to support our conjecture and achieve the state-of-the-art sparse training performance with ResNet-50 on ImageNet. More impressively, ITOP achieves dominant performance over the overparameterization-based sparse methods at extreme sparsities. When trained with ResNet-34 on CIFAR-100, ITOP can match the performance of the dense model at an extreme sparsity 98%.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether a network needs many parameters active simultaneously to obtain the benefits associated with dense training. It proposes In-Time Over-Parameterization, or ITOP: start with a random sparse network and change its connectivity during training, allowing the training process to explore a much larger collection of possible parameters over time.

The authors use this perspective to explain dynamic sparse training. Their proposed mechanism is that changing connectivity searches for a strong sparse structure while considering parameters beyond those active at any single moment. They argue that, when enough parameters have been explored reliably, dynamic sparse training can outperform a dense network by a large margin. Experiments support this conjecture about why the approach works.

The reported results include state-of-the-art sparse training with ResNet-50 on ImageNet and particularly strong performance at extreme sparsity. With ResNet-34 on CIFAR-100, ITOP matches dense-model performance at 98% sparsity. These findings support the possibility of obtaining substantial expressive benefits through connectivity exploration across training, without maintaining the full dense parameter set throughout the process.
summary.tldr: ITOP attributes strong sparse training to reliably exploring many possible connections over time.

title: Do We Actually Need Dense Over-Parameterization? In-Time Over-Parameterization in Sparse Training

abstract: Densest subgraph detection is a fundamental graph mining problem, with a large number of applications. There has been a lot of work on efficient algorithms for finding the densest subgraph in massive networks. However, in many domains, the network is private, and returning a densest subgraph can reveal information about the network. Differential privacy is a powerful framework to handle such settings. We study the densest subgraph problem in the edge privacy model, in which the edges of the graph are private. We present the first sequential and parallel differentially private algorithms for this problem. We show that our algorithms have an additive approximation guarantee. We evaluate our algorithms on a large number of real-world networks, and observe a good privacy-accuracy tradeoff when the network has high density.

paragraphs: Finding a densely connected part of a network is a fundamental graph-mining task. When network connections are private, however, releasing the result can reveal information about those connections. This paper studies how to find a dense subgraph while providing differential privacy in the edge privacy model, where graph edges are the protected information.

The authors present the first sequential and parallel differentially private algorithms for this problem. Providing both forms addresses different ways of carrying out the computation. They also establish an additive approximation guarantee: the quality guarantee allows an additive discrepancy from the target density, giving a formal account of the accuracy available under privacy protection.

Evaluation across many real-world networks finds a favorable privacy-accuracy tradeoff when the network has high density. That condition is part of the reported empirical finding. The contribution therefore combines formal privacy and approximation properties with evidence that useful dense-subgraph results can be retained for the high-density networks studied.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces sequential and parallel private densest-subgraph algorithms with additive accuracy guarantees and favorable results on high-density networks.

title: Differentially Private Densest Subgraph Detection

abstract: The performance of a language model has been shown to be effectively modeled as a power-law in its parameter count. Here we study the scaling behaviors of Routing Networks: architectures that conditionally use only a subset of their parameters while processing an input. For these models, parameter count and computational requirement form two independent axes along which an increase leads to better performance. In this work we derive and justify scaling laws defined on these two variables which generalize those known for standard language models and describe the performance of a wide range of routing architectures trained via three different techniques. Afterwards we provide two applications of these laws: first deriving an Effective Parameter Count along which all models scale at the same rate, and then using the scaling coefficients to give a quantitative comparison of the three routing techniques considered. Our analysis derives from an extensive evaluation of Routing Networks across five orders of magnitude of size, including models with hundreds of experts and hundreds of billions of parameters.

paragraphs: Routed language models use only a subset of their parameters for each input. This separates total model capacity from the computation used to process an input. The paper studies how performance scales along these two independent axes, extending scaling laws that describe standard language models primarily through parameter count.

The authors derive and justify laws that describe a broad range of routing architectures trained with three different techniques. These laws account jointly for model size and computational requirements. Their analysis draws on evaluations spanning five orders of magnitude in size, including models with hundreds of experts and hundreds of billions of parameters.

The paper applies the laws in two ways. It defines an effective parameter count under which the studied models scale at the same rate, giving a shared basis for comparison. It also uses the fitted scaling coefficients to compare the three routing techniques quantitatively. The contribution is a unified account of how conditional parameter use changes the relationship among capacity, computation, and language-model performance.
summary.tldr: Two-variable scaling laws describe routed language-model performance through both total parameters and computation, enabling comparisons across routing techniques.

title: Unified Scaling Laws for Routed Language Models

abstract: A fundamental concept in control theory is that of controllability, where any system state can be reached through an appropriate choice of control inputs. Indeed, a large body of classical and modern approaches are designed for controllable linear dynamical systems. However, in practice, we often encounter systems in which a large set of state variables evolve exogenously and independently of the control inputs; such systems are only partially controllable. The focus of this work is on a large class of partially controllable linear dynamical systems, specified by an underlying sparsity pattern. Our main results establish structural conditions and finite-sample guarantees for learning to control such systems. In particular, our structural results characterize those state variables which are irrelevant for optimal control, an analysis which departs from classical control techniques. Our algorithmic results adapt techniques from high-dimensional statistics{—}specifically soft-thresholding and semiparametric least-squares{—}to exploit the underlying sparsity pattern in order to obtain finite-sample guarantees that significantly improve over those based on certainty-equivalence. We also corroborate these theoretical improvements over certainty-equivalent control through a simulation study.

paragraphs: A controllable system can be moved to any state through suitable control inputs. Many real systems only partly satisfy that description: some state variables evolve independently of the controls. This paper studies a broad class of partially controllable linear systems whose dependencies follow an underlying sparsity pattern.

The authors first establish structural conditions that identify which state variables are irrelevant to optimal control. This distinction matters because being unable to control a variable and having no need to consider it are different questions. The analysis characterizes irrelevance through the system’s structure, providing a basis for concentrating learning on the information that optimal control requires.

The algorithmic contribution adapts soft-thresholding and semiparametric least-squares methods from high-dimensional statistics to exploit that sparsity. The resulting finite-sample guarantees substantially improve on those based on certainty-equivalent control, and simulations corroborate the theoretical improvements. The findings show how structural knowledge about partially controllable systems can translate into stronger guarantees for learning to control them from limited data.
summary.tldr: Exploiting sparse dependencies in partially controllable linear systems identifies irrelevant state variables and improves finite-sample control guarantees.

title: Sparsity in Partially Controllable Linear Systems

abstract: Recovering global rankings from pairwise comparisons has wide applications from time synchronization to sports team ranking. Pairwise comparisons corresponding to matches in a competition can be construed as edges in a directed graph (digraph), whose nodes represent e.g. competitors with an unknown rank. In this paper, we introduce neural networks into the ranking recovery problem by proposing the so-called GNNRank, a trainable GNN-based framework with digraph embedding. Moreover, new objectives are devised to encode ranking upsets/violations. The framework involves a ranking score estimation approach, and adds an inductive bias by unfolding the Fiedler vector computation of the graph constructed from a learnable similarity matrix. Experimental results on extensive data sets show that our methods attain competitive and often superior performance against baselines, as well as showing promising transfer ability. Codes and preprocessed data are at: \url{https://github.com/SherylHYX/GNNRank}.

paragraphs: Pairwise comparisons describe how two items relate, but many applications need a single ranking of all items. GNNRank approaches this problem by representing comparisons as a directed graph. Competitors or other ranked entities become nodes, and their comparisons become directed edges. This representation lets a neural network learn from the pattern of comparisons across the graph.

The framework combines directed-graph embeddings with ranking-score estimation and new objectives that capture ranking upsets or violations. It also incorporates a specific structural preference by unfolding the computation of a Fiedler vector for a graph built from a learnable similarity matrix. This places a graph-based ranking computation inside the trainable approach.

Experiments across extensive datasets show performance that is competitive with, and often better than, the evaluated baselines. The authors also report promising transfer ability. Together, these findings support learning a graph representation for ranking recovery, while retaining an explicit connection to the structure of ranking disagreements and to a graph-derived ordering mechanism.
summary.tldr: GNNRank learns global rankings from directed comparison graphs using ranking-aware objectives and a graph-structured scoring approach.

title: GNNRank: Learning Global Rankings from Pairwise Comparisons via Directed Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Variational inference is a powerful paradigm for approximate Bayesian inference with a number of appealing properties, including support for model learning and data subsampling. By contrast MCMC methods like Hamiltonian Monte Carlo do not share these properties but remain attractive since, contrary to parametric methods, MCMC is asymptotically unbiased. For these reasons researchers have sought to combine the strengths of both classes of algorithms, with recent approaches coming closer to realizing this vision in practice. However, supporting data subsampling in these hybrid methods can be a challenge, a shortcoming that we address by introducing a surrogate likelihood that can be learned jointly with other variational parameters. We argue theoretically that the resulting algorithm allows an intuitive trade-off between inference fidelity and computational cost. In an extensive empirical comparison we show that our method performs well in practice and that it is well-suited for black-box inference in probabilistic programming frameworks.

paragraphs: Approximate Bayesian inference offers different strengths through variational methods and Markov chain Monte Carlo. Variational inference supports model learning and training with subsets of data. MCMC methods such as Hamiltonian Monte Carlo remain attractive for their asymptotic lack of bias. Combining these strengths is appealing, but supporting data subsampling in hybrid algorithms can be difficult.

This paper addresses that difficulty with a surrogate likelihood learned together with the other variational parameters. The surrogate becomes part of the inference procedure's learned components, providing a mechanism for handling the data-subsampling challenge in variational annealed importance sampling. The approach therefore targets an obstacle to making hybrid inference computationally practical.

The authors give a theoretical argument that the resulting algorithm offers an understandable trade-off between inference fidelity and computational cost. An extensive empirical comparison finds that it performs well in practice and is suitable for black-box inference in probabilistic programming frameworks. These findings support learned likelihood surrogates as a way to balance the quality and expense of approximate inference within this hybrid approach.
summary.tldr: A jointly learned surrogate likelihood supports data subsampling in hybrid Bayesian inference while providing a fidelity–computation trade-off.

title: Surrogate Likelihoods for Variational Annealed Importance Sampling

abstract: We propose computationally tractable accelerated first-order methods for Riemannian optimization, extending the Nesterov accelerated gradient (NAG) method. For both geodesically convex and geodesically strongly convex objective functions, our algorithms are shown to have the same iteration complexities as those for the NAG method on Euclidean spaces, under only standard assumptions. To the best of our knowledge, the proposed scheme is the first fully accelerated method for geodesically convex optimization problems. Our convergence analysis makes use of novel metric distortion lemmas as well as carefully designed potential functions. A connection with the continuous-time dynamics for modeling Riemannian acceleration in (Alimisis et al., 2020) is also identified by letting the stepsize tend to zero. We validate our theoretical results through numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Accelerated gradient methods can reduce the number of optimization steps needed in ordinary Euclidean spaces. This paper extends that idea to Riemannian optimization, where the space has a curved geometry. It considers geodesically convex objectives and the stronger geodesically strongly convex case, adapting the acceleration principle associated with Nesterov's method.

The proposed algorithms are computationally tractable first-order methods, meaning their updates use gradient information. Under the standard assumptions invoked in the paper, their iteration complexities match those of Nesterov acceleration in Euclidean spaces for both objective classes. The authors describe their scheme as the first fully accelerated method for geodesically convex optimization, qualified by their knowledge of prior work.

The analysis introduces results controlling metric distortion and carefully constructed potential functions to track progress. It also connects the discrete algorithms to previously studied continuous-time acceleration dynamics as the step size approaches zero. Numerical experiments support the theoretical results. Together, these contributions address both how to implement acceleration on curved spaces and how to justify its convergence.
summary.tldr: Tractable accelerated methods match Euclidean Nesterov iteration complexities for geodesically convex and strongly convex optimization under standard assumptions.

title: Accelerated Gradient Methods for Geodesically Convex Optimization: Tractable Algorithms and Convergence Analysis

abstract: Multi-objective optimization (MOO) and multi-task learning (MTL) have gained much popularity with prevalent use cases such as production model development of regression / classification / ranking models with MOO, and training deep learning models with MTL. Despite the long history of research in MOO, its application to machine learning requires development of solution strategy, and algorithms have recently been developed to solve specific problems such as discovery of any Pareto optimal (PO) solution, and that with a particular form of preference. In this paper, we develop a novel and generic framework to discover a PO solution with multiple forms of preferences. It allows us to formulate a generic MOO / MTL problem to express a preference, which is solved to achieve both alignment with the preference and PO, at the same time. Specifically, we apply the framework to solve the weighted Chebyshev problem and an extension of that. The former is known as a method to discover the Pareto front, the latter helps to find a model that outperforms an existing model with only one run. Experimental results demonstrate not only the method achieves competitive performance with existing methods, but also it allows us to achieve the performance from different forms of preferences.

paragraphs: When a model must serve several objectives or tasks, improving one outcome can come at the expense of another. Pareto optimality describes solutions where no objective can improve without worsening another. However, finding such a solution does not by itself express which tradeoffs a user prefers. This paper develops a framework that combines these two goals.

The framework accommodates multiple forms of preference within a common formulation for multi-objective optimization and multi-task learning. Its aim is to find a solution that both aligns with the stated preference and achieves Pareto optimality. The authors apply it to weighted Chebyshev optimization, a method for exploring the Pareto front, and to an extension designed to help find a model that improves on an existing model in a single run.

Experiments report competitive performance relative to existing methods while demonstrating different ways to specify preferences. The contribution is therefore a more flexible route to selecting desirable tradeoffs, alongside the optimization needed to achieve them.
summary.tldr: A unified optimization framework seeks Pareto-optimal models while accommodating several forms of user preference.

title: A Multi-objective / Multi-task Learning Framework Induced by Pareto Stationarity

abstract: The ability to align points across two related yet incomparable point clouds (e.g. living in different spaces) plays an important role in machine learning. The Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) framework provides an increasingly popular answer to such problems, by seeking a low-distortion, geometry-preserving assignment between these points. As a non-convex, quadratic generalization of optimal transport (OT), GW is NP-hard. While practitioners often resort to solving GW approximately as a nested sequence of entropy-regularized OT problems, the cubic complexity (in the number $n$ of samples) of that approach is a roadblock. We show in this work how a recent variant of the OT problem that restricts the set of admissible couplings to those having a low-rank factorization is remarkably well suited to the resolution of GW: when applied to GW, we show that this approach is not only able to compute a stationary point of the GW problem in time $O(n^2)$, but also uniquely positioned to benefit from the knowledge that the initial cost matrices are low-rank, to yield a linear time $O(n)$ GW approximation. Our approach yields similar results, yet orders of magnitude faster computation than the SoTA entropic GW approaches, on both simulated and real data.

paragraphs: Matching two point clouds is difficult when their points live in different spaces and cannot be compared directly. Gromov-Wasserstein methods seek assignments that preserve their internal geometry. This leads to a non-convex, quadratic optimal transport problem that is NP-hard. A commonly used approximate solution involves nested entropy-regularized transport problems with cubic complexity in the number of samples.

The paper instead restricts transport couplings to those with a low-rank factorization. This structured representation is particularly useful for Gromov-Wasserstein optimization: the authors show that it can compute a stationary point in quadratic time. On simulated and real data, the approach produces similar results to state-of-the-art entropic Gromov-Wasserstein methods while running orders of magnitude faster. The computational claims concern stationary-point computation and approximation, with linear scaling depending on low-rank costs as well as couplings. The work shows how these two forms of structure can make geometry-based matching substantially more practical.
summary.tldr: Low-rank couplings enable faster Gromov-Wasserstein optimization, with linear-time approximation when the cost matrices are also low-rank.

title: Linear-Time Gromov Wasserstein Distances using Low Rank Couplings and Costs

abstract: Off-policy learning (OPL) aims at finding improved policies from logged bandit data, often by minimizing the inverse propensity scoring (IPS) estimator of the risk. In this work, we investigate a smooth regularization for IPS, for which we derive a two-sided PAC-Bayes generalization bound. The bound is tractable, scalable, interpretable and provides learning certificates. In particular, it is also valid for standard IPS without making the assumption that the importance weights are bounded. We demonstrate the relevance of our approach and its favorable performance through a set of learning tasks. Since our bound holds for standard IPS, we are able to provide insight into when regularizing IPS is useful. Namely, we identify cases where regularization might not be needed. This goes against the belief that, in practice, clipped IPS often enjoys favorable performance than standard IPS in OPL.
