paragraphs: Off-policy learning uses logged bandit feedback to learn a policy different from the one that collected the data. A common approach estimates risk using inverse propensity scoring, or IPS, which accounts for how likely the logged actions were. This paper studies a smooth regularization of that estimator and develops guarantees for learning with it.

The main theoretical contribution is a two-sided PAC-Bayes generalization bound. It provides a tractable and scalable way to relate estimated performance to generalization and produce learning certificates. The bound also applies to ordinary IPS without assuming that its importance weights are bounded. That coverage allows the authors to examine both regularized and unregularized estimation within the same analysis.

The reported learning tasks demonstrate the relevance and favorable performance of the approach. The analysis also identifies cases where regularization might be unnecessary. This qualifies the common expectation that clipping IPS weights tends to be preferable in practice. The result supports a more conditional view: whether regularization helps depends on the learning situation, rather than being a universal requirement.
summary.tldr: A PAC-Bayes analysis of smoothly regularized IPS provides learning certificates and identifies cases where ordinary IPS may need no regularization.

title: Exponential Smoothing for Off-Policy Learning

abstract: We develop a transformer-based sequence-to-sequence model that recovers scalar ordinary differential equations (ODEs) in symbolic form from irregularly sampled and noisy observations of a single solution trajectory. We demonstrate in extensive empirical evaluations that our model performs better or on par with existing methods in terms of accurate recovery across various settings. Moreover, our method is efficiently scalable: after one-time pretraining on a large set of ODEs, we can infer the governing law of a new observed solution in a few forward passes of the model.
originalAbstract: We develop a transformer-based sequence-to-sequence model that recovers scalar ordinary differential equations (ODEs) in symbolic form from irregularly sampled and noisy observations of a single solution trajectory. We demonstrate in extensive empirical evaluations that our model performs better or on par with existing methods in terms of accurate recovery across various settings. Moreover, our method is efficiently scalable: after one-time pretraining on a large set of ODEs, we can infer the governing law of a new observed solution in a few forward passes of the model.

paragraphs: This paper addresses recovering a mathematical law from observations of a changing quantity. The target is a scalar ordinary differential equation, expressed symbolically, and the input consists of measurements from a single solution trajectory. The method is designed to handle observations that are both noisy and taken at irregular times.

The authors develop a transformer-based sequence-to-sequence model that maps those observations to an equation. They pretrain the model once on a large collection of ordinary differential equations. After this preparation, the governing law for a newly observed solution can be inferred with only a few forward passes through the model, making the distinction between training effort and new-instance inference central to the approach.

Extensive empirical evaluations show recovery accuracy that matches or exceeds existing methods across the tested settings. These findings support the use of a pretrained transformer for symbolic equation recovery from imperfect observations. The stated scope is scalar equations and a single observed trajectory; within that scope, the paper combines competitive empirical recovery with an efficient inference procedure after pretraining.
summary.tldr: A pretrained transformer recovers symbolic scalar differential equations from one noisy, irregularly sampled trajectory using a few forward passes.

title: Predicting Ordinary Differential Equations with Transformers

abstract: Resource-constrained perception systems such as edge computing and vision-for-robotics require vision models to be both accurate and lightweight in computation and memory usage. While knowledge distillation is a proven strategy to enhance the performance of lightweight classification models, its application to structured outputs like object detection and instance segmentation remains a complicated task, due to the variability in outputs and complex internal network modules involved in the distillation process. In this paper, we propose a simple yet surprisingly effective sequential approach to knowledge distillation that progressively transfers the knowledge of a set of teacher detectors to a given lightweight student. To distill knowledge from a highly accurate but complex teacher model, we construct a sequence of teachers to help the student gradually adapt. Our progressive strategy can be easily combined with existing detection distillation mechanisms to consistently maximize student performance in various settings. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to successfully distill knowledge from Transformer-based teacher detectors to convolution-based students, and unprecedentedly boost the performance of ResNet-50 based RetinaNet from 36.5% to 42.0% AP and Mask R-CNN from 38.2% to 42.5% AP on the MS COCO benchmark. Code available at https://github.com/Shengcao-Cao/MTPD.

paragraphs: Object detectors for resource-constrained systems must balance accuracy with computation and memory use. Knowledge distillation can help a small model learn from a larger one, but detection involves variable structured outputs and complicated internal modules. This makes transferring knowledge more challenging than in the classification setting where distillation is already well established.

The paper proposes teaching a lightweight detector progressively through a sequence of teacher models. This sequence helps the student gradually adapt before absorbing knowledge from a highly accurate, complex teacher. The strategy can be combined with existing detection distillation mechanisms, making the ordering of teachers an additional tool for improving the student.

The authors report successful transfer from Transformer-based teachers to convolution-based students. On MS COCO, ResNet-50 RetinaNet improves from 36.5% to 42.0% AP, while Mask R-CNN improves from 38.2% to 42.5% AP. These results demonstrate substantial gains in the reported configurations and support progressive teaching as a useful approach to bridging differences between teacher and student models.
summary.tldr: A sequence of teacher detectors progressively improves lightweight students, including successful transfer from Transformer teachers to convolutional models.

title: Learning Lightweight Object Detectors via Multi-Teacher Progressive Distillation

abstract: Recent works successfully leveraged Large Language Models’ (LLM) abilities to capture abstract knowledge about world’s physics to solve decision-making problems. Yet, the alignment between LLMs’ knowledge and the environment can be wrong and limit functional competence due to lack of grounding. In this paper, we study an approach (named GLAM) to achieve this alignment through functional grounding: we consider an agent using an LLM as a policy that is progressively updated as the agent interacts with the environment, leveraging online Reinforcement Learning to improve its performance to solve goals. Using an interactive textual environment designed to study higher-level forms of functional grounding, and a set of spatial and navigation tasks, we study several scientific questions: 1) Can LLMs boost sample efficiency for online learning of various RL tasks? 2) How can it boost different forms of generalization? 3) What is the impact of online learning? We study these questions by functionally grounding several variants (size, architecture) of FLAN-T5.

paragraphs: A language model can contain useful abstract knowledge about how the world works while still making poor decisions in a particular environment. The problem is alignment between that knowledge and what actions actually accomplish. This paper studies functional grounding: connecting a model's decision-making behavior to feedback obtained through interaction with an environment.

The proposed approach, GLAM, uses a large language model as the agent's policy. Online reinforcement learning progressively updates that policy as the agent interacts and works toward goals. The learning process therefore gives the model opportunities to adapt its behavior using experience from the environment in which its decisions are applied.

The study uses an interactive textual environment with spatial and navigation tasks, examining FLAN-T5 variants that differ in size and architecture. It asks whether language models improve sample efficiency, how they affect different forms of generalization, and what online learning contributes. The abstract presents these as research questions rather than reporting specific answers, so the stated contribution is the grounding approach and its experimental investigation.
summary.tldr: GLAM studies how online reinforcement learning can ground language-model policies through interaction in textual spatial and navigation tasks.

title: Grounding Large Language Models in Interactive Environments with Online Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The recent advances in neural language models have also been successfully applied to the field of chemistry, offering generative solutions for classical problems in molecular design and synthesis planning. These new methods have the potential to fuel a new era of data-driven automation in scientific discovery. However, specialized models are still typically required for each task, leading to the need for problem-specific fine-tuning and neglecting task interrelations. The main obstacle in this field is the lack of a unified representation between natural language and chemical representations, complicating and limiting human-machine interaction. Here, we propose the first multi-domain, multi-task language model that can solve a wide range of tasks in both the chemical and natural language domains. Our model can handle chemical and natural language concurrently, without requiring expensive pre-training on single domains or task-specific models. Interestingly, sharing weights across domains remarkably improves our model when benchmarked against state-of-the-art baselines on single-domain and cross-domain tasks. In particular, sharing information across domains and tasks gives rise to large improvements in cross-domain tasks, the magnitude of which increase with scale, as measured by more than a dozen of relevant metrics. Our work suggests that such models can robustly and efficiently accelerate discovery in physical sciences by superseding problem-specific fine-tuning and enhancing human-model interactions.

paragraphs: Language models can support molecular design and synthesis planning, but specialized models for separate tasks can leave useful connections unexplored. This paper targets the divide between chemical representations and natural language. It proposes a single language model that handles multiple tasks in both domains, allowing chemical and textual information to be processed together.

The model shares weights across domains and tasks without requiring expensive pretraining within individual domains or separate task-specific models. Benchmark comparisons show that this sharing improves performance on both single-domain and cross-domain tasks. The largest highlighted gains occur on tasks spanning the two domains, where improvements grow with scale across more than a dozen evaluation metrics.

These results suggest that a common representation can make information learned in one domain useful in another. The authors argue that such models could make scientific discovery more efficient by reducing reliance on problem-specific fine-tuning and improving human interaction with models. The demonstrated contribution is the multi-task model and its benchmark performance; acceleration of broader physical-science discovery is presented as a prospective implication.
summary.tldr: A shared multi-task language model improves chemical and textual benchmarks, with especially strong cross-domain gains that increase with scale.

title: Unifying Molecular and Textual Representations via Multi-task Language Modelling

abstract: We propose Automatic Feature Explanation using Contrasting Concepts (FALCON), an interpretability framework to explain features of image representations. For a target feature, FALCON captions its highly activating cropped images using a large captioning dataset (like LAION-400m) and a pre-trained vision-language model like CLIP. Each word among the captions is scored and ranked leading to a small number of shared, human-understandable concepts that closely describe the target feature. FALCON also applies contrastive interpretation using lowly activating (counterfactual) images, to eliminate spurious concepts. Although many existing approaches interpret features independently, we observe in state-of-the-art self-supervised and supervised models, that less than 20% of the representation space can be explained by individual features. We show that features in larger spaces become more interpretable when studied in groups and can be explained with high-order scoring concepts through FALCON. We discuss how extracted concepts can be used to explain and debug failures in downstream tasks. Finally, we present a technique to transfer concepts from one (explainable) representation space to another unseen representation space by learning a simple linear transformation.

paragraphs: FALCON explains features inside image representations by finding concepts shared by images that activate them strongly. It captions highly activating image crops using a large captioning dataset and a pretrained vision-language model. Words in those captions are scored and ranked to produce a compact collection of human-readable concepts.

The method also examines images that activate the target feature weakly. This contrast helps remove concepts that appear relevant but do not distinguish strong activation from weak activation. The authors then question the practice of explaining each feature separately: in the supervised and self-supervised models studied, individual features explain less than 20 percent of the representation space.

Studying features in groups makes larger representation spaces more interpretable, and FALCON can describe these groups with higher-order concept scores. The paper discusses using extracted concepts to understand and debug downstream failures. It also presents a learned linear transformation that transfers concepts from an explainable representation space to an unseen one, extending the approach beyond interpreting a single fixed representation.
summary.tldr: FALCON uses contrasting image captions to explain individual features and feature groups, revealing interpretable structure beyond single coordinates.

title: Identifying Interpretable Subspaces in Image Representations

abstract: Finding the mixed Nash equilibria (MNE) of a two-player zero sum continuous game is an important and challenging problem in machine learning. A canonical algorithm to finding the MNE is the noisy gradient descent ascent method which in the infinite particle limit gives rise to the Mean-Field Gradient Descent Ascent (GDA) dynamics on the space of probability measures. In this paper, we first study the convergence of a two-scale Mean-Field GDA dynamics for finding the MNE of the entropy-regularized objective. More precisely we show that for each finite temperature (or regularization parameter), the two-scale Mean-Field GDA with a suitable finite scale ratio converges exponentially to the unique MNE without assuming the convexity or concavity of the interaction potential. The key ingredient of our proof lies in the construction of new Lyapunov functions that dissipate exponentially along the Mean-Field GDA. We further study the simulated annealing of the Mean-Field GDA dynamics. We show that with a temperature schedule that decays logarithmically in time the annealed Mean-Field GDA converges to the MNE of the original unregularized objective.

paragraphs: In a two-player zero-sum continuous game, finding a mixed Nash equilibrium means finding suitable distributions over the players' choices. Noisy gradient descent-ascent leads, in an infinite-particle limit, to mean-field dynamics over probability measures. This paper studies a two-scale version of those dynamics, where the players evolve at different rates.

For an entropy-regularized objective at each finite temperature, the authors prove exponential convergence to the unique mixed Nash equilibrium when the finite scale ratio is suitably chosen. The result does not require the interaction potential to be convex or concave. The proof constructs new Lyapunov functions that decrease exponentially along the dynamics, providing a way to track progress toward equilibrium.

The paper also considers gradually removing the entropy regularization through simulated annealing. With temperature decreasing logarithmically over time, the annealed dynamics converge to a mixed Nash equilibrium of the original unregularized objective. These are guarantees for the specified mean-field dynamics and schedules, connecting fixed-temperature convergence with a route toward solving the original game.
summary.tldr: Suitably scaled mean-field gradient dynamics converge to regularized game equilibria, while logarithmic annealing reaches an equilibrium of the original game.

title: Two-Scale Gradient Descent Ascent Dynamics Finds Mixed Nash Equilibria of Continuous Games: A Mean-Field Perspective

abstract: We consider the problem of ranking n experts based on their performances on d tasks. We make a monotonicity assumption stating that for each pair of experts, one outperforms the other on all tasks. We consider the sequential setting where in each round the learner has access to noisy evaluations of actively chosen pair of expert-task, given the information available up to the actual round. Given a confidence parameter $\delta \in (0, 1)$, we provide strategies allowing to recover the correct ranking of experts and develop a bound on the total number of queries made by our algorithm that hold with probability at least $1-\delta$. We show that our strategy is adaptive to the complexity of the problem (our bounds are instance dependent), and develop matching lower bounds up to a ploy-logarithmic factor. Finally, we adapt our strategy to the relaxed problem of best expert identification and provide numerical simulation consistent with our theoretical results

paragraphs: This paper studies how to rank experts when their performance can be measured across many tasks, but each measurement is noisy. Its central assumption is strong: for any pair of experts, the better expert performs better on every task. Thus, tasks provide different opportunities to gather evidence about a consistent underlying ordering.

The learner operates sequentially, choosing which expert to evaluate on which task using information collected so far. The authors give strategies for recovering the correct ranking and bound the number of evaluations with probability at least one minus a chosen failure tolerance. These bounds depend on the particular problem instance, allowing the analysis to reflect differences in difficulty.

Matching lower bounds, up to polylogarithmic factors, show that the proposed evaluation requirements are close to the theoretical limits in this setting. The authors also adapt the strategy to identifying only the best expert. Numerical simulations agree with the theory, supporting adaptive evaluation as a way to avoid unnecessary measurements under the shared-ordering assumption.
summary.tldr: Adaptive evaluations can efficiently rank experts under an assumption that their relative performance order is consistent across tasks.

title: Active Ranking of Experts Based on their Performances in Many Tasks

abstract: To mitigate the privacy leakages and communication burdens of Federated Learning (FL), decentralized FL (DFL) discards the central server and each client only communicates with its neighbors in a decentralized communication network. However, existing DFL suffers from high inconsistency among local clients, which results in severe distribution shift and inferior performance compared with centralized FL (CFL), especially on heterogeneous data or sparse communication topologies. To alleviate this issue, we propose two DFL algorithms named DFedSAM and DFedSAM-MGS to improve the performance of DFL. Specifically, DFedSAM leverages gradient perturbation to generate local flat models via Sharpness Aware Minimization (SAM), which searches for models with uniformly low loss values. DFedSAM-MGS further boosts DFedSAM by adopting Multiple Gossip Steps (MGS) for better model consistency, which accelerates the aggregation of local flat models and better balances communication complexity and generalization. Theoretically, we present improved convergence rates $\small \mathcal{O}\big(\frac{1}{\sqrt{KT}}+\frac{1}{T}+\frac{1}{K^{1/2}T^{3/2}(1-\lambda)^2}\big)$ and $\small \mathcal{O}\big(\frac{1}{\sqrt{KT}}+\frac{1}{T}+\frac{\lambda^Q+1}{K^{1/2}T^{3/2}(1-\lambda^Q)^2}\big)$ in non-convex setting for DFedSAM and DFedSAM-MGS, respectively, where $1-\lambda$ is the spectral gap of gossip matrix and $Q$ is the number of MGS. Empirically, our methods can achieve competitive performance compared with CFL methods and outperform existing DFL methods.

paragraphs: Decentralized federated learning removes the central server and lets clients exchange information only with neighboring clients. However, their local models can become inconsistent, especially when clients have different data distributions or communication links are sparse. The paper targets this inconsistency as a source of poorer performance compared with centralized federated learning.

DFedSAM uses Sharpness Aware Minimization to find local models with low loss across nearby parameter settings. Its gradient perturbations encourage flatter solutions. DFedSAM-MGS adds multiple gossip steps, increasing the mixing of these local models across the communication network. This additional communication is intended to improve agreement while balancing communication cost and generalization.

The authors derive improved convergence rates for both algorithms in a nonconvex setting. The bounds explicitly depend on the communication network's spectral gap, and the second also incorporates the number of gossip steps. Empirically, the methods outperform existing decentralized approaches and can compete with centralized ones. The results connect local optimization choices and network communication to better model consistency.
summary.tldr: Flatter local models and additional gossip steps improve model agreement, convergence, and empirical performance in decentralized federated learning.

title: Improving the Model Consistency of Decentralized Federated Learning

abstract: Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins that neutralize pathogens and constitute the core of our adaptive immune system. De novo generation of new antibodies that target specific antigens holds the key to accelerating vaccine discovery. However, this co-design of the amino acid sequence and the 3D structure subsumes and accentuates, some central challenges from multiple tasks including protein folding (sequence to structure), inverse folding (structure to sequence), and docking (binding). We strive to surmount these challenges with a new generative model AbODE that extends graph PDEs to accommodate both contextual information and external interactions. Unlike existing approaches, AbODE uses a single round of full-shot decoding, and elicits continuous differential attention that encapsulates, and evolves with, latent interactions within the antibody as well as those involving the antigen. We unravel fundamental connections between AbODE and temporal networks as well as graph-matching networks. The proposed model significantly outperforms existing methods on standard metrics across benchmarks.

paragraphs: Designing an antibody for a particular antigen requires coordinating its amino acid sequence with its three-dimensional structure and its interactions with the target. These requirements combine challenges usually studied separately: predicting structure from sequence, finding sequences for a structure, and modeling binding. AbODE addresses this coupled design problem with a generative model.

The model extends graph-based differential equations to represent contextual information and external interactions. Its continuous differential attention evolves alongside hidden interactions within the antibody and between the antibody and antigen. This makes the changing interaction representation part of the generation process. AbODE also produces its output through a single full-shot decoding round.

The paper develops connections between this design and temporal networks, as well as networks for graph matching. Across the reported benchmarks, AbODE significantly outperforms existing methods on standard evaluation metrics. These findings support the proposed approach to joint sequence and structure generation; the stated evidence concerns benchmark performance rather than demonstrated vaccine discovery.
summary.tldr: AbODE jointly generates antibody sequences and structures using evolving representations of internal and antigen interactions, improving performance across reported benchmarks.

title: AbODE: Ab initio antibody design using conjoined ODEs

abstract: It has been recognized that the data generated by the denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) improves adversarial training. After two years of rapid development in diffusion models, a question naturally arises: can better diffusion models further improve adversarial training? This paper gives an affirmative answer by employing the most recent diffusion model which has higher efficiency ($\sim 20$ sampling steps) and image quality (lower FID score) compared with DDPM. Our adversarially trained models achieve state-of-the-art performance on RobustBench using only generated data (no external datasets). Under the $\ell_\infty$-norm threat model with $\epsilon=8/255$, our models achieve $70.69\\%$ and $42.67\\%$ robust accuracy on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, respectively, i.e. improving upon previous state-of-the-art models by $+4.58\\%$ and $+8.03\\%$. Under the $\ell_2$-norm threat model with $\epsilon=128/255$, our models achieve $84.86\\%$ on CIFAR-10 ($+4.44\\%$). These results also beat previous works that use external data. We also provide compelling results on the SVHN and TinyImageNet datasets. Our code is at https://github.com/wzekai99/DM-Improves-AT.

paragraphs: Adversarial training aims to make classifiers withstand deliberately chosen input perturbations. Earlier work had already shown that images generated by diffusion models could help. This paper asks whether improvements in the image generator translate into further robustness gains, and reports that they do in the evaluated settings.

The authors use a diffusion model with better image quality and greater sampling efficiency than DDPM, requiring approximately 20 sampling steps. Their approach uses generated data without adding external datasets. This connects progress in image generation to robust classification: the generator supplies training material whose usefulness is measured through the resulting classifier’s resistance to attacks.

Under an infinity-norm perturbation budget of 8/255, the reported robust accuracies are 70.69% on CIFAR-10 and 42.67% on CIFAR-100. Under a Euclidean-norm budget of 128/255, CIFAR-10 accuracy reaches 84.86%. The authors report state-of-the-art RobustBench results, including improvements over previous approaches using external data, and additional positive results on SVHN and TinyImageNet. These findings apply to the specified threat models and evaluations.
summary.tldr: Higher-quality diffusion-generated images improve adversarial training, producing reported robustness gains without external datasets.

title: Better Diffusion Models Further Improve Adversarial Training

abstract: This paper introduces a distributed, GPU-centric experience replay system, GEAR, designed to perform scalable reinforcement learning (RL) with large sequence models (such as transformers). With such models, existing systems such as Reverb face considerable bottlenecks in memory, computation, and communication. GEAR, however, optimizes memory efficiency by enabling the memory resources on GPU servers (including host memory and device memory) to manage trajectory data. Furthermore, it facilitates decentralized GPU devices to expedite various trajectory selection strategies, circumventing computational bottlenecks. GEAR is equipped with GPU kernels capable of collecting trajectories using zero-copy access to host memory, along with remote-directed-memory access over InfiniBand, improving communication efficiency. Cluster experiments have shown that GEAR can achieve performance levels up to 6× greater than Reverb when training state-of-the-art large RL models. GEAR is open-sourced at https:// github.com/bigrl-team/gear.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning systems reuse stored trajectories to train their models. When those models are large sequence networks such as transformers, supplying that experience can become a bottleneck in memory, computation, and communication. GEAR is a distributed experience replay system designed to address all three bottlenecks with a GPU-centered architecture.

The system manages trajectory data using both host memory and GPU device memory on GPU servers. It distributes trajectory-selection work across GPU devices so that selection does not become a centralized computational obstacle. For data movement, specialized GPU kernels access host memory without an intermediate copy, while remote direct memory access over InfiniBand supports efficient communication between machines.

Cluster experiments report performance up to six times that of Reverb when training large reinforcement learning models. This is a systems result about the infrastructure delivering training experience. The contribution shows how coordinating memory placement, trajectory selection, and communication can improve the performance of experience replay as the models consuming that experience grow larger.
summary.tldr: GEAR reorganizes trajectory storage, selection, and transfer around GPUs to accelerate experience replay for large reinforcement learning models.

title: GEAR: A GPU-Centric Experience Replay System for Large Reinforcement Learning Models

abstract: Coarse-graining (CG) accelerates molecular simulations of protein dynamics by simulating sets of atoms as singular beads. Backmapping is the opposite operation of bringing lost atomistic details back from the CG representation. While machine learning (ML) has produced accurate and efficient CG simulations of proteins, fast and reliable backmapping remains a challenge. Rule-based methods produce poor all-atom geometries, needing computationally costly refinement through additional simulations. Recently proposed ML approaches outperform traditional baselines but are not transferable between proteins and sometimes generate unphysical atom placements with steric clashes and implausible torsion angles. This work addresses both issues to build a fast, transferable, and reliable generative backmapping tool for CG protein representations. We achieve generalization and reliability through a combined set of innovations: representation based on internal coordinates; an equivariant encoder/prior; a custom loss function that helps ensure local structure, global structure, and physical constraints; and expert curation of high-quality out-of-equilibrium protein data for training. Our results pave the way for out-of-the-box backmapping of coarse-grained simulations for arbitrary proteins.

Rule-based methods produce poor all-atom geometries, needing computationally costly refinement through additional simulations. paragraphs: Coarse-grained protein simulations gain speed by representing groups of atoms as single beads. Backmapping reconstructs the atom-level detail that this simplification removes. summary.tldr: A generative backmapping method combines structural representations, physical constraints, and curated data to improve reliability and transfer between proteins.

title: Chemically Transferable Generative Backmapping of Coarse-Grained Proteins

abstract: We study the feasibility of identifying epistemic uncertainty (reflecting a lack of knowledge), as opposed to aleatoric uncertainty (reflecting entropy in the underlying distribution), in the outputs of large language models (LLMs) over free-form text. In the absence of ground-truth probabilities, we explore a setting where, in order to (approximately) disentangle a given LLM’s uncertainty, a significantly larger model stands in as a proxy for the ground truth. We show that small linear probes trained on the embeddings of frozen, pretrained models accurately predict when larger models will be more confident at the token level and that probes trained on one text domain generalize to others. Going further, we propose a fully unsupervised method that achieves non-trivial accuracy on the same task. Taken together, we interpret these results as evidence that LLMs naturally contain internal representations of different types of uncertainty that could potentially be leveraged to devise more informative indicators of model confidence in diverse practical settings. Code can be found at: https://github.com/KempnerInstitute/llm_uncertainty

paragraphs: A language model can be uncertain because it lacks knowledge or because the text itself allows multiple plausible continuations. The paper investigates whether these sources of uncertainty can be distinguished in free-form text. That distinction matters because additional knowledge could reduce the first kind, whereas variability in the underlying distribution remains even for a better-informed model.

The authors do not have ground-truth probabilities, so they use a substantially larger model as an approximate reference. They train small linear probes on representations from frozen pretrained models to predict when the larger model will be more confident about a token. These probes make accurate predictions and transfer across text domains. A fully unsupervised method also achieves non-trivial accuracy.

These findings support the authors’ interpretation that language models contain internal signals about different kinds of uncertainty. The conclusion remains approximate because greater confidence from a larger model stands in for ground truth. The results suggest a possible route toward more informative confidence indicators, rather than establishing a definitive separation of knowledge gaps from unavoidable uncertainty.
summary.tldr: Small probes can predict when a larger language model will be more confident, offering evidence of internal signals about uncertainty types.

title: Distinguishing the Knowable from the Unknowable with Language Models

abstract: Recent works have shown that machine learning models improve at a predictable rate with the amount of training data, leading to scaling laws that describe the relationship between error and dataset size. These scaling laws can help determine a model’s training dataset, but they take an aggregate view of the data by only considering the dataset’s size. We consider a new perspective by investigating scaling behavior for the value of individual data points: we find that a data point’s contribution to model’s performance shrinks predictably with the size of the dataset in a log-linear manner. Interestingly, there is significant variability in the scaling exponent among different data points, indicating that certain points are more valuable in small datasets and other points are relatively more useful as a part of large datasets. We provide learning theory support for our scaling laws and we observe empirically that it holds across several model classes. We further propose a maximum likelihood estimator and an amortized estimator to efficiently learn the individualized scaling behaviors from a small number of noisy observations per data point. Using our efficient estimators, we provide insights into factors that influence the scaling behavior of different data points. Finally we demonstrate applications of the individualized scaling laws to data valuation and data subset selection.

This paper studies scaling at that finer level. The authors find that a data point’s contribution to performance shrinks predictably with dataset size according to a log-linear relationship.

Different examples have substantially different scaling exponents. Consequently, points that are valuable in small datasets need not be the ones that are relatively most useful in larger datasets. The authors provide learning-theoretic support and observe the behavior across several model classes, suggesting that data value should be considered in relation to the size of the surrounding training set.

These estimators support analysis of factors associated with different scaling patterns. The authors also demonstrate applications to data valuation and subset selection, connecting the observed laws to decisions about which examples to retain or prioritize.
summary.tldr: Individual training examples follow different value-scaling patterns, making their relative usefulness depend on dataset size.

title: Scaling Laws for the Value of Individual Data Points in Machine Learning

abstract: Large language models such as GPT and Llama are trained with a next-token prediction loss. In this work, we suggest that training language models to predict multiple future tokens at once results in higher sample efficiency. More specifically, at each position in the training corpus, we ask the model to predict the following $n$ tokens using $n$ independent output heads, operating on top of a shared model trunk. Considering multi-token prediction as an auxiliary training task, we measure improved downstream capabilities with no overhead in training time for both code and natural language models. The method is increasingly useful for larger model sizes, and keeps its appeal when training for multiple epochs. Gains are especially pronounced on generative benchmarks like coding, where our models consistently outperform strong baselines by several percentage points. Our 13B parameter models solves 12% more problems on Human Eval and 17% more on MBPP than comparable next-token models. Experiments on small algorithmic tasks demonstrate that multi-token prediction is favorable for the development of induction heads and algorithmic reasoning capabilities. As an additional benefit, models trained with 4-token prediction are up to $3\times$ faster at inference, even with large batch sizes.

The findings make multi-token prediction relevant to both learning efficiency and generation speed, with the reported improvements tied to the evaluated model and task settings.
summary.tldr: Training models to predict several future tokens improves measured capabilities and enables inference speedups of up to threefold.

title: Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) problems where the learner attempts to infer an unobserved reward from some feedback variables have been studied in several recent papers. The setting of Interaction-Grounded Learning (IGL) is an example of such feedback-based reinforcement learning tasks where the learner optimizes the return by inferring latent binary rewards from the interaction with the environment. In the IGL setting, a relevant assumption used in the RL literature is that the feedback variable $Y$ is conditionally independent of the context-action $(X,A)$ given the latent reward $R$. In this work, we propose Variational Information-based IGL (VI-IGL) as an information-theoretic method to enforce the conditional independence assumption in the IGL-based RL problem. The VI-IGL framework learns a reward decoder using an information-based objective based on the conditional mutual information (MI) between the context-action $(X,A)$ and the feedback variable $Y$ observed from the environment. To estimate and optimize the information-based terms for the continuous random variables in the RL problem, VI-IGL leverages the variational representation of mutual information and results in a min-max optimization problem. Theoretical analysis shows that the optimization problem can be sample-efficiently solved. Furthermore, we extend the VI-IGL framework to general $f$-Information measures in the information theory literature, leading to the generalized $f$-VI-IGL framework to address the RL problem under the IGL condition. Finally, the empirical results on several reinforcement learning settings indicate an improved performance in comparison to the previous IGL-based RL algorithm.

paragraphs: Interaction-grounded learning considers agents that receive feedback but cannot directly observe the reward they should optimize. Here, the hidden reward is binary. A central assumption is that, once the reward is known, the feedback contains no further dependence on the context and action. Learning a reward decoder must respect that structure.

VI-IGL translates this assumption into an information-based learning objective. It uses conditional mutual information to capture the relevant dependence between context-action pairs and environmental feedback. A variational representation makes the information terms estimable and optimizable for continuous variables, yielding a min-max problem in which opposing optimization components are trained together.

The theoretical analysis shows that this optimization problem can be solved sample-efficiently. The authors also extend the framework beyond mutual information to general f-information measures. Experiments in several reinforcement-learning settings indicate better performance than the previous IGL-based algorithm. These results support information-theoretic reward decoding within the stated conditional-independence setting, connecting an assumption about feedback to a concrete learning procedure.
summary.tldr: VI-IGL learns hidden rewards through an information-based objective that enforces the conditional-independence structure assumed in interaction-grounded learning.

title: An Information Theoretic Approach to Interaction-Grounded Learning

abstract: The success of large language models in text processing has inspired their adaptation to speech modeling. However, since speech is continuous and complex, it is often discretized for autoregressive modeling. Speech tokens derived from self-supervised models (known as semantic tokens) typically focus on the linguistic aspects of speech but neglect prosodic information. As a result, models trained on these tokens can generate speech with reduced naturalness. Existing approaches try to fix this by adding pitch features to the semantic tokens. However, pitch alone cannot fully represent the range of paralinguistic attributes, and selecting the right features requires careful hand-engineering. To overcome this, we propose an end-to-end variational approach that automatically learns to encode these continuous speech attributes to enhance the semantic tokens. Our approach eliminates the need for manual extraction and selection of paralinguistic features. Moreover, it produces preferred speech continuations according to human raters. Code, samples and models are available at https://github.com/b04901014/vae-gslm.

paragraphs: Spoken language models often turn continuous speech into discrete tokens so they can generate speech autoregressively. However, tokens derived from self-supervised models tend to preserve linguistic content more strongly than prosody. A model can therefore retain information about what is said while losing information that contributes to how natural the resulting speech sounds.

Existing methods supplement these semantic tokens with pitch features, but the paper argues that pitch captures only part of the relevant information. Choosing additional features by hand also requires careful engineering. The proposed variational framework instead learns continuous speech attributes automatically and uses them to enrich the semantic tokens through an end-to-end approach.

This changes the representation-learning problem: the system learns which continuous attributes to encode instead of relying on a manually selected feature set. Human raters preferred the speech continuations produced by the proposed approach. That finding supports its intended benefit for perceived naturalness, while the removal of manual feature extraction makes the representation process less dependent on hand-engineered choices.
summary.tldr: A variational framework automatically enriches speech tokens with continuous attributes, producing speech continuations preferred by human raters.

title: A Variational Framework for Improving Naturalness in Generative Spoken Language Models

abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) are widely used post-training techniques for foundation models. However, their roles in enhancing model generalization capabilities remain unclear. This paper studies the difference between SFT and RL on generalization and memorization, focusing on text-based rule variants and visual variants. We introduce GeneralPoints, an arithmetic reasoning card game, and adopt V-IRL, a real-world navigation environment, to assess how models trained with SFT and RL generalize to unseen variants in both textual and visual domains. We show that RL, especially when trained with an outcome-based reward, generalizes across both rule-based textual and visual variants. SFT, in contrast, tends to memorize training data and struggles to generalize out-of-distribution scenarios. Further analysis reveals that RL improves the model’s underlying visual recognition capabilities, contributing to its enhanced generalization in the visual domain. Despite RL’s superior generalization, we show that SFT remains essential for effective RL training; SFT stabilizes the model’s output format, enabling subsequent RL to achieve its performance gains. These findings demonstrates the capability of RL for acquiring generalizable knowledge in complex, multi-modal tasks.

summary.tldr: In the studied multimodal tasks, RL generalizes better to unseen variants, while SFT supplies the stable output format needed for effective RL training.

title: SFT Memorizes, RL Generalizes: A Comparative Study of Foundation Model Post-training

abstract: Diagnosing deep neural networks (DNNs) by analyzing the eigenspectrum of their weights has been an active area of research in recent years. One of the main approaches involves measuring the heavytailness of the empirical spectral densities (ESDs) of weight matrices. This analysis has been shown to provide insights to help diagnose whether a model is well-trained or undertrained, and has been used to guide training methods involving layer-wise hyperparameter assignment. In this paper, we address an often-overlooked challenge in estimating the heavytailness of these ESDs: the impact of the aspect ratio of weight matrices. We demonstrate that matrices of varying sizes (and aspect ratios) introduce a non-negligible bias in estimating the heavytailness of ESDs, leading to inaccurate model diagnosis and layer-wise hyperparameter assignment. To overcome this challenge, we propose FARMS (Fixed-Aspect-Ratio Matrix Subsampling), a method that normalizes the weight matrices by subsampling submatrices with a fixed aspect ratio. Instead of measuring the heavytailness of the original ESD, we measure the average ESD of these subsampled submatrices. We show that this method effectively mitigates the aspect ratio bias. We validate our approach across various optimization techniques and application domains that involve eigenspectrum analysis of weights, including image classification in computer vision (CV) models, scientific machine learning (SciML) model training, and large language model (LLM) pruning. Our results show that despite its simplicity, FARMS uniformly improves the accuracy of eigenspectrum analysis while enabling more effective layer-wise hyperparameter assignment. In one of the LLM pruning experiments, FARMS reduces the perplexity of the LLaMA-7B model by 17.3% when compared with state-of-the-art methods.

This paper shows that matrix dimensions and aspect ratios can bias that measurement, making differences in shape look like differences in training quality.

summary.tldr: FARMS uses fixed-aspect-ratio submatrices to reduce bias in spectral diagnostics and improve their use in training and pruning.

title: Eigenspectrum Analysis of Neural Networks without Aspect Ratio Bias

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization is challenging because distribution shifts come in many forms. Numerous algorithms exist to address specific settings, but choosing the right training algorithm for the right dataset without trial and error is difficult. Indeed, real-world applications often involve multiple types and combinations of shifts that are hard to analyze theoretically. Method. This work explores the possibility of learning the selection of a training algorithm for OOD generalization. We propose a proof of concept (OOD-Chameleon) that formulates the selection as a multi-label classification over candidate algorithms, trained on a dataset of datasets representing a variety of shifts. We evaluate the ability of OOD-Chameleon to rank algorithms on unseen shifts and datasets based only on dataset characteristics, i.e., without training models first, unlike traditional model selection. Findings. Extensive experiments show that the learned selector identifies high-performing algorithms across synthetic, vision, and language tasks. Further inspection shows that it learns non-trivial decision rules, which provide new insights into the applicability of existing algorithms. Overall, this new approach opens the possibility of better exploiting and understanding the plethora of existing algorithms for OOD generalization.

paragraphs: Algorithms for out-of-distribution generalization address different kinds of changes between training and deployment data. Choosing among them becomes difficult when several shifts occur together. OOD-Chameleon asks whether an algorithm selector can learn this choice from dataset characteristics, reducing the need to train candidate models through trial and error.

The proposed proof of concept treats selection as multi-label classification over a set of candidate algorithms. Its training examples are themselves datasets representing varied distribution shifts. The learned selector is then evaluated on its ability to rank algorithms for unseen datasets and shifts using dataset characteristics alone, without first training those candidate models.

Experiments across synthetic, vision, and language tasks show that the selector identifies high-performing algorithms. Inspection also reveals non-trivial decision rules, offering insight into when existing methods are applicable. The paper presents this as evidence that algorithm selection can itself be learned and as a possible route to making better use of available generalization methods, rather than a universal solution to every distribution shift.
summary.tldr: OOD-Chameleon learns to rank generalization algorithms from dataset characteristics without first training the candidate models.

title: OOD-Chameleon: Is Algorithm Selection for OOD Generalization Learnable?

abstract: In this paper, we consider combinatorial reinforcement learning with preference feedback, where a learning agent sequentially offers an action—an assortment of multiple items—to a user, whose preference feedback follows a multinomial logistic (MNL) model. This framework allows us to model real-world scenarios, particularly those involving long-term user engagement, such as in recommender systems and online advertising. However, this framework faces two main challenges: (1) the unknown value of each item, unlike traditional MNL bandits that only address single-step preference feedback, and (2) the difficulty of ensuring optimism while maintaining tractable assortment selection in the combinatorial action space with unknown values. In this paper, we assume a contextual MNL preference model, where the mean utilities are linear, and the value of each item is approximated by a general function. We propose an algorithm, MNL-VQL, that addresses these challenges, making it both computationally and statistically efficient. As a special case, for linear MDPs (with the MNL preference feedback), we establish the first regret lower bound in this framework and show that MNL-VQL achieves near-optimal regret. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to provide statistical guarantees in combinatorial RL with preference feedback.

paragraphs: This paper studies an agent that repeatedly presents a collection of items to a user and learns from the user's preference feedback. The setting captures decisions where the aim includes long-term engagement, as in recommendations or advertising. Their algorithm, MNL-VQL, addresses efficient assortment selection while maintaining the optimism needed for its learning guarantees.

The paper establishes computational and statistical efficiency within this framework. For the special case of linear Markov decision processes with the specified preference feedback, it derives a regret lower bound and shows that MNL-VQL is near-optimal. The authors describe this as the first statistical guarantee for combinatorial reinforcement learning with preference feedback, qualified by their knowledge of prior work.
summary.tldr: MNL-VQL learns assortments from preference feedback and achieves near-optimal regret in the studied linear-MDP special case.

title: Combinatorial Reinforcement Learning with Preference Feedback

abstract: Composition—the ability to generate myriad variations from finite means—is believed to underlie powerful generalization. However, compositional generalization remains a key challenge for deep learning. A widely held assumption is that learning disentangled (factorized) representations naturally supports this kind of extrapolation. Yet, empirical results are mixed, with many generative models failing to recognize and compose factors to generate out-of-distribution (OOD) samples. In this work, we investigate a controlled 2D Gaussian "bump" generation task with fully disentangled $(x,y)$ inputs, demonstrating that standard generative architectures still fail in OOD regions when training with partial data, by re-entangling latent representations in subsequent layers. By examining the model’s learned kernels and manifold geometry, we show that this failure reflects a "memorization" strategy for generation via data superposition rather than via composition of the true factorized features. We show that when models are forced—through architectural modifications with regularization or curated training data—to render the disentangled latents into the full-dimensional representational (pixel) space, they can be highly data-efficient and effective at composing in OOD regions. These findings underscore that disentangled latents in an abstract representation are insufficient and show that if models can represent disentangled factors directly in the output representational space, it can achieve robust compositional generalization.

paragraphs: A model can receive clearly separated factors and still fail to combine them in unfamiliar ways. This paper demonstrates that issue in a controlled task: generating a two-dimensional Gaussian bump from separate horizontal and vertical coordinates. With only partial training coverage, standard generative architectures fail in regions outside the training distribution despite receiving fully disentangled inputs.

Analysis of learned kernels and representation geometry indicates that later layers re-entangle those inputs. The models generate through a memorization strategy based on superposing training data, rather than composing the underlying factors. This identifies a concrete reason why providing a factorized input representation does not by itself ensure compositional behavior.

The authors modify architectures with regularization or curate training data to force the separated factors to be rendered into the full pixel space. Under these interventions, models can become highly data-efficient and generate effectively in unseen regions. The findings support preserving factor structure through the rendering process, with the controlled bump task providing evidence for where compositional generalization can break down and how it can improve.
summary.tldr: A controlled generation study shows that disentangled inputs can be re-entangled, while forcing factorized rendering enables effective unseen combinations.

title: Compositional Generalization via Forced Rendering of Disentangled Latents

abstract: Despite the tremendous success of deep learning in computer vision, models still fall behind humans in generalizing to new input distributions. Existing benchmarks do not investigate the specific failure points of models by analyzing performance under many controlled conditions. Our study systematically dissects where and why models struggle with contour integration - a hallmark of human vision – by designing an experiment that tests object recognition under various levels of object fragmentation. Humans (n=50) perform at high accuracy, even with few object contours present. This is in contrast to models which exhibit substantially lower sensitivity to increasing object contours, with most of the over 1,000 models we tested barely performing above chance. Only at very large scales ($\sim5B$ training dataset size) do models begin to approach human performance. Importantly, humans exhibit an integration bias - a preference towards recognizing objects made up of directional fragments over directionless fragments. We find that not only do models that share this property perform better at our task, but that this bias also increases with model training dataset size, and training models to exhibit contour integration leads to high shape bias. Taken together, our results suggest that contour integration is a hallmark of object vision that underlies object recognition performance, and may be a mechanism learned from data at scale.

paragraphs: Humans can recognize objects from incomplete outlines, making contour integration a useful way to examine differences between human and machine vision. This study varies how much of an object’s contour remains visible, creating controlled recognition conditions. That design probes a specific visual capability rather than relying only on broad recognition benchmarks.

The study compares 50 human participants with more than 1,000 models. Humans maintain high accuracy even when few contours remain, whereas most tested models barely exceed chance and benefit much less as more contours appear. Models begin approaching human performance only at very large training scales, around five billion training examples.

Humans also prefer directional fragments over directionless fragments when recognizing objects. Models sharing this integration bias perform better on the task, and the bias increases with training dataset size. Training models to integrate contours also produces a strong preference for shape. Together, the findings suggest that contour integration supports object recognition and may emerge through learning from data at scale.
summary.tldr: Controlled fragmentation tests link human-like object recognition to contour integration, a capability that may emerge in models through large-scale training.

title: Contour Integration Underlies Human-Like Vision

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise as robotic planners but often struggle with long-horizon and complex tasks, especially in specialized environments requiring external knowledge. While hierarchical planning and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) address some of these challenges, they remain insufficient on their own and a deeper integration is required for achieving more reliable systems. To this end, we propose a neuro-symbolic approach that enhances LLMs-based planners with Knowledge Graph-based RAG for hierarchical plan generation. This method decomposes complex tasks into manageable subtasks, further expanded into executable atomic action sequences. To ensure formal correctness and proper decomposition, we integrate a Symbolic Validator, which also functions as a failure detector by aligning expected and observed world states. Our evaluation against baseline methods demonstrates the consistent significant advantages of integrating hierarchical planning, symbolic verification, and RAG across tasks of varying complexity and different LLMs. Additionally, our experimental setup and novel metrics not only validate our approach for complex planning but also serve as a tool for assessing LLMs’ reasoning and compositional capabilities. Code available at https://github.com/corneliocristina/HVR.

paragraphs: LLMs can help plan robotic actions, but complex tasks become difficult when they require many steps and specialized external knowledge. This paper integrates hierarchical planning, knowledge-graph retrieval, and symbolic verification into a single planning approach. The goal is to make the resulting plans more reliable through coordination among these components.

Knowledge Graph-based RAG supplies information for generating a hierarchy of plans. Complex tasks are divided into subtasks, which are expanded into executable atomic actions. A Symbolic Validator checks formal correctness and the decomposition of tasks. It also detects failures by comparing the world state expected from a plan with the state actually observed.

Evaluation across tasks of different complexity and several LLMs shows consistent, significant advantages over baseline methods. The paper also introduces an experimental setup and metrics for examining reasoning and compositional capabilities. Its contribution is the integrated relationship between knowledge retrieval, task decomposition, and validation: retrieved knowledge informs planning, while symbolic checks assess whether the resulting structure and execution fit the expected world state.
summary.tldr: Combining knowledge-graph retrieval, hierarchical planning, and symbolic validation improves LLM planning across tasks and models.

title: Hierarchical Planning for Complex Tasks with Knowledge Graph-RAG and Symbolic Verification

abstract: Consistency Training (CT) has recently emerged as a strong alternative to diffusion models for image generation. However, non-distillation CT often suffers from high variance and instability, motivating ongoing research into its training dynamics. We propose Variational Consistency Training (VCT), a flexible and effective framework compatible with various forward kernels, including those in flow matching. Its key innovation is a learned noise-data coupling scheme inspired by Variational Autoencoders, where a data-dependent encoder models noise emission. This enables VCT to adaptively learn noise-to-data pairings, reducing training variance relative to the fixed, unsorted pairings in classical CT. Experiments on multiple image datasets demonstrate significant improvements: our method surpasses baselines, achieves state-of-the-art FID among non-distillation CT approaches on CIFAR-10, and matches SoTA performance on ImageNet 64x64 with only two sampling steps. Code is available at https://github.com/sony/vct.

paragraphs: Consistency training offers an alternative to diffusion models for image generation, but training without distillation can suffer from high variance and instability. Variational Consistency Training addresses this through the relationship between noise and data during training. Its central change is to learn noise-to-data pairings instead of using the fixed, unsorted pairings of classical consistency training.

Inspired by variational autoencoders, VCT introduces a data-dependent encoder that models noise emission. This allows the pairing scheme to adapt to the data and reduces training variance relative to the classical setup. The framework supports different forward kernels, including those used in flow matching, so the learned coupling idea is not tied to only one forward-process choice.

Experiments on multiple image datasets report improvements over baselines. VCT achieves state-of-the-art FID among non-distillation consistency-training approaches on CIFAR-10 and matches state-of-the-art performance on ImageNet at 64-by-64 resolution using two sampling steps. These findings show that changing how training examples are coupled with noise can improve generation quality while retaining very short sampling procedures.
summary.tldr: VCT learns data-dependent noise pairings to reduce consistency-training variance and improve image generation with few sampling steps.

title: VCT: Training Consistency Models with Variational Noise Coupling

abstract: Subgraph GNNs have emerged as promising architectures that overcome the expressiveness limitations of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) by processing bags of subgraphs. Despite their compelling empirical performance, these methods are afflicted by a high computational complexity: they process bags whose size grows linearly in the number of nodes, hindering their applicability to larger graphs. In this work, we propose an effective and easy-to-implement approach to dramatically alleviate the computational cost of Subgraph GNNs and unleash broader applications thereof. Our method, dubbed HyMN, leverages walk-based centrality measures to sample a small number of relevant subgraphs and drastically reduce the bag size. By drawing a connection to perturbation analysis, we highlight the strength of the proposed centrality-based subgraph sampling, and further prove that these walk-based centralities can be additionally used as Structural Encodings for improved discriminative power. A comprehensive set of experimental results demonstrates that HyMN provides an effective synthesis of expressiveness, efficiency, and downstream performance, unlocking the application of Subgraph GNNs to dramatically larger graphs. Not only does our method outperform more sophisticated subgraph sampling approaches, it is also competitive, and sometimes better, than other state-of-the-art approaches for a fraction of their runtime.

paragraphs: Subgraph neural networks gain expressive power by processing collections of subgraphs rather than treating a graph only as a single object. Their computational burden grows because those collections typically expand with the number of nodes. HyMN addresses this bottleneck by choosing a small collection of relevant subgraphs, reducing the amount of material the network must process.

The selection uses walk-based centrality measures, which characterize structural importance through walks on the graph. The authors connect this sampling strategy to perturbation analysis to explain its strengths. They also prove that the same centrality measures can serve as structural encodings that improve discriminative power. Thus, the structural information helps both select subgraphs and enrich their representations.

Experiments show a useful balance of efficiency, expressiveness, and downstream performance, including application to substantially larger graphs. HyMN outperforms more elaborate subgraph sampling methods and is competitive with, sometimes better than, other leading approaches while using a fraction of their runtime. Those comparisons support selective processing as a practical route to scaling subgraph networks.
summary.tldr: HyMN uses walk-based centrality to select fewer subgraphs and improve structural representations, making expressive graph networks more efficient.

title: Balancing Efficiency and Expressiveness: Subgraph GNNs with Walk-Based Centrality

abstract: Accelerating the inference of large language models (LLMs) is a critical challenge in generative AI. Speculative decoding (SD) methods offer substantial efficiency gains by generating multiple tokens using a single target forward pass. However, existing SD approaches require the drafter and target models to share the same vocabulary, thus limiting the pool of possible drafters, often necessitating the training of a drafter from scratch. We present three new SD methods that remove this shared-vocabulary constraint. All three methods preserve the target distribution (i.e., they are lossless) and work with off-the-shelf models without requiring additional training or modifications. Empirically, on summarization, programming, and long-context tasks, our algorithms demonstrate significant speedups of up to 2.8x over standard autoregressive decoding. By enabling any off-the-shelf model to serve as a drafter and requiring no retraining, this work substantially broadens the applicability of the SD framework in practice.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding accelerates language generation by using a draft model to propose tokens and a target model to process multiple proposals in one forward pass. A practical obstacle is that existing approaches require both models to use the same vocabulary. That restriction narrows the available draft models and can make training a compatible model necessary.

This paper introduces three algorithms that remove the shared-vocabulary requirement. They work with existing models without additional training or modifications. All three preserve the target model’s output distribution, which is the meaning of lossless here: acceleration does not replace the target’s distribution with an approximation supplied by the drafter.

Experiments cover summarization, programming, and long-context tasks, with reported speedups reaching 2.8 times standard autoregressive decoding. That figure is an observed maximum across the evaluations. The broader contribution is flexibility in model pairing: removing vocabulary compatibility as a requirement substantially expands the pool of usable drafters and makes speculative decoding easier to apply without a separate training effort.
summary.tldr: Three lossless speculative decoding algorithms allow different draft and target vocabularies, achieving speedups of up to 2.8 times without retraining.

title: Accelerating LLM Inference with Lossless Speculative Decoding Algorithms for Heterogeneous Vocabularies

abstract: Recent advances in Dynamic Sparse Training (DST) have pushed the frontier of sparse neural network training in structured and unstructured contexts, matching dense-model performance while drastically reducing parameter counts to facilitate model scaling. However, unstructured sparsity often fails to translate into practical speedups on modern hardware. To address this shortcoming, we propose DynaDiag, a novel structured sparse-to-sparse DST method that performs at par with unstructured sparsity. DynaDiag enforces a diagonal sparsity pattern throughout training and preserves sparse computation in forward and backward passes. We further leverage the diagonal structure to accelerate computation via a custom CUDA kernel, rendering the method hardware-friendly. Empirical evaluations on diverse neural architectures demonstrate that our method maintains accuracy on par with unstructured counterparts while benefiting from tangible computational gains. Notably, with 90% sparse linear layers in ViTs, we observe up to a 3.13x speedup in online inference without sacrificing model performance and a 1.59x speedup in training on a GPU compared to equivalent unstructured layers.

DynaDiag enforces a diagonal sparsity pattern throughout training and preserves sparse computation in forward and backward passes. Empirical evaluations on diverse neural architectures demonstrate that our method maintains accuracy on par with unstructured counterparts while benefiting from tangible computational gains. paragraphs: Sparse networks can reduce parameter counts while retaining strong predictive performance, but fewer parameters do not automatically produce faster computation. Irregularly placed weights can be difficult for modern hardware to exploit. DynaDiag addresses this gap by imposing a diagonal sparsity pattern during dynamic sparse training.

The method preserves sparse computation in both the forward and backward passes. It also uses a custom CUDA kernel built around the diagonal structure, connecting the training design to an implementation that can benefit from that structure. Across diverse neural architectures, the authors report accuracy comparable to unstructured sparse alternatives alongside practical computational gains.

For Vision Transformers with linear layers that are 90% sparse, the reported online inference speedup reaches 3.13 times without sacrificing model performance. Training is 1.59 times faster on a GPU than with equivalent unstructured layers. These measurements illustrate the paper’s central point: a carefully chosen sparsity pattern can preserve the benefits of sparse learning while making the reduced computation useful on hardware.
summary.tldr: DynaDiag combines diagonal sparse training with a custom CUDA kernel to match unstructured sparsity’s accuracy while delivering measured GPU speedups.

title: Dynamic Sparse Training of Diagonally Sparse Networks

abstract: Solving mathematical problems using computer-verifiable languages like Lean has significantly impacted the mathematical and computer science communities. State-of-the-art methods utilize a single Large Language Model (LLM) to generate complete proof or perform tree search, but they fail to balance these tasks. We propose MA-LoT: Model-CollAboration Lean-based Long Chain-of-Thought, a comprehensive framework for Lean4 theorem proving to solve this issue. It separates the cognition tasks of general NL for whole-proof generation and error analysis for proof correction using the model-collaboration method. We achieve this by structured interaction of the LLM and Lean4 verifier in Long CoT. To implement the framework, we propose the novel LoT-Transfer Learning training-inference pipeline, which enables the Long CoT thinking capability to LLMs without special data annotation. Extensive experiment shows that our framework achieves a 61.07% accuracy rate on the Lean4 version of the MiniF2F-Test dataset, largely outperforming DeepSeek-V3 (33.61%), single-model tree search (InternLM-Step-Prover, 50.70%), and whole-proof generation (Godel-Prover, 55.33%) baselines. Furthermore, our findings highlight the potential of combining Long CoT with formal verification for a more insightful generation in a broader perspective.

paragraphs: Formal theorem proving requires a proposed proof to satisfy a computer-verifiable language such as Lean4. Generating an entire proof and diagnosing errors place different demands on a language model. MA-LoT addresses the difficulty of balancing these activities by using model collaboration to separate whole-proof generation from error analysis and correction.

The framework organizes extended reasoning around structured interaction between language models and the Lean4 verifier. It also introduces a training-and-inference pipeline called LoT-Transfer Learning, intended to give models long-chain reasoning capabilities without special data annotation. The contribution therefore includes both a collaborative proving process and a way to prepare models for that process.

The stated comparisons are 33.61% for DeepSeek-V3, 50.70% for InternLM-Step-Prover’s single-model tree search, and 55.33% for Godel-Prover’s whole-proof generation. These results support combining extended reasoning, distinct model roles, and formal feedback for this benchmark. The paper also presents the combination of long reasoning and verification as a promising direction for more insightful proof generation.
summary.tldr: MA-LoT coordinates proof generation and correction through language-model collaboration and Lean4 verification, reaching 61.07% on MiniF2F-Test.

title: MA-LoT: Model-Collaboration Lean-based Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning enhances Formal Theorem Proving

abstract: Contrast-enhanced MRI enhances pathological visualization but often necessitates Pre-Contrast images for accurate quantitative analysis and comparative assessment. However, Pre-Contrast images are frequently unavailable due to time, cost, or safety constraints, or they may suffer from degradation, making alignment challenging. This limitation hinders clinical diagnostics and the performance of tools requiring combined image types. To address this challenge, we propose a novel staged, physics-grounded learning framework with a hyperintensity prior to synthesize Pre-Contrast images directly from Post-Contrast MRIs. The proposed method can generate high-quality Pre-Contrast images, thus, enabling comprehensive diagnostics while reducing the need for additional imaging sessions, costs, and patient risks. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first Pre-Contrast synthesis model capable of generating images that may be interchangeably used with standard-of-care Pre-Contrast images. Extensive evaluations across multiple datasets, sites, anatomies, and downstream tasks demonstrate the model’s robustness and clinical applicability, positioning it as a valuable tool for contrast-enhanced MRI workflows.
