paragraphs: Contrast-enhanced MRI workflows often need images acquired before contrast administration for comparison and quantitative analysis. Those pre-contrast images may be absent, degraded, or difficult to align with later scans. This paper addresses that gap by synthesizing pre-contrast images directly from post-contrast MRI, aiming to supply information needed by workflows that use both image types.

The proposed learning framework proceeds in stages and incorporates physical grounding together with a hyperintensity prior. These are the stated foundations of its synthesis approach. Producing the missing image from an existing post-contrast scan could reduce the need for additional imaging sessions and the associated costs and patient burdens.

The authors evaluate the model across datasets, clinical sites, anatomies, and downstream tasks, reporting robustness and clinical applicability. They describe it, to their knowledge, as the first pre-contrast synthesis model whose outputs may be used interchangeably with standard-of-care pre-contrast images. That wording expresses a possibility supported by their evaluations, rather than establishing unconditional equivalence. The stated findings position the method as a potentially useful addition to contrast-enhanced MRI workflows.
summary.tldr: A staged, physics-grounded model synthesizes pre-contrast MRI from post-contrast scans, with evaluations supporting potential clinical use.

title: Staged and Physics-Grounded Learning Framework with Hyperintensity Prior for Pre-Contrast MRI Synthesis

abstract: Recent large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities across challenging tasks, enabling their widespread adoption in agentic systems that interact with external tools. In such deployments, however, LLMs are typically trained with general-purpose tokenizers designed for broad language coverage, while their usage is dominated by narrow, structured tool-calling interactions. This training–deployment mismatch leads to inefficient tokenization, where repetitive structural patterns and frequent semantic units in function calls are fragmented into long sequences of low-level tokens, increasing decoding overhead. To address this gap, we introduce $\textbf{AgentVocab}$, a structure-aware vocabulary adaptation framework for efficient LLM agents. AgentVocab derives specialized vocabulary entries from real tool-calling traces and adapts the model vocabulary to better reflect structural and semantic regularities, without task-specific schema engineering. Experiments on $\tau$-bench and $\tau^2$-bench show that AgentVocab preserves tool-calling performance while reducing latency relative to the vanilla baseline by 17.7% and 19.5%, respectively. Our approach is orthogonal to existing fine-tuning and agent-training methods and integrates seamlessly into standard agent pipelines. Source code and models will be available at https://github.com/Starry-159/AgentVocab.

paragraphs: Language models used as agents often spend much of their time producing structured tool calls. Their tokenizers, however, are usually designed for language in general. Repeated pieces of function calls can therefore be split into many small tokens, adding decoding work even when the interaction follows a familiar pattern.

AgentVocab adapts the model vocabulary to this setting. It derives specialized vocabulary entries from actual tool-calling traces, using recurring structural patterns and meaningful units to guide the adaptation. This lets the vocabulary reflect how the agent is deployed without requiring someone to engineer a separate schema for each task.

On τ-bench and τ²-bench, the authors report preserved tool-calling performance alongside latency reductions of 17.7% and 19.5% relative to the vanilla baseline. These findings show that vocabulary design can address a concrete source of agent overhead. The framework is described as compatible with existing fine-tuning and agent-training methods, making vocabulary adaptation an additional efficiency mechanism within standard agent pipelines.
summary.tldr: AgentVocab adapts vocabularies to recurring tool-call patterns, reducing latency while preserving tool-calling performance in the reported benchmarks.

title: AgentVocab: Structure-Aware Vocabulary Adaptation for Efficient LLM Agents

abstract: We study continual pre-training (CPT) as a mechanism for adapting general-purpose large language models to specialized domains: mathematics, instruction, code, and natural text. Using singular value decomposition of weight matrices, we find that CPT leaves singular value spectra largely invariant, with adaptation driven mainly by changes in singular vectors. An analysis of attention-head projection matrices reveals strong, domain-dependent head heterogeneity, which we exploit to define a head importance criterion: up to 60% of head updates can be removed without measurable quality loss. Selectively rewinding low-importance heads to their pre-trained state improves benchmark accuracy by up to 4% versus the fully trained baseline. Finally, we identify domain connectivity—linear interpolation between CPT checkpoints yields smooth domain-quality interpolation without notable degradation on either domain—and release Diffract, an open-source toolkit for scalable spectral analysis of billion-parameter models.

This paper examines what changes inside model weights during adaptation to mathematics, instructions, code, and natural text. It uses singular value decomposition to separate the strength of weight-matrix components from their directions.

The authors find that component strengths remain largely unchanged, while adaptation mainly changes their directions. Attention heads also differ substantially in how important their updates are, and those differences depend on the domain. Using a head-importance criterion, the authors remove up to 60% of head updates without measurable quality loss. Together, these results show that adaptation is unevenly distributed across heads and that some learned updates can be unnecessary or counterproductive. Diffract provides an open-source toolkit for conducting this spectral analysis at scale.
summary.tldr: Spectral analysis finds that domain adaptation mainly changes weight directions, with many attention-head updates removable without measurable quality loss.

title: Diffract: Spectral View of LLM Domain Adaptation

abstract: As AI models continue to develop powerful capabilities, it becomes critical that we are able to verify that their output is aligned with our intentions. A recent line of work focuses on verification via debate, a model of interactive proofs where two competing powerful provers, or AI models, debate each other to convince a weak verifier, or a human, of the correctness of their claim. However, debate assumes that the two AI models possess equal abilities and that one of them is truthful, which may not be realistic. In this work, we show how to avoid debate: we initiate the study of single-prover interactive proofs for AI safety. Prior results in single-prover interactive proofs do not immediately carry over to the AI safety setting because they do not work when the computation has access to an oracle, such as to human judgment or an external database such as the web. We present doubly-efficient single-prover interactive proofs for oracle-aided computations (also known as relativizing proofs), in the settings where (1) the computation is robust, in the sense that the output does not change if at most a small fraction of the answers to oracle queries are incorrect, or (2) the oracle is a low-degree polynomial. These results suggest that interactive verification is possible even without debate, under structured or noise-tolerant oracle access.

paragraphs: Verification through AI debate asks two powerful models to compete before a weaker verifier. The setup assumes equally capable participants and a truthful participant, assumptions that may be unrealistic. This paper investigates whether a single prover can instead support interactive verification in settings relevant to AI safety.

A central obstacle is access to external information. Computations may consult human judgment or a database such as the web, represented mathematically as an oracle. Existing single-prover results do not immediately apply to these oracle-aided computations. The authors develop doubly-efficient interactive proofs that accommodate this access in two specified settings.

The first setting requires robustness: changing a small fraction of oracle answers does not alter the computation’s output. The second requires the oracle to be a low-degree polynomial. These are substantive conditions on the computation or information source. Under them, the results suggest that verification can proceed without a debate between two models. The contribution establishes a conditional route to single-prover verification for structured or noise-tolerant oracle access.
summary.tldr: Single-prover interactive proofs can support oracle-aided verification when the computation tolerates oracle errors or the oracle has low-degree polynomial structure.

title: How to Avoid Debate: Scalable AI Safety via Doubly-Efficient Interactive Proofs

abstract: Probabilistic forecasting with exogenous variables is vital for decision-making but remains underexplored compared to deterministic methods. We propose KITE, a knowledge-guided probabilistic modeling framework designed to bridge this gap by addressing two key bottlenecks: (1) topological disparity in sampling initialization and (2) spurious covariate correlations during the iterative conditional generation process. KITE introduces a History-Conditional Manifold to construct an informative source distribution from historical dynamics, effectively anchoring the starting point closer to the target space. Additionally, a Knowledge-Guided Conditioning module is developed to regularize variable interactions using statistical priors, suppressing spurious correlations and enhancing the robustness of covariate conditioning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that KITE outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both deterministic and probabilistic forecasting.

paragraphs: KITE addresses time-series forecasting that uses external variables and represents uncertainty in future outcomes. The paper identifies two obstacles in iterative conditional generation: an initial sampling distribution whose structure is poorly aligned with the target, and misleading correlations among conditioning variables. Both can interfere with generating forecasts that reflect the relevant historical and external information.

The History-Conditional Manifold constructs an informative starting distribution from historical dynamics, placing the initial samples closer to the target space. The Knowledge-Guided Conditioning module uses statistical priors to regularize interactions between variables. Its purpose is to suppress spurious associations and make conditioning on external variables more robust during generation.

Experiments report that KITE outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both deterministic and probabilistic forecasting. These results support addressing initialization and conditioning together: historical structure improves where generation begins, while statistical knowledge shapes how covariates influence its progress. The framework therefore links the starting distribution and subsequent variable interactions within a single probabilistic forecasting approach.
summary.tldr: KITE improves time-series forecasting by initializing generation from historical dynamics and using statistical priors to regulate external-variable interactions.

title: KITE: Knowledge-Guided Probabilistic Modeling for Time Series Forecasting with Exogenous Variables

abstract: The training of neural networks often entails objective functions that are not globally $L$-smooth. For these functions, it is both theoretically and practically difficult to reply to the question: what is the largest possible step size that ensures the convergence of gradient descent (GD)? We address this longstanding open question in deep learning by providing a unifying definition of "large" step sizes that requires only local Lipschitz (or even Hölder) continuity of the gradient. We design first-order adaptive methods that provably yield large step sizes and show that they operate at the edge of stability (EoS) right from the start of the training. In particular, the loss decreases nonmonotonically and the product between the step size and sharpness, i.e., the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian, stays above the EoS threshold of 2 throughout training. Using our method, we are also able to minimize the sharpness all the way down to its global minimum. Contrary to expectation, we find that encountering globally-flat regions too early in the training may both slow down convergence and jeopardize the generalization ability of the network. Exploiting a self-stabilization argument, we allow GD to enter slightly sharper valleys and turn unsuccessful training runs into very successful ones.

paragraphs: Choosing a large gradient-descent step while retaining convergence is difficult when a training objective lacks a global smoothness bound. The findings connect convergence behavior to when and how training encounters flat regions.
summary.tldr: Adaptive large-step gradient methods reveal that reaching extremely flat regions too early can impede convergence and generalization.

title: Flatland: The Adventures of Gradient Descent with Large Step Sizes

abstract: Traditional whole slide image (WSI) analysis methods typically rely on the multiple instance learning (MIL) paradigm, which extracts patch-level features at high magnification and aggregates them for slide-level prediction. However, such exhaustive patch-level processing is computationally expensive, severely limiting the efficiency and scalability of WSI analysis. To address this challenge, we propose PathCTM (a Pathology-oriented Continuous Thought Model) that enables token-efficient scale-space continuous reasoning for gigapixel WSIs. PathCTM formulates diagnostic inference as a dynamic sequential information pursuit. It progressively transitions from low-magnification global to high-magnification local inspection, and adaptively terminates inference when sufficient evidence is gathered to effectively bound decision uncertainty. Specifically, it uses conditional computation for dynamic scale switching with attention-guided region pruning, coupled with confidence-aware early stopping. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, compared with standard MIL-based methods, PathCTM reduces the number of required image patches by 95.95% and shortens inference time by approximately 95.62%, while maintaining AUC without degradation. Code is available at https://github.com/JSGe-AI/PathCTM.

paragraphs: Whole-slide pathology images are so large that processing many high-magnification patches becomes expensive. Standard multiple instance learning methods extract patch features and aggregate them into a slide-level prediction. PathCTM instead treats inference as a sequence of information-gathering decisions, determining where and at what scale additional inspection is useful.

The model starts with low-magnification global information and progressively moves toward higher-magnification local regions. Conditional computation controls scale changes, attention guides the removal of regions from further consideration, and confidence-aware early stopping ends inference once sufficient evidence has accumulated. Its efficiency comes from deciding what evidence to inspect and when further inspection is unnecessary.
summary.tldr: PathCTM adaptively inspects pathology slides across scales, cutting patch use and inference time by about 96% without reported AUC degradation.

title: Thinking in Scales: Accelerating Gigapixel Pathology Image Analysis via Adaptive Continuous Reasoning

abstract: Can we bridge the gap between perceiving camera trajectories and rendering novel views within a single generative framework? Recovering camera parameters from images and rendering scenes from novel viewpoints are considered the forward and inverse problems in the field of computer vision and graphics. Previous approaches treat these problems in isolation, often failing when image coverage is sparse or camera poses are ambiguous. In this work, we propose Rays as Pixels, a specialized Video Diffusion Model (VDM) that learns a joint distribution of videos and camera trajectories. We represent cameras as dense ray pixels (raxels) and simultaneously denoise them alongside video frames using a novel Decoupled Self-Cross Attention. This joint formulation enables us to: i) generate a video from multiple input images following a defined camera trajectory, ii) perform novel view synthesis from sparse views (without necessarily requiring camera poses), and iii) predict the camera trajectory from a raw video. We evaluate our model on pose estimation, camera-controlled video generation and validate its self-consistency. Please reference supplementary material for more qualitative results.

paragraphs: Estimating camera motion from images and generating images from new viewpoints describe closely related problems. They are often handled separately, which can become difficult when only a few views are available or camera poses are ambiguous. Rays as Pixels places both problems inside one video diffusion framework.

The model represents cameras through dense ray pixels, called raxels, and learns a joint distribution over these camera representations and video frames. A Decoupled Self-Cross Attention mechanism allows the two to be denoised together. This gives the generative process a shared representation of what a video shows and how the camera moves.

The resulting model supports several directions of inference: generating video along a specified camera path from multiple images, synthesizing new views from sparse images without necessarily having camera poses, and predicting a camera trajectory from raw video. The authors evaluate pose estimation and camera-controlled generation and validate self-consistency. The contribution is this unified set of capabilities, connecting perception and rendering through joint generation.
summary.tldr: Rays as Pixels jointly models video and camera trajectories to support camera estimation, controlled generation, and sparse-view synthesis.

title: Rays as Pixels: Learning A Joint Distribution of Videos and Camera Trajectories

abstract: Analyzing large-scale text corpora is a core challenge in machine learning, crucial for tasks like identifying undesirable model behaviors. Current methods often rely on costly LLM-based techniques (e.g. annotating dataset differences) or dense embedding models (e.g. for clustering), which lack control over the properties of interest. We propose using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to create SAE embeddings: representations whose dimensions map to interpretable concepts. Through four data analysis tasks, we show that SAE embeddings are more cost-effective and reliable than LLMs and offer the controllability that dense embeddings lack. Using the large hypothesis space of SAEs, we can uncover insights such as (1) semantic differences between datasets and (2) unexpected concept correlations in documents. For instance, by comparing model responses, we find that Grok-4 clarifies ambiguities more often than nine other frontier models. Relative to LLMs, SAE embeddings uncover bigger differences at 2-8x lower cost and identify biases more reliably. Additionally, SAE embeddings are controllable: by filtering concepts, we can (3) cluster documents along axes of interest and (4) outperform dense embeddings on property-based retrieval. Using SAE embeddings, we study model behavior with two case studies: investigating how OpenAI model behavior has changed over time and finding "trigger" phrases learned by Tulu-3 (Lambert et al., 2024) from its training data. These results position SAEs as a versatile tool for unstructured data analysis and highlight the neglected importance of interpreting models through their data.

title: Interpretable Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders: A Data Analysis Toolkit

abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) extend context lengths to millions of tokens, enabling coherent, personalized responses grounded in long conversational history. However, the Key-Value (KV) cache grows linearly with the extended dialogue history, causing the model’s memory footprint to quickly exceed device limits. While recent KV cache compression methods attempt to reduce memory usage, most apply cache eviction after processing the entire context, incurring unbounded peak memory usage. Additionally, query-dependent eviction narrows the cache semantics to a single query, leading to failure cases in multi-turn conversations. In this paper, we introduce EpiCache, a training-free KV cache management framework for long conversational question answering (LongConvQA) under fixed memory budgets. EpiCache bounds cache growth through block-wise prefill and preserves topic-relevant context via episodic KV compression, which clusters conversation history into coherent episodes and performs episode-specific KV cache eviction. Across three LongConvQA benchmarks (LongMemEval, Realtalk, and LoCoMo), EpiCache improves accuracy by up to 30%, achieves near-full-cache accuracy under $4$–$6\times$ compression, and reduces latency and peak memory by up to $2.4\times$ and $3.7\times$, respectively.

paragraphs: Long conversation histories can make a language model’s key-value cache exceed device memory. Compressing the cache only after processing the entire history does not control the peak memory needed to get there. Separately, retaining information according to one query can discard material that becomes relevant in later conversational turns.

EpiCache addresses both problems without additional model training. It processes the history in blocks to bound cache growth during prefill. It also groups the conversation into coherent episodes and evicts cached entries separately within those episodes. This organization is designed to preserve topic-relevant context under a fixed memory budget while avoiding a cache shaped entirely around a single question.

Reported latency and peak-memory reductions reach factors of 2.4 and 3.7, respectively. The findings show the value of managing memory throughout context processing and retaining the episodic structure of conversations when supporting long-term question answering.
summary.tldr: EpiCache combines block-wise processing with episode-specific cache compression to support long conversations under fixed memory budgets.

title: EpiCache: Episodic KV Cache Management for Long-Term Conversation on Resource-Constrained Environments

abstract: Deep generative models can help with data scarcity and privacy by producing synthetic training data, but they struggle in low-data, imbalanced tabular settings to fully learn the complex data distribution. We argue that striving for the full joint distribution could be overkill; for greater data efficiency, models should prioritize learning the conditional distribution $P(y\mid \mathbf{X})$, as suggested by recent theoretical analysis. Therefore, we overcome this limitation with ReTabSyn, a Reinforced Tabular Synthesis pipeline that provides direct feedback on feature correlation preservation during synthesizer training. This objective encourages the generator to prioritize the most useful predictive signals when training data is limited, thereby strengthening downstream model utility. We empirically fine-tune a language model-based generator using this approach, and across benchmarks with small sample sizes, class imbalance, and distribution shift, ReTabSyn consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Moreover, our approach can be readily extended to control various aspects of synthetic tabular data, such as applying expert-specified constraints on generated observations.

paragraphs: Synthetic tabular data can supplement scarce training examples, but generators struggle when datasets are small or classes are imbalanced. ReTabSyn questions whether learning the entire joint data distribution is always the most useful goal. For prediction, it argues that prioritizing the relationship between input features and the target can improve data efficiency.

The pipeline uses reinforcement learning to provide a synthesizer with direct feedback about preserving feature correlations. This encourages attention to predictive signals that matter for models trained on the generated data. The authors implement the approach by fine-tuning a language-model-based generator, connecting generation quality to downstream usefulness when real examples are limited.

Across benchmarks involving small samples, class imbalance, and distribution shift, ReTabSyn consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. The framework can also be extended to control other properties of generated observations, including expert-specified constraints. Its contribution is therefore a feedback-driven synthesis approach that prioritizes useful statistical relationships and offers a route to incorporating explicit requirements on synthetic records.
summary.tldr: ReTabSyn uses reinforcement-learning feedback to preserve predictive relationships in synthetic tables, improving downstream utility in challenging data settings.

title: ReTabSyn: Realistic Tabular Data Synthesis via Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The widespread availability of fine-tuned LoRA modules for open pre-trained models has led to an interest in methods that can adaptively merge LoRAs to improve performance. These methods typically include some way of selecting LoRAs from a pool and tune merging coefficients based on a task-specific dataset. While adaptive merging methods have demonstrated improvements in some settings, no past work has attempted to recycle LoRAs found “in the wild” on model repositories like the Hugging Face Hub. To address this gap, we consider recycling from a pool of nearly 1,000 user-contributed LoRAs trained from the Llama 3.1 8B-Instruct language model. Our empirical study includes a range of adaptive and non-adaptive merging methods in addition to a new method designed via a wide search over the methodological design space. We demonstrate that adaptive merging methods can improve performance over the base model but provide limited benefit over training a new LoRA on the same data used to set merging coefficients. We additionally find not only that the specific choice of LoRAs to merge has little importance, but that using LoRAs with randomly initialized parameter values yields similar performance. To better understand why past work has proven successful, we confirm that positive transfer is indeed possible when there are highly relevant LoRAs in the pool. We release the model checkpoints and code online at https://github.com/r-three/realistic-adaptive-merging.

paragraphs: This paper tests whether publicly available LoRA modules can be recycled effectively through adaptive merging. Such methods select modules from a pool and tune their mixing coefficients using task-specific data. The study uses nearly 1,000 user-contributed LoRAs based on Llama 3.1 8B-Instruct, examining a repository-derived pool rather than only specially assembled modules.

The authors compare adaptive and non-adaptive merging approaches, including a new method developed through a broad methodological search. Adaptive merging improves on the base model, but offers limited benefit over training a fresh LoRA with the same data used to tune the merging coefficients. In the study, the particular modules selected matter little, and randomly initialized LoRA parameters produce similar performance.

Those findings question how much useful prior task knowledge is being recovered in this setting. However, the paper also confirms positive transfer when the pool contains highly relevant LoRAs. Its conclusion is therefore conditional: recycling can help with suitable source modules, but gains over a base model alone do not establish an advantage over directly training a new adapter.
summary.tldr: Recycling repository LoRAs offers limited gains over training a fresh adapter in this study, although highly relevant modules can provide positive transfer.

title: The Appeal and Reality of Recycling LoRAs with Adaptive Merging

abstract: Shampoo is one of the leading approximate second-order optimizers: a variant of it has won the MLCommons AlgoPerf competition, and it has been shown to produce models with lower activation outliers that are easier to compress. Yet, applying Shampoo currently comes at the cost of significant computational slowdown, due to its expensive internal operations. In this paper, we take a significant step to address this shortcoming by proposing DASH (for Distributed Accelerated SHampoo), a faster implementation of Distributed Shampoo based on two main new techniques: First, we show that preconditioner blocks can be stacked into 3D tensors to significantly improve GPU utilization; second, we introduce the Newton-DB iteration and the Chebyshev polynomial approximations as novel and faster approaches for computing the inverse matrix roots required by Shampoo. Along with these algorithmic contributions, we provide a first in-depth analysis of how matrix scaling critically affects Shampoo convergence. On the practical side, our GPU-aware implementation achieves up to $5.6\times$ faster optimizer steps compared to the well-optimized Distributed Shampoo, while Newton-DB attains the lowest validation perplexity per iteration among all tested methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/IST-DASLab/DASH.

paragraphs: Shampoo is an approximate second-order optimizer that uses matrix-based information to shape training updates. Its appeal comes with substantial computational overhead: the internal calculations needed to construct those updates can be expensive. DASH targets that implementation cost, aiming to make Distributed Shampoo faster while retaining its optimization approach.

The first technique groups preconditioner blocks into three-dimensional tensors so GPUs can process them more efficiently. The second targets inverse matrix roots, a costly operation inside Shampoo. The authors introduce Newton-DB iteration and Chebyshev polynomial approximations as faster ways to compute these quantities. They also analyze how matrix scaling affects convergence, connecting numerical choices inside the implementation to optimization behavior.

The resulting implementation achieves optimizer steps up to 5.6 times faster than the well-optimized Distributed Shampoo comparison. This is a speedup for the optimizer step, rather than a reported equivalent reduction in total training time. Among the tested methods, Newton-DB also produces the lowest validation perplexity per iteration. Together, the findings show that GPU batching and improved matrix calculations can substantially reduce Shampoo’s overhead while supporting strong optimization results.
summary.tldr: DASH accelerates Shampoo optimizer steps through GPU-friendly batching and faster inverse-matrix-root calculations.

title: DASH: Faster Shampoo via Batched Block Preconditioning and Efficient Inverse-Root Solvers

abstract: The rapid rise of synthetic media has made deepfake detection a critical challenge for online safety and trust. Progress remains constrained by the scarcity of large, high-quality datasets. Although multimodal large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong reasoning capabilities, their performance on deepfake detection is poor, often producing explanations that are misaligned with visual evidence or hallucinatory. To address this limitation, we introduce a reasoning-annotated dataset for deepfake detection and propose Paragraph-level Relative Policy Optimization (PRPO), a reinforcement learning algorithm that aligns LLM reasoning with image content at the paragraph level. Experiments show that PRPO improves detection accuracy by a wide margin and achieves the highest reasoning score of 4.55/5.0. Ablation studies further demonstrate that PRPO significantly outperforms GRPO under test-time conditions. These results underscore the importance of grounding multimodal reasoning in visual evidence to enable more reliable and interpretable deepfake detection.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models can produce explanations for deepfake judgments, but those explanations may fail to match the image or contain invented evidence. This paper treats that mismatch as a central obstacle to useful detection. It also addresses the shortage of large, high-quality datasets by introducing data annotated with reasoning.

The proposed Paragraph-level Relative Policy Optimization algorithm uses reinforcement learning to align explanations with image content at paragraph granularity. That choice makes chunks of reasoning the focus of optimization. The dataset and training method work together to improve both the detection decision and the explanation supporting it, with visual evidence as the grounding target.

Experiments report a wide improvement in detection accuracy and the highest reasoning score of 4.55 out of 5. Ablation studies also show significant gains over GRPO under the tested inference conditions. The results support the value of explicitly training evidence-grounded reasoning for deepfake detection, where a convincing explanation is useful only insofar as it reflects the actual visual content.
summary.tldr: PRPO combines reasoning-annotated data with paragraph-level reinforcement learning to improve deepfake detection and visually grounded explanations.

title: PRPO: Paragraph-level Policy Optimization for Vision-Language Deepfake Detection

abstract: We study the error rate of LLMs on tasks like arithmetic that require a deterministic output, and repetitive processing of tokens drawn from a small set of alternatives. We argue that incorrect predictions arise when small errors in the attention mechanism accumulate to cross a threshold, and use this insight to derive a quantitative two-parameter relationship between the accuracy and the complexity of the task. The two parameters vary with the prompt and the model; they can be interpreted in terms of an elementary noise rate, and the number of plausible erroneous tokens that can be predicted. Our analysis is inspired by an "effective field theory” perspective: the LLM’s many raw parameters can be reorganized into just two parameters that govern the error rate. We perform extensive empirical tests, using Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro and DeepSeek R1, and find excellent agreement between the predicted and observed accuracy for a variety of tasks, although we also identify deviations in some cases. Our model provides an alternative to suggestions that errors made by LLMs on long repetitive tasks indicate the "collapse of reasoning”, or an inability to express "compositional” functions. Finally, we show how to construct prompts to reduce the error rate.

paragraphs: Why do language models make mistakes on long, repetitive tasks even when each individual step seems simple? This paper studies tasks such as arithmetic, where outputs are deterministic and processing repeatedly involves a small set of possible tokens. It proposes that small inaccuracies in attention accumulate until they cross a threshold and produce an incorrect prediction.

The authors turn this explanation into a quantitative relationship between task complexity and accuracy using just two parameters. These depend on the model and prompt, and represent an elementary noise rate and the number of plausible wrong tokens. The aim is to summarize error behavior without tracking the model’s enormous collection of individual parameters.

Experiments with Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and DeepSeek R1 show close agreement between predicted and observed accuracy across several tasks, alongside deviations in some cases. The results offer an alternative explanation to claims that repetitive-task failures demonstrate a collapse of reasoning. The paper also shows how prompt construction can reduce errors.
summary.tldr: A two-parameter model links repetitive-task errors to accumulating attention noise and closely predicts accuracy in several tested language models.

title: A model of errors in transformers

abstract: As a lightweight model for sequence processing, an LSSL that uses the HiPPO matrix has been proposed. In this paper, as the continuous limit of the HiPPO Matrix, we propose Continuized-HiPPO Operator. Furthermore, as examples of advantages obtained by using this operator, we show that one can analyze the asymptotic behavior of eigenvalues of a matrix related to the HiPPO matrix, and that the LSSL induced by the continuous limit Continuized-HiPPO Operator admits an explicit solution.
originalAbstract: As a lightweight model for sequence processing, an LSSL that uses the HiPPO matrix has been proposed. In this paper, as the continuous limit of the HiPPO Matrix, we propose Continuized-HiPPO Operator. Furthermore, as examples of advantages obtained by using this operator, we show that one can analyze the asymptotic behavior of eigenvalues of a matrix related to the HiPPO matrix, and that the LSSL induced by the continuous limit Continuized-HiPPO Operator admits an explicit solution.

paragraphs: The HiPPO matrix has been used within an LSSL, a lightweight model for processing sequences. This paper introduces a mathematical object called the Continuized-HiPPO Operator by taking a continuous limit of that matrix. The contribution focuses on what this operator formulation makes possible to analyze about the associated state-space model.

One result concerns the asymptotic behavior of eigenvalues of a matrix related to HiPPO. Instead of treating the matrix only as a finite computational object, the continuous-limit construction provides a route to studying its spectral behavior. This is one of the concrete analytical advantages the authors establish for the proposed operator.

The other result is an explicit solution for the LSSL induced by the continuous-limit operator. The two contributions address complementary questions: how a related matrix’s eigenvalues behave asymptotically, and how the limiting sequence model can be solved explicitly. The paper thus supplies an analytical formulation of HiPPO-based sequence processing whose stated benefits are spectral analysis and a solution formula.
summary.tldr: A continuous-limit HiPPO operator enables asymptotic eigenvalue analysis and an explicit solution for its induced sequence-processing model.

title: State Space Model with Continuous Limit of HiPPO Matrix: Eigenvalue Analysis and Explicit Solution Formula

abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds large language models with external evidence, but many implementations rely on pre-built indices that remain static after construction. Related queries therefore repeat similar multi-hop traversal, increasing latency and compute. Motivated by schema-based learning in cognitive neuroscience, we propose GAM-RAG, a training-free framework that accumulates retrieval experience from recurring or related queries and updates retrieval memory over time. GAM-RAG builds a lightweight, relation-free hierarchical index whose links capture potential co-occurrence rather than fixed semantic relations. During inference, successful retrieval episodes provide sentence-level feedback, updating sentence memories so evidence useful for similar reasoning types becomes easier to activate later. To balance stability and adaptability under noisy feedback, we introduce an uncertainty-aware, Kalman-inspired gain rule that jointly updates memory states and uncertainty estimates. It applies fast updates for reliable novel signals and conservative refinement for stable or noisy memories. We provide a theoretical analysis of the update dynamics, and empirically show that GAM-RAG improves average performance by 3.95% over the strongest baseline and by 8.19% with 5-turn memory, while reducing inference cost by 61%.

GAM-RAG introduces a training-free retrieval memory that accumulates experience from successful queries, making evidence useful for similar reasoning patterns easier to activate during later retrieval.

title: GAM-RAG: Gain-Adaptive Memory for Evolving Retrieval in Retrieval-Augmented Generation

abstract: Meta-Reinforcement Learning (Meta-RL) faces significant challenges in non-parametric settings, where vastly different return scales across diverse tasks cause severe gradient interference. Existing categorical solutions attempt to normalize these scales but often fail due to rigid discretization and quantization errors. To address this, we propose Reflect-then-Correct (RTC), a framework that models meta-values using Sinkhorn divergence. By treating distributions as adaptive floating particles, RTC achieves a geometry-aware alignment of distinct meta-task structures. However, while Sinkhorn updates harmonize gradients, they introduce statistical bias via sampling estimation. RTC overcomes this issue by "reflecting” on the temporal accumulation of Bellman inconsistencies through a recursive error model and "correcting” the optimization via adaptive importance weights, which prioritize more accurate transitions for meta-value estimation. We provide theoretical guarantees for this reweighting strategy and demonstrate that RTC outperforms existing baselines on the challenging Meta-World ML-10 and ML-45 benchmarks.

paragraphs: Meta-reinforcement learning must learn across tasks whose reward scales can differ greatly. In the non-parametric settings studied here, these differences cause severe interference between gradient updates. Existing categorical approaches attempt to normalize the scales, but fixed discretization introduces quantization errors. Reflect-then-Correct instead models value distributions with adaptive particles.

RTC uses Sinkhorn divergence to align those distributions in a way that accounts for their geometry. The particles can move rather than remain tied to rigid categories, helping align distinct task structures and harmonize gradients. However, the authors identify a cost of these updates: estimating them through samples introduces statistical bias.

The framework responds with a second stage. A recursive error model tracks how Bellman inconsistencies accumulate over time, and adaptive importance weights give greater influence to transitions judged more accurate for meta-value estimation. The authors provide theoretical guarantees for this reweighting and report better performance than existing baselines on Meta-World ML-10 and ML-45. The contribution joins flexible distribution alignment with an explicit correction for estimation error introduced by that alignment.
summary.tldr: RTC aligns task value distributions with Sinkhorn divergence and corrects sampling-related error through adaptive weighting, improving results on two Meta-World benchmarks.

title: Reflect-then-Correct: Rebalancing Task Optimization for Generalizable Meta-Reinforcement Learning via Distributional Value Error Reduction

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) employing Chain-of-Thought reasoning achieve strong performance but suffer from excessive token consumption that inflates inference costs. Existing efficiency methods—such as explicit length penalties, difficulty estimators, or multi-stage curricula—either degrade reasoning quality or require complex training pipelines. We introduce Batched Contextual Reinforcement (BCR), a minimalist, single-stage training paradigm that unlocks efficient reasoning through a simple structural modification: training the model to solve N problems simultaneously within a shared context window, rewarded purely by per-instance accuracy. This formulation creates an implicit token budget that yields several key findings: (1) We identify a novel task-scaling law: as the number of concurrent problems N increases at inference time, per-problem token usage decreases monotonically—a phenomenon that arises purely at inference, holds for models both before and after training, and is unrelated to accuracy or the training procedure. BCR makes this regime practical by degrading accuracy far more gracefully than baselines as N grows, establishing N as a controllable throughput dimension. (2) BCR challenges the traditional accuracy-efficiency trade-off by demonstrating a "free lunch" phenomenon at standard single-problem (N=1) inference. Across both 1.5B and 4B model families, BCR reduces token usage by 15.8% to 62.6% while consistently maintaining or improving accuracy across five major mathematical benchmarks (e.g., +13.3% on AIME25 for the 4B model). (3) Qualitative analyses reveal emergent self-regulated efficiency, where models autonomously eliminate redundant metacognitive loops without explicit length supervision. (4) Crucially, we empirically demonstrate that implicit budget constraints successfully circumvent the adversarial gradients and catastrophic optimization collapse inherent to explicit length penalties, offering a highly stable, constraint-based alternative for length control. These results establish BCR as a highly practical framework, demonstrating how simple structural training incentives can unlock latent high-density reasoning modes in LLMs.

paragraphs: Batched Contextual Reinforcement trains a language model to solve several problems inside one shared context window, rewarding it only for each problem’s correctness. Sharing the window creates an implicit constraint on how much reasoning each problem can consume. The approach uses a single training stage and does not explicitly penalize long answers or supervise reasoning length.

The paper separates two findings. Increasing the number of simultaneous problems at inference reduces tokens per problem, an observed pattern present even before BCR training and independent of accuracy. BCR makes that pattern more useful by preserving accuracy more gracefully as the batch grows. The number of concurrent problems therefore becomes a practical control for throughput, with accuracy still needing consideration.

Benefits also appear when solving just one problem at a time. Across the tested 1.5B and 4B model families and five mathematical benchmarks, BCR reduces token use by 15.8%–62.6% while maintaining or improving accuracy. Qualitative analysis finds fewer redundant self-reflection loops, and experiments report more stable optimization than explicit length penalties. These results support shared-context training as a way to encourage economical reasoning.
summary.tldr: BCR trains models on multiple problems in a shared context, reducing reasoning tokens while maintaining or improving accuracy in the reported single-problem evaluations.

title: Batched Contextual Reinforcement

abstract: With recent advancements in large-scale pre-trained text-to-image (T2I) models, training-free image editing methods have demonstrated remarkable success. Typically, these methods involve adding noise to a clean image via an inversion process, followed by separate denoising steps for the reconstruction and editing paths during the forward process. However, since the reconstruction path is approximated using noisy latents from mismatched timesteps, existing methods inevitably suffer from accumulated drift, which fundamentally limits reconstruction fidelity. To address this challenge, we systematically analyze the inversion process within the flow transformer and propose DirectEdit, a simple yet effective editing method that eliminates the inherent reconstruction error without introducing additional neural function evaluations (NFEs). Unlike most prior works that attempt to rectify the inversion path, DirectEdit focuses on directly aligning the forward paths, enabling precise reconstruction and reliable feature sharing. Furthermore, we introduce a preservation mechanism based on attention feature injection and multi-branch mask-guided noise blending, which effectively balances fidelity and editability. Extensive experiments across diverse scenarios demonstrate that DirectEdit achieves efficient and accurate image editing, delivering superior performance that outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Code and examples are available at https://desongyang.github.io/Directedit.

paragraphs: Training-free image editing commonly turns an image into a noisy representation, then follows separate forward paths to reconstruct and edit it. This paper identifies a source of reconstruction drift: existing methods approximate the reconstruction path using noisy representations associated with mismatched timesteps. Those errors accumulate and reduce fidelity to the original image.

DirectEdit addresses this by directly aligning the forward paths within a flow transformer. The authors describe this alignment as eliminating the inherent reconstruction error without adding neural function evaluations. Accurate reconstruction also supports reliable sharing of features between the reconstruction and editing processes, connecting inversion accuracy to the editing method itself.

A preservation mechanism combines attention feature injection with mask-guided noise blending across multiple branches. Its purpose is to retain desired image content while still allowing the requested edit. Experiments across diverse scenarios report efficient, accurate editing and better performance than state-of-the-art methods. The contribution joins step-level alignment with explicit preservation controls, addressing both reconstruction fidelity and editability.
summary.tldr: DirectEdit aligns forward editing paths to eliminate inherent reconstruction error without extra neural function evaluations.

title: DirectEdit: Step-Level Accurate Inversion for Flow-Based Image Editing

abstract: Inference-time steering offers a promising way to control language models (LMs) without retraining. However, standard approaches typically rely on activation addition, which inevitably alters the hidden-state magnitudes raising concerns about representation collapse and degraded open-ended generation. In this work, we explore Spherical Steering, a training-free primitive that resolves this trade-off through activation rotation. Rather than shifting activations with a fixed vector, our method rotates them along a geodesic toward a target direction, preserving signal integrity while steering toward the target concept. To further enhance adaptivity, we incorporate a confidence gate that dynamically modulates steering strength based on input uncertainty. Extensive experiments across multiple-choice benchmarks demonstrate that Spherical Steering significantly outperforms addition-based baselines (notably by +10% on TruthfulQA, COPA, and Storycloze), while simultaneously maintaining the model’s general open-ended generation quality. This work highlights the value of geometric consistency, suggesting that norm-preserving rotation is a robust and effective primitive for precise inference-time control. The code is available at: https://github.com/chili-lab/Spherical-Steering.

paragraphs: Inference-time steering modifies a language model's internal activations to influence its behavior without retraining. Common methods add a vector, changing both the direction and magnitude of hidden states. This paper investigates rotation as a way to steer toward a target concept while preserving activation magnitude and avoiding the associated concerns about degraded representations.

Spherical Steering rotates an activation along a geodesic toward a target direction. Keeping its norm fixed maintains geometric consistency while changing the information emphasized by its direction. A confidence gate adjusts the steering strength according to input uncertainty, making the intervention adaptive rather than applying the same strength to every input.

Across multiple-choice benchmarks, the method significantly outperforms addition-based baselines, with reported gains of 10% on TruthfulQA, COPA, and Storycloze. It simultaneously maintains general open-ended generation quality. These findings support norm-preserving rotation as an effective primitive for the tested steering tasks, linking the geometry of the intervention to both improved targeted performance and preservation of broader generation quality.
summary.tldr: Spherical Steering rotates hidden activations without changing their magnitude, improving targeted performance while maintaining open-ended generation quality.

title: Spherical Steering: Geometry-Aware Activation Rotation for Language Models

abstract: Comprehensive urban understanding requires integrating macroscopic spatial structure with fine-grained street-level semantics. However, existing urban Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) primarily rely on satellite imagery, limiting their ability to capture detailed urban appearance and cross-view relationships. We propose UrbanMLLM, a unified MLLM that jointly learns from satellite and street-view imagery for cross-view urban perception and reasoning. To support this, we construct a large-scale dataset with paired cross-view urban images, geospatial alignment, and textual annotations. UrbanMLLM introduces a cross-view perceiver to explicitly model interactions between satellite and street-view representations, and adopts a structural interleaved pre-training paradigm that organizes cross-view image–text content as coherent urban documents to enhance cross-view knowledge fusion. We evaluate UrbanMLLM on 13 diverse urban understanding tasks spanning satellite, street-view, and cross-view settings. Experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements over strong open-source and proprietary MLLMs, highlighting effectiveness and scalability of UrbanMLLM for urban environment understanding.

paragraphs: Understanding an urban area requires both its broad spatial organization and detailed street-level appearance. Satellite-focused multimodal models have limited access to the latter and to relationships between viewpoints. UrbanMLLM jointly learns from satellite and street-view images to support perception and reasoning across those complementary views.

The authors construct a large-scale dataset pairing the two image types with geospatial alignment and textual annotations. A cross-view perceiver explicitly models interactions between their representations. During pre-training, a structured interleaving scheme organizes images and text into coherent urban documents, helping the model combine information across viewpoints within a shared context.

Evaluation covers 13 urban understanding tasks involving satellite imagery, street-view imagery, and cross-view inputs. The authors report consistent improvements over strong open-source and proprietary multimodal models. These findings support both the joint representation design and the organized training material as parts of a unified approach. The resulting model connects large-scale spatial information with fine-grained urban semantics across a diverse set of evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: UrbanMLLM jointly learns aligned satellite and street-view imagery, improving performance across 13 urban understanding tasks.

title: UrbanMLLM: Joint Learning of Cross-view Imagery for Urban Understanding

abstract: We study the posterior contraction rate of Bayesian Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) for solving a general class of elliptic partial differential equations (PDEs). We focus on learning of the elliptic equation with a non-homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition from independent and noisy measurements collected both inside the domain and on the boundary. Assuming that the PDE admits a strong solution in a Hölder space and using with a suitably constructed prior on the neural network weights, we prove that the posterior distribution concentrates around the exact solution at a near-minimax rate. Furthermore, the chosen prior is rate-adaptive: the posterior contracts at an (almost) optimal rate without prior knowledge of the smoothness level of the exact solution. Our results provide statistical guarantees for uncertainty quantification of PDEs via Bayesian PINNs.

paragraphs: Bayesian physics-informed neural networks represent uncertainty about a differential equation's solution through a posterior distribution. This paper asks how quickly that distribution becomes concentrated near the exact solution as measurements accumulate. It studies a general class of elliptic equations using independent, noisy observations collected both inside the domain and on its boundary.

The analysis includes non-homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions, which specify boundary values that need not be zero. Its guarantees assume that the equation has a strong solution in a Hölder space and use a suitably constructed prior over network weights. Under these conditions, the authors prove posterior concentration at a near-minimax rate, meaning nearly the best statistical rate for the considered problem class.

The chosen prior is also rate-adaptive: achieving an almost optimal contraction rate does not require knowing the exact solution's smoothness beforehand. This strengthens the statistical justification for the Bayesian construction under the stated assumptions. The paper's contribution is a theoretical foundation for uncertainty quantification with Bayesian PINNs, linking their posterior behavior to the accuracy of PDE solution learning.
summary.tldr: Under stated solution and prior assumptions, Bayesian PINNs for elliptic PDEs achieve nearly optimal, smoothness-adaptive posterior concentration.

title: Posterior Concentration of Bayesian Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Elliptic PDEs

abstract: Offline policy improvement faces an inherent conflict between maximizing value and fitting the data distribution. While in-sample weighted regression is stable, it suffers from over-conservatism that suppresses high-value actions in the distribution tail; conversely, gradient-based approaches often exhibit a fitting-optimization conflict of gradients, which drive the policy off the data manifold. To address this, we propose Support-Preserving Action Rectification (SPAR), which reframes global learning as a local residual rectification anchored to a frozen pure behavior cloning policy. This framework performs fine-grained fitting and local policy improvement in the residual space, thereby contracting the search space. We further introduce Latent Self-Imitation, utilizing a latent-sampling weighted-regression mechanism to address fitting-improvement gradient conflict in the residual space. Theoretically, we prove this mechanism eliminates the manifold-normal drift of standard value gradients, while extensive D4RL experiments show SPAR extracts significant gains from suboptimal baselines to achieve state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Improving a policy from a fixed dataset requires balancing better actions against staying close to behavior supported by the data. Weighted regression can be overly cautious about valuable but uncommon actions. Direct value-gradient updates can instead conflict with data fitting and push a policy away from the data manifold.

SPAR anchors learning to a frozen policy trained by pure behavior cloning. It learns local residual corrections around that reference, narrowing the space in which fitting and improvement take place. This turns policy improvement into adjusting an existing behavior locally rather than searching globally for an entirely new policy.

Within the residual space, Latent Self-Imitation uses latent sampling and weighted regression to address conflicting fitting and improvement gradients. The paper proves that this mechanism eliminates the component of standard value-gradient drift normal to the data manifold. Experiments on D4RL report substantial improvements from suboptimal baselines and state-of-the-art performance. The combined contribution is a constrained local improvement framework and a learning mechanism designed to keep improvement aligned with data-supported behavior.
summary.tldr: SPAR improves offline policies through local corrections to frozen behavior cloning, using latent self-imitation to avoid drift away from data-supported actions.

title: SPAR: Support-Preserving Action Rectification

abstract: Treating the outcome of machine learning as a stable, identifiable artifact is implicit in language, tooling, and governance. This position paper examines whether a trained system admits context-appropriate criteria of identity. I show that neither functional behavior nor internal structure suffices: behavioral equivalence is underdetermined by finite data, while modern architectures admit multiple, structurally distinct realizations of the same function. Consequently, practices that treat learned systems as stable objects presuppose equivalence relations that are rarely made explicit. I do not propose abandoning such practices. Instead, I articulate the reasonably minimal conditions under which identity claims grounded in behavior, structure, or training process can be meaningfully interpreted, with implications for reproducibility, traceability, and governance.

paragraphs: This position paper examines what it means to identify a trained machine-learning system as the same model across contexts. Research language, tools, and governance commonly assume a stable artifact. The author asks which criteria make that assumption meaningful and argues that neither observed behavior nor internal structure provides a sufficient basis on its own.

Behavioral evidence has a basic limitation: finite observations cannot fully determine whether systems implement equivalent behavior. Structure presents a different problem because modern architectures can realize the same function through multiple, structurally distinct configurations. Consequently, claims of sameness rely on rules for deciding which differences matter, even when those rules remain unstated.

The paper develops reasonably minimal conditions for interpreting identity claims grounded in behavior, structure, or the training process. It retains the practical use of model identity while calling for its criteria to be explicit and appropriate to the context. This matters for reproducibility, traceability, and governance because each practice needs a clear account of what is being identified and which changes preserve that identity.
summary.tldr: Meaningful claims about model identity require explicit, context-appropriate rules for deciding which behavioral, structural, or training differences matter.

title: Position: Model identity in machine learning is a convention, not a property

abstract: Identifying and disentangling sources of predictive uncertainty is essential for trustworthy supervised learning. We argue that widely used second-order decomposition-based approaches to uncertainty quantification are fundamentally incomplete. First, we show that unaccounted bias contaminates uncertainty estimates by overestimating aleatoric (data-related) uncertainty and underestimating the epistemic (model-related) counterpart, leading to systematically incorrect uncertainty quantification. Second, we demonstrate that existing methods capture only partial contributions to the variance-driven part of epistemic uncertainty; different approaches account for different variance sources, yielding estimates that are incomplete and difficult to interpret. Together, these results highlight that current epistemic uncertainty estimates can only be used in safety-critical and high-stakes decision-making when limitations are fully understood by end users and acknowledged by AI developers.

paragraphs: Uncertainty estimates often separate uncertainty associated with data from uncertainty associated with a model. This paper challenges widely used approaches that make this separation through second-order decompositions. The authors argue that their estimates are incomplete in two distinct ways, affecting both how uncertainty is divided and how much model-related uncertainty is captured.

First, bias that the decomposition does not account for distorts the result. The paper shows that this inflates the estimate of data-related, or aleatoric, uncertainty while reducing the estimate of model-related, or epistemic, uncertainty. The result can misleadingly attribute uncertainty to the data when model limitations are contributing to it.

Second, existing methods capture only some sources of the variance-related component of epistemic uncertainty. Different methods include different sources, making their outputs incomplete and difficult to interpret. Together, these findings mean that an epistemic uncertainty estimate should not be assumed to cover every relevant model-related contribution. For high-stakes use, the authors insist that developers acknowledge these limitations and that end users fully understand them.
summary.tldr: The paper shows that unaccounted bias and omitted variance sources make widely used epistemic uncertainty estimates incomplete.

title: Position: Epistemic Uncertainty Estimation Methods are Fundamentally Incomplete

abstract: How do we fundamentally discover new things? In a letter to Maurice Solovine, Albert Einstein conceptualized discovery as a cyclical process involving an intuitive ’jump’ from sensory experience to axioms, followed by logical deduction. While Generative AI has mastered Induction (statistical pattern matching) and is rapidly conquering Deduction (formal proof), we argue it lacks the mechanism for Abduction—the generation of novel explanatory hypotheses. Using Einstein’s formulation of General Relativity as a computational case study, we demonstrate that the prevailing theory of "creativity as data compression" (induction) fails to account for discoveries where observational data is scarce. This position paper argues that while a modern Large Language Model could plausibly execute the deductive phase of proving theorems from established premises, it is structurally incapable of the abductive ’Jump’ required to formulate those premises. We identify the translation of simulation into formal axioms as the critical bottleneck in artificial scientific invention, and propose that physically consistent, multimodal world models offer the necessary sensory grounding to bridge this divide.

paragraphs: This position paper distinguishes three activities involved in scientific discovery: learning patterns from observations, deriving consequences from premises, and inventing explanatory premises. The authors argue that generative AI has advanced in the first two but lacks a mechanism for the third, called abduction. They frame this distinction through Einstein’s account of an intuitive jump from experience to axioms.

Using the formulation of general relativity as a computational case study, they challenge the view that creativity can be explained by compressing observed data. Their argument concerns discoveries made with scarce observational evidence. They contend that a modern language model could plausibly carry out deductions from established premises while being structurally unable to generate the abductive jump that establishes those premises.

The paper identifies converting simulation into formal axioms as the critical obstacle for artificial scientific invention. It proposes physically consistent multimodal world models as a source of sensory grounding that could help bridge this divide. The contribution is a conceptual argument about what discovery requires and a proposed direction for supplying that grounding.
summary.tldr: The authors argue that LLMs lack the abductive mechanism needed to invent scientific premises and propose grounded world models as a path forward.

abstract: Previous work has shown that the difficulties in learning deep generative or discriminative models can be overcome by an initial unsupervised learning step that maps inputs to useful itermediate representations. We introduce and motivate a new training principle for unsupervised learning of a representation based on the idea of making the learned representations robust to partial corruption of the input pattern. This approach can be used to train autoencoders, and these denoising autoencoders can be stacked to initialize deep architectures. The algorithm can be motivated from a manifold learning and information theoretic perspective or from a generative model perspective. Comparative experiments clearly show the surprising advantage of corrupting the input of autoencoders on a pattern classification benchmark suite.

paragraphs: Learning a deep model can be helped by an initial unsupervised stage that turns inputs into useful intermediate representations. This paper introduces a training principle for that stage: learned representations should remain useful when part of the input has been corrupted. Robustness to partial corruption becomes a goal of representation learning itself.

The principle can be used to train denoising autoencoders. These models can then be stacked to initialize a deeper architecture, allowing representations learned at successive stages to be composed. The paper motivates this approach from several perspectives, including manifold learning, information theory, and generative modeling, connecting the same training idea to different ways of understanding representation learning.

Comparative experiments on a suite of pattern classification benchmarks show an advantage from corrupting autoencoder inputs during training. The finding gives practical support to the proposed principle: deliberately damaging part of the input can help produce features that serve a later classification task. The reported advantage concerns the benchmark comparisons, rather than a guarantee for every kind of corruption or dataset.
summary.tldr: Training autoencoders to handle partially corrupted inputs produces useful representations that can be stacked to initialize deep models.

title: Extracting and composing robust features with denoising autoencoders
